  (stencilFor signature change) or a growable-mutable-vector builder. Left as
  a possible follow-up if option 2's numbers ever stop being enough --
  currently they are.

Shipped as commit 6a98dff on worktree-sized-grid-adr.15, merged to master.
Did NOT re-record bench/baseline-ghc9.12.3-aarch64-darwin.csv: a concurrent
worktree session (sized-grid-adr-9) was active during two full-suite runs,
and unrelated benchmarks (transposeGrid, tabulateGrid unboxed) moved 15-30%
with byte-identical allocation counts -- contention, not a real change, per
bench/README.md's own warning about comparing across sessions. The stencil
numbers above are trustworthy (both sides measured back-to-back in the same
window) but the checked-in baseline still needs a deliberate idle-machine
re-record; filed as a note rather than a new issue since bench/README.md
already documents the procedure.
close_reason: Closed

title: Represent Coord as its row-major position: the port adr.8 measured the ceiling for
description:
sized-grid-adr.8 spiked this and the answer came back well above the bar it
set for itself, so this is the plan half of that issue. Read adr.8's notes
first: they carry the measured ceiling, the method, and the two
arguments-against that the spike settled.

The change: `Coord cs` stops being `NP I cs` and becomes the row-major
position it can already compute.

    newtype Coord cs = Coord Int
    type role Coord nominal

The measured ceiling, guarded (i.e. with the spike paying unsafeOrdinal's
range check on every axis value it builds, as this library does), two
back-to-back runs on ghc-9.12.3 aarch64-darwin:

  offsetCoord x360000, checked        4.6x
  (.+^) x10000, Periodic 300x300      5.1x, 2.68 MB -> 17 B
  imapGrid over neighbours 50x50      2.6x, 16.4 MB -> 2.6 MB
  tabulate 300x300                    2.25x
  onBoundary x360000                  2.2x
  coordDistance x360000               1.7x
  index x90000                        1.60x
  ifoldl' 300x300                     1.53x
  imap 300x300                        1.41x
  (.+^) x360000, four corner reads    1.33x
  transposeGrid 300x300               1.26x
  axis list opaque at run time        1.64x

Nothing measured got slower, including the case built to make it: a tabulate
whose rule destructures its coordinate per cell, where `(:|)` stops being a
field read and becomes a quotRem. It still came out 2.24x, because producing
a coordinate costs more than decoding one.

WHAT MUST NOT CHANGE, and how it is kept:

  * The axis list still indexes the type and still carries the boundary
    policy. `Coord '[Clamped 5, Periodic 3]` means what it meant.
  * The role stays nominal, so `coerce :: Coord '[C 9] -> Coord '[C 3]` stays
    shut. tests/compile-fail must keep proving it.
  * `(:|)` and `EmptyCoord` stay the public interface and stay `COMPLETE`;
    they become bidirectional pattern synonyms doing the quotRem/multiply.
    `Coord(..)`'s `unCoord` can keep handing back an `NP I cs`, rebuilt.
  * The invariant becomes "the Int is in [0, MaxCoordSize cs)", maintained by
    the constructors -- the same trade `Ordinal` made when it stopped being a
    GADT. Keep the guard: the spike measured what dropping it is worth
    (1.33x -> 1.62x on (.+^)) and that is not the trade adr.14 and
    sized-grid-sxy settled.

WHAT THE SPIKE DID NOT COVER, and so is where the risk is:

  * Reflective and Reflect101 -- the only policies with a non-trivial
    axisFrameFlips. Separable, so they fit, but not measured. Do these first:
    if any of them cannot be expressed per-axis on a position, the whole plan
    changes shape.
  * Stencils. Should only improve (a stencil table is already a vector of
    positions), but unmeasured.
  * weakenCoord/strengthenCoord, windows/tiles, scanAxis/mapAxis,
    Show/ToJSON/FromJSON/Random, PuncturedCoord and centreCoord.
  * The one real cost nobody has priced: this is a breaking change for a
    consumer who pattern-matches `Coord` directly rather than through `(:|)`.
    ../aoc is the consumer to check.

SUGGESTED ORDER. Reflective/Reflect101 on a position first (the gate), then
Coord plus the two pattern synonyms plus the IsCoordList methods, then the
instances that need an NP rebuilt, then Stencil, then the shape algebra. Keep
spike/adr8-intcoord/ until the port's own benchmark run reproduces its
ratios; it is the acceptance test.
acceptance_criteria: The paired benchmarks in spike/adr8-intcoord reproduce, in the library itself, within ~10% of the spike's ratios on the same machine; the full test suite passes unchanged, including tests/compile-fail (the nominal role) and the downstream suite; Coord's public interface is still (:|)/EmptyCoord, both COMPLETE; ../aoc builds and its grid puzzles do not regress.
close_reason: Ported and merged to master as a357144. Coord cs is its row-major position; IsCoord untouched (which is also how the Reflective/Reflect101 gate cleared -- both already compute from a bare index). Displacements split out to Data.Grid.Sized.Coord.Delta, indexed by the diff list so the difference space stays shared across grid shapes. Nothing slower across 57 benchmarks; tabulate 2.31x, indexGrid 2.36x, neighbours 2.58x (16.4 MB -> 2.6 MB, adr.8's figure exactly), extend 2.51x, ifoldl' 2.07x, offsetCoord 2.60x, torus walk 3.74x (2.68 MB -> 20 B). 592 tests plus downstream, readme and both atlas suites. Nominal role now proved by tests/compile-fail/CoordCoerceAcrossSizes.hs. Four measured findings recorded in the commits: the indexed traversals had to move to the vector's own index (imap was 0.27x without it), (:|) needs an INLINE because a constrained pattern synonym's matcher does not inline on its own (9.20 ms/36 MB vs 1.13 ms/4.8 MB), the decode was re-checking a proved bound, and mooreNeighbours was building a list only to drop it. Also corrected adr.8's own 4.6x on offsetCoord to 3.25x -- both sides used isJust, which let the Int side elide the reconstruction. ../aoc migration itemised in sized-grid-3xw; it does not build in this environment before or after, for want of blas/lapack.

title: Stencil API: precompute neighbour positions per grid type, not per cell
description:
Cellular-automaton workloads pay per cell for a neighbourhood that is a function
of the *type*, not of the cell.

gameOfLife's whole step is:

    imapGrid (\c here -> runRule rule here (map (indexGrid g) (neighbours c))) g

Per cell that allocates a list of `Coord`s from `neighbours`, each `Coord` an
`NP I cs` spine of boxes, and then throws every one of them away again through
`coordPosition`. The same shape drives `extend`.

Baseline (bench/Main.hs):
- `extend neighbourSum 50x50`               2.67 s,   15.3 MB
- `extend neighbourSum 50x50, Periodic`     3.53 s,   18.1 MB
- `iterate (extend neighbourSum) x100`    319 s,     1.53 GB
- Periodic x100                           402 s,     1.81 GB

For a fixed radius and axis list, every interior cell has the *same* neighbour
offsets in flat-vector terms. Only cells near a boundary differ, and how they
differ is per axis, decided by that axis's boundary-policy type -- which is
exactly the information the coordinate type already carries.

Sketch: a stencil API that computes the position table once per (axis list,
radius) and then runs a flat loop.

    stencilGrid :: Int -> (a -> [a] -> b) -> GridOf v cs a -> GridOf v cs b

backed by a `Vector Int` of `n * k` neighbour positions with a sentinel for
"off-grid on a bounded axis" (a `Periodic` axis never produces one). The table
is a function of `cs` alone, so it can be shared per specialisation the way
`coordListSize` already constant-folds.

Type safety: unchanged and, if anything, better -- the caller stops writing
`map (indexGrid g) (neighbours c)` by hand, and the offsets come from the same
per-axis `IsCoord` instances `stepsWithin` uses today, so a `Periodic` axis
wraps and a `Clamped` one drops exactly as before. Prove that with a property
test: `stencilGrid r f g == imapGrid (\c x -> f x (map (indexGrid g) (mooreNeighbours r c))) g`
on mixed-policy axis lists.

Rewrite gameOfLife and ising-example on top of it; they are the readers who tell
us whether the API is the right shape.
notes:
Landed 1674e56 as Data.Grid.Sized.Stencil.

API departs from the sketch in one way that matters. Not 'stencilGrid :: Int -> ...': the table is a value the caller holds (Stencil cs, built by stencilFor / mooreStencil / vonNeumannStencil). Building it is a full pass of the neighbourhood computation it replaces, so the Int form would have made the single-shot case SLOWER than the code it replaces, and its sharing would have depended on GHC floating a CAF -- which fires only where the axis-list dictionary is static and then retains the table for the process lifetime.

Measured at 50x50 against imapGrid-over-neighbours (not extend neighbourSum, which also pays for a FocusedGrid the rule never reads):
  loop, one pass          3.3 ms   16 MB
  build the table         5.7 ms   14 MB
  one pass, table built  0.28 ms  2.4 MB
  x100 loop                361 ms  1.5 GB
  x100 stencil              65 ms  237 MB
Second pass breaks even; each one after is 12x cheaper and allocates a seventh as much. No other benchmark moved. bench/baseline CSV re-recorded.

stencilGrid needs no IsCoordList constraint -- all axis-list work happens at build time.

Width is DISCOVERED, not derived from the radius: axisSteps deduplicates (a Periodic 3 axis at r=2 reaches values from both directions), so (2r+1)^d - 1 is an over-estimate. Test.Stencil covers that case.

Consumer feedback (this is what the issue asked the readers for):
- gameOfLife: holds the Stencil in WorldState; applyRule lost its IsCoordList constraint. Clean fit.
- ising: does NOT fit stencilGrid. Its Metropolis update reads one site, so rebuilding the grid would compute 3,600 cells to use four. That is why stencilAt (one row of the table, by coordinate) exists -- the API was the wrong shape until a real reader said so. Knock-on: singleEnergy stopped needing a FocusedGrid, and ising no longer imports Control.Comonad at all.
close_reason: Closed

title: onBoundary/isCorner/coordDistance/coordManhattan build a list to answer a fold
description:
Four coordinate predicates build a list per call to answer a question that is a
fold.

    onBoundary     = any isJust . axisBoundaries    -- [Maybe Extremum]
    isCorner       = all isJust . axisBoundaries    -- [Maybe Extremum]
    coordDistance  = foldl' max 0 . axisDistances   -- [Int]
    coordManhattan = sum . axisDistances            -- [Int]

`axisBoundaries`/`axisDistances` are `npBoundaries`/`npDistances`, `IsCoordList`
methods that cons per axis. The cost is measured, not suspected:

- `onBoundary x360000, Clamped 300x300`     13.93 s,  98.3 MB  (273 B/call)
- `coordDistance x360000, Clamped 300x300`  12.60 s,  78.5 MB  (218 B/call)

For comparison `(.+^) x360000` over the same grid is 1.83 s and 43 *bytes*
total, because `sizeAndPosition` is a method whose per-axis fold unrolls and
constant-folds. These four do not get that because the list is built before
anything folds it.

Fix in the same idiom the class already uses: add fused methods that produce the
answer directly, no intermediate list.

    npAnyBoundary :: NP I cs -> Bool
    npAllBoundary :: NP I cs -> Bool
    npMaxDistance :: NP I cs -> NP I cs -> Int
    npSumDistance :: NP I cs -> NP I cs -> Int

Two instances each, `INLINE` on both, exactly as `sizeAndPosition` and
`coordListSize` are written -- and for the reason set out at length on
`IsCoordList`: as a method the dictionary is known at compile time so the fold
unrolls, as a self-recursive `where` helper it never can.

`axisBoundaries` and `axisDistances` stay as they are; a caller who wants the
per-axis answers still gets them. Type safety is untouched: these are internal
methods of a class whose two instances already cover every type-level list, and
`Data.Grid.Sized.Coord` re-exports the class without its methods.

Guard with a property test that each fused method agrees with the list version
on mixed-policy axis lists, so `Periodic`'s wrap-around distance cannot drift
apart from the fused one.
close_reason: Fused into IsCoordList methods (npAnyBoundary/npAllBoundary/npMaxDistance/npSumDistance) in b201418. onBoundary sweep 22.3 ms/123 MB -> 11.5 ms/60 MB, coordDistance 19.7 ms/135 MB -> 13.4 ms/60 MB; baseline CSV re-recorded. Property tests added in Test.Boundary and Test.Neighbours over mixed Clamped/Periodic/Reflective/Reflect101 axis lists. Residual per-call allocation filed as sized-grid-2xv.

title: tabulate is 16x pure: find out how much of that is coordinate plumbing
description:
`tabulate` at 300x300 is 6.32 s and 10.1 MB. `pure` over the same grid -- same
vector, no coordinate -- is 0.39 s and 0.72 MB. The 16x gap is the coordinate
plumbing, and `imap` is evidence that most of it is plumbing rather than
coordinate arithmetic: `imap 300x300` does the same per-cell `coordPosition`
work and comes in at 2.39 s, 2.6x faster than `tabulate`.

The difference is how the coordinates reach the vector:

    tabulateGrid func = Grid $ VG.fromListN (coordSpaceSize @cs) $ map func allCoord
    imap func (Grid v) = Grid $ V.zipWith func (V.fromList allCoord) v

The note on the `FunctorWithIndex` instance already records that `V.fromList` is
load-bearing there -- `V.zipWith` fuses with it, so each coordinate dies in the
nursery, and swapping in `fromListN` made `imap` 59% slower with 90,000
coordinates live at once. `tabulateGrid` applies `fromListN` to the *result*
list rather than the coordinate list so it is not the same mistake, but it is
worth checking whether it fuses with `map func allCoord` at all.

Things to spike, measured against `tabulate 300x300`:
1. `VG.unfoldrExactN (coordSpaceSize @cs)` with an odometer successor on
   `Coord` -- increment the last axis, carry -- which reuses the spine and
   needs no `divMod`.
2. `VG.generate` over positions with `coordFromPosition`, for comparison; this
   is `divMod` per axis per cell but allocates no list.
3. Leaving the list but making it fuse, the way `imap` does.

Whichever wins, `Representable`'s `tabulate` gets it for free -- its body is
`tabulateGrid` -- and so does every unboxed grid, where `tabulateGrid` is the
only way to build from a function.

No type-safety question here at all: the signature does not move, and the only
obligation is producing exactly `coordSpaceSize @cs` elements in row-major
order, which `unfoldrExactN` states in its own type.
notes:
RESOLVED 2026-08-19. Spiked all three options the description proposed, measured against the VG.fromListN baseline (tabulate 300x300, same machine, same run):

1. Odometer (VG.unfoldrExactN + hand-rolled Coord successor, incrementing the last axis and carrying): WORSE. 78-93% slower, more allocation not less. The NP state threaded through unfoldrExactN's generator does not specialise the way a plain Int accumulator would -- every step partially rebuilds that structure -- and that cost outweighs the list it avoids. Code was written, benchmarked, and reverted (added/removed npZero/npSuccessor on IsCoordList in Coord/Class.hs); not merged.

2. VG.generate + coordFromPosition (per-axis quotRem from scratch, no list, no per-step state): WORSE, badly. 297-650% slower, ~5x the allocation. Re-deriving every axis from the flat position costs far more than either building the list or walking it.

3. Make the list fuse, the way imap does: WINNER. imap's FunctorWithIndex instance fuses because it has a second vector (the grid's own elements) to V.zipWith against; tabulateGrid has none, since producing the vector is the job. Handing it a throwaway one -- V.replicate size () -- is enough to trigger the same fusion RULE, so V.fromList allCoord never materialises as a whole list; each coordinate is produced, consumed by func, and dies in the nursery, same as imap.

Landed as the new tabulateGrid body in src/Data/Grid/Sized/Internal/Grid.hs. Measured same-run, same-machine improvement over the old VG.fromListN version:
  tabulate 300x300:            3.15 ms / 9.6 MB / 6.4 MB copied  ->  2.53 ms / 7.6 MB / 4.6 MB copied
  tabulateGrid 300x300 boxed:  3.11 ms / 9.6 MB / 6.2 MB copied  ->  2.42 ms / 7.6 MB / 4.3 MB copied
  tabulateGrid 300x300 unboxed:906 us / 9.6 MB / 525 KB copied  ->  530 us / 4.8 MB /  15 KB copied
Downstream (summed-area build, which composes tabulateGrid with scanAxis/transposeGrid) improved proportionally too. Full 57-benchmark suite passes against baseline with --fail-if-slower 30 and no failures; laptop baseline CSV regenerated to reflect the new numbers. All 589 tests pass unchanged (pure vector-construction rewrite, no type or behaviour change).

Left as a noted-but-not-taken further step: the VG.convert at the end of tabulateGrid is a real copy-of-a-vector-to-itself for the v ~ V.Vector (boxed) case, same as collapseGrid/gridFromList used to be before their [~1] RULE. Not added here -- the win already lands without it and the boxed number above already accounts for paying that cost -- but it's the next lever if boxed tabulate needs to close further on unboxed.

Answering the issue's original question: the 16x gap was never really about "a list exists vs not" (both the odometer and the original all still allocate a comparable coordinate structure) -- it was specifically about *fusion*: whether that structure is ever forced into a standalone heap object before being consumed, or whether producer and consumer run as one loop. Options 1 and 2 replace the list with something that superficially looks list-free but doesn't fuse either, and lose to the list. Option 3 keeps the list literally in the source text but makes it fuse, and wins.
close_reason: Closed

title: mapAxis/scanAxis transpose the whole grid twice; scanAxis loses to hand-rolled boxed, wins unboxed
description:
`mapAxisHere` -- the engine under `mapAxis` and `scanAxis` -- makes four full
passes over the grid and three whole intermediate copies to run a function along
one axis:

    Grid $ transposeFlat restSize axisSize
         $ VG.concat
         $ map (unGrid . f . Grid)
         $ splitVectorBySize axisSize
         $ transposeFlat axisSize restSize v

Transpose, split into a list of vectors, map, concat, transpose back.

It shows in the benchmark, and it shows in the worst possible way -- the
library's own combinator loses to what a user writes by hand:

- summed-area build 300x300, boxed:      26.92 s,  33.3 MB
- via `scanAxis`,   300x300, boxed:      34.08 s,  53.5 MB
- summed-area build 300x300, unboxed:    12.83 s,  33.3 MB
- via `scanAxis`,   300x300, unboxed:    11.02 s,  59.2 MB

The boxed case is 27% slower and 61% more allocation than the hand-rolled
version. A combinator that exists so callers do not have to hand-roll the thing
should not be the slower of the two.

An axis map is a strided traversal. For axis `n` the stride is
`MaxCoordSize` of the axes below it and the count is the product of the rest --
both known from the type, both already computed by `AllSizedKnown`. So the
transposes are avoidable: gather the axis's elements by stride into a
`coordListSize`-sized buffer, apply `f`, scatter back. One intermediate of the
axis's length instead of three of the grid's.

Whether `f`'s `GridOf v '[c] x -> GridOf v '[c] y` signature survives that is
the design question -- it wants a contiguous vector, and a strided view is not
one. Options: keep the gather (one small copy per line, still far below three
full-grid copies), or offer a second entry point for the length-preserving case
where a fold along the stride is enough, which is what `scanAxis` needs.

Type safety: the signature and the `MapAxis n cs c` fundep stay exactly as they
are; this is a body swap behind them. `mapAxis`'s existing property tests (it
agrees with the naive `tabulate`-based definition) are what keeps it honest.
notes:
RE-MEASURED 2026-08-19, quiet machine, 48/48 same as baseline. The description's numbers are from 2026-08-18 and predate the -O2 library flags (b60e202); every one of them is roughly 2x too slow now. More importantly, half the claim in the original title no longer holds.

Current:

  summed-area build 300x300  boxed:            13.95 ms, 36.0 MB
  summed-area build (scanAxis) 300x300  boxed: 17.75 ms, 53.4 MB   (+27% time, +48% alloc)

  summed-area build 300x300 unboxed:            6.76 ms, 38.9 MB
  summed-area build (scanAxis) 300x300 unboxed: 5.56 ms, 59.1 MB   (-18% time, +52% alloc)

So scanAxis loses to the hand-rolled pipeline BOXED, by the 27% the description describes, and BEATS it UNBOXED by 18%. The allocation penalty is the constant across both -- roughly +50% either way, which is the three whole-grid intermediates mapAxisHere builds -- but unboxed those intermediates are cheap enough that scanAxis's single strided pass wins anyway, while boxed they are three copies of 90,000 pointers and it does not.

That splits the issue in two, and the split is worth keeping in mind before rewriting anything:

- The allocation story is unchanged and is the real defect. Three full-grid intermediates to run a function along one axis, on both representations.
- The time story is representation-dependent. 'A combinator that exists so callers do not have to hand-roll the thing should not be the slower of the two' is still true for boxed grids and is now false for unboxed ones.

A strided gather/scatter fixes both at once, so the plan in the description does not change. What changes is the acceptance test: it has to hold the unboxed win, not just recover the boxed loss. A rewrite that made boxed match hand-rolled while giving back the 18% unboxed would be a regression for the representation the summed-area workload actually uses.

Also note the sign of the allocation column against the DESCRIPTION's numbers: boxed scanAxis was 53.5 MB then and is 53.4 MB now. Allocation did not move across the -O2 flags, which is the usual tell -- the flags bought inlining, not a different algorithm. The intermediates are still there.
close_reason:
Fixed by d3869b1. mapAxisHere's two whole-grid transposes are gone: MapAxis now yields only the axis's size and stride (axisSizeAndStride replaces mapAxisImpl, and the data recursion with it), mapAxis gathers/scatters one fibre at a time, and scanAxis walks the grid once in order with no gather at all.

Measured 300x300, aarch64-darwin GHC 9.12.3, before -> after, with the hand-rolled transposeGrid pipeline for comparison:

  scanAxis 0   boxed  11.5 ms/37 MB -> 575 us/2.1 MB   (hand-rolled 1.56 ms/5.6 MB)
  scanAxis 0 unboxed  3.62 ms/41 MB -> 67.8 us/703 KB  (hand-rolled 636 us/5.6 MB)
  mapAxis 0    boxed  13.7 ms/38 MB -> 4.39 ms/10 MB
  mapAxis 0  unboxed  3.49 ms/37 MB -> 168 us/2.1 MB
  summed-area  boxed  15.8 ms/46 MB -> 3.61 ms/11 MB   (hand-rolled 5.67 ms/14 MB)
  summed-area unboxed 4.42 ms/48 MB -> 634 us/5.6 MB   (hand-rolled 1.37 ms/10 MB)

Both halves of the split in the NOTES are settled: the allocation defect is gone (46 MB -> 11 MB on the summed-area build, and the isolated scanAxis 0 allocates its result and nothing else -- 703 KB for 90,000 Ints), and scanAxis now beats the hand-rolled pipeline in BOTH representations rather than winning one and losing the other.

Correction to the NOTES' acceptance test, for the record: the 18% unboxed win it said a rewrite had to hold no longer existed by the time this was worked. Re-measured before touching anything, scanAxis was 2.8x SLOWER than hand-rolled boxed and 3.2x slower unboxed. The notes' 5.56 vs 6.76 ms pair did not reproduce because sized-grid-adr.16 made tabulateGrid ~2.4x faster, and tabulateGrid is most of what satBuild measures -- the hand-rolled side got faster while scanAxis stood still. That is also why bench/Main.hs now measures scanAxis and mapAxis on a grid that already exists: the summed-area pair hid the operation behind its input.

Two implementation findings worth keeping:
- The scan reads the element one stride back out of the result vector rather than carrying it in an accumulator argument. Carrying it is the obvious shape and is slower (1.2x boxed, 3.7x unboxed): it saves a read but takes the grid in stride-sized jumps.
- INLINE, not INLINABLE, on the loops and on mapAxis/scanAxis is worth 2.1x boxed and 8.7x unboxed. Behind a call f is unknown, so every combined value is a boxed thunk and the pass allocates a word per cell.

Tests: tests/Test/Axis.hs checks every axis of a 3x5 and a 2x3x4 against a Coord-indexed reference that shares no code with the stride arithmetic, with a fibre reversal and a non-commutative operator so a mis-gathered fibre or a wrong-way fold cannot pass. Both mutations were confirmed to fail the tests. Laptop baseline refreshed in a166d71.

title: Library builds at -O1 with no cross-package unfoldings
description:
The library is built at cabal's default `-O1`, with no `-O2` and none of the
flags that let a downstream package specialise across the package boundary.

That matters more here than in most libraries. This codebase's entire
performance story -- see the long note on `IsCoordList` -- is that a per-axis
fold written as a class method unrolls and constant-folds *once the dictionary
is known*, and for a downstream caller at a concrete axis list that happens at
specialisation. Specialisation across a package boundary needs the unfoldings to
be in the interface file. If they are not, `../aoc` and the example packages pay
the generic worker cost that the library's own benchmarks never see, because the
benchmarks are compiled against the same package's Core.

Measure, on the library component, in this order:
1. `-O2` alone.
2. `-fexpose-all-unfoldings -fspecialise-aggressively`.
3. Both.

against the benchmark suite *and* against a consumer -- gameOfLife or ising, or
better `../aoc`, which is the real one. A win visible only in-package is not the
win we are looking for.

Watch out for two things already documented in the .cabal:
- `-fno-ignore-asserts` is set deliberately on the library so `unsafeOrdinal`'s
  precondition check survives into every consumer's build. `-O2` does not change
  that, but confirm it rather than assume it -- the whole point is that the
  check is stripped once, here, when the unfolding is written.
- Bigger unfoldings mean slower downstream compiles. Record the cost. If the
  trade is bad, `-fexpose-all-unfoldings` can go on selectively, or the fold
  methods can carry explicit `SPECIALISE` pragmas for the common axis lists
  instead.

Zero type-safety cost either way; these are codegen flags.
notes:
Measured and merged (b60e202). Library now carries -O2 -fexpose-all-unfoldings -fspecialise-aggressively -fno-ignore-asserts, in that order.

Result, honestly: 2 of 48 benchmarks move, none regress. imap 300x300 2.0x (alloc 0.64x), ifoldl' 300x300 1.5x (alloc to ~0). Everything else inside the noise, and ../aoc does not move at all -- two grid puzzles within a percent, their time being parsing and list building rather than coord arithmetic. Kept because the cost is near zero: library builds 5% slower, .hi files +10%, downstream recompile unchanged at 8.1s.

MEASUREMENT TRAP, worth remembering: the first pass applied the flags via a 'package grid-sized' stanza in a cabal.project. That applies to EVERY component of the package, so it rebuilt the benchmark itself with -O2 -fspecialise-aggressively and reported 16 moved benchmarks and a 27x on toEnum/fromEnum -- all of it the benchmark's own compilation, not the library's unfoldings. The honest experiment edits only the library stanza and holds the benchmark at -O1 on both sides. The Allocated column is the tell: it does not drift with machine load.

Spun out sized-grid-sxy (the -O2/assert-order bug, fixed here with a guard in the downstream suite).
close_reason: Closed

title: permuteGrid: transposeGrid is a backpermute written as a per-cell tabulate
description:
`transposeGrid` is defined as the obvious thing:

    transposeGrid g = tabulateGrid (indexGrid g . tranposeCoord)

which costs a `Coord` built, permuted and destroyed per cell: 5.14 s and 8.6 MB
at 300x300 boxed, 2.30 s unboxed. `transposeFlat` -- already in this module,
used by `mapAxisHere` -- does the 2D case in a `VG.generate` with a `divMod` and
an `unsafeIndex`, no coordinate at all.

The general point is that `tabulate (index g . f)` for a coordinate
endomorphism `f` is a permutation of the vector, and the permutation depends
only on the axis list and `f`, not on the elements. So it can be built once as a
`Vector Int` and applied with `VG.unsafeBackpermute`, which is a tight loop.

Sketch a combinator:

    permuteGrid :: (Coord cs -> Coord ds) -> GridOf v ds a -> GridOf v cs a

with the index vector computed from the type, and define `transposeGrid` on top
of it. `unsafeBackpermute` is licensed here for the same reason as in
sized-grid-adr.1: every entry of the table is a `coordPosition`, so
it is in `[0, MaxCoordSize ds)` by construction.

Check the other `tabulate (index . f)` shapes in the library while you are here
-- `Monad`'s `>>=` is `imap (\p a -> f a `index` p)`, which is a different
shape, but `dropGrid`/`takeGrid`/`combineHigherDim` may be permutations in
disguise.

Type safety: `permuteGrid`'s signature says the shapes involved, and the table
is built from the same `coordPosition` every safe read uses. A caller cannot
supply a bad permutation because they supply a *coordinate function*, and
`Coord ds` is only inhabited by in-range coordinates.
notes:
Done. Added permuteGrid (Coord cs -> Coord ds) -> GridOf v ds a -> GridOf v cs a,
built on VG.unsafeBackpermute over a table of coordPosition . f; transposeGrid
is now permuteGrid tranposeCoord. Both exported from Data.Grid.Sized.

The one real finding: permuteGrid MUST be INLINE, not INLINABLE. Left
INLINABLE, transposeGrid 300x300 measured 22-29 ms / 85-92 MB -- worse than
the per-cell tabulateGrid/indexGrid it replaced, and unchanged by building the
whole project at -O2, so it wasn't an optimisation-level gap. It was that an
offered-but-declined unfolding leaves f/cs/ds opaque wherever permuteGrid is
actually called (this library's own bench executable included), and
coordPosition/allCoord only unroll into flat arithmetic when the axis list is
known at the inline site. Forcing INLINE: 812 us / 720 KB boxed and 428 us /
720 KB unboxed, 82-84% under the old per-cell baseline on both time and
allocation -- checked into bench/baseline-ghc9.12.3-aarch64-darwin.csv.

Also checked whether unsafeBackpermute itself (needing an extra VG.Vector v
Int constraint) was the expensive part, by comparing against a
Stencil.hs-style concrete VU.Vector Int table walked with VG.generate: with
INLINE, backpermute was actually faster and lower-allocation than the manual
table (838 us -> 812 us boxed measured across runs), so backpermute stayed.

Checked the rest of the library for other tabulate (index . f) shapes:
dropGrid/takeGrid/combineHigherDim/splitHigherDim are already direct vector
ops (VG.drop/VG.take/VG.++/VG.splitAt), not tabulate/index in disguise, so
transposeGrid was the only instance to fix.

All 589 grid-sized tests pass, plus atlas-topology and grid-atlas. Full
57-benchmark suite passes against the regenerated baseline with no
--fail-if-slower 25 failures.
close_reason: done

title: Spike: what would Coord as a flat Int cost, and what would it buy?
description:
Spike, not a commitment.

`Coord cs = Coord (NP I cs)` is a boxed heterogeneous cons list: per axis, a
`:*` cell, an `I` box, and the axis newtype's own box around an `Ordinal`, which
is a boxed `Int`. Every coordinate the library produces pays that, and the
benchmarks are full of places where a coordinate is built only to be collapsed
to an `Int` by `coordPosition` and dropped -- `tabulate`, `imap`, `neighbours`,
`extend`, `transposeGrid`.

The other end of the design space: represent a coordinate *as* its row-major
position.

    newtype Coord cs = Coord Int
    type role Coord nominal

with `(:|)` and `EmptyCoord` as bidirectional pattern synonyms doing the
`divMod`, and `NP I cs` recovered only when someone asks for it. `coordPosition`
becomes `coerce` -- free -- and so does the whole of `index`, `tabulate`'s
odometer, and the stencil tables.

Arguments that it does not cost type safety:
- The axis list still indexes the type and still carries the boundary policy.
  Nothing about what `Coord '[Clamped 5, Periodic 3]` means changes.
- The public interface is already the pattern synonyms, both marked `COMPLETE`.
  `Coord(..)` exports `unCoord`, but that is an `NP` accessor that a synonym can
  keep providing.
- The role stays nominal, so the `Ordinal`-style `coerce :: Coord '[C 9] ->
  Coord '[C 3]` hole stays shut.
- The invariant becomes "the Int is in `[0, MaxCoordSize cs)`", maintained by
  constructors, which is precisely the trade `Ordinal` already made when it
  stopped being a GADT -- and that change is what made this library fast in the
  first place. Read that module header before starting.

Arguments against, to be settled by measurement not by argument:
- Per-axis operations get `divMod`-heavy. `offsetCoord`, `axisSteps`,
  `neighbours` and every boundary policy work axis at a time; today they walk a
  spine, after this they divide. On a 2- or 3-axis grid with sizes that
  constant-fold, GHC turns `divMod` by a literal into multiply-shift, but that
  only happens where the size is a literal -- i.e. exactly where the current
  design already constant-folds. Check whether the win survives at a
  non-constant-folded call site.
- `All Eq cs` / `Ord` / `Show` / `ToJSON` instances currently fold over the `NP`
  with per-axis dictionaries. As an `Int` some get cheaper (`Eq`, `Ord`) and
  some need the `NP` rebuilt (`Show`, JSON).
- `Coord` is exposed; a representation change is a breaking change for anyone
  pattern-matching `Coord` directly rather than through `:|`.

How to settle it: do not port the library. Write a throwaway `Int`-coordinate
grid outside the package, run the existing benchmark bodies against it, and get
a number for the ceiling. If the ceiling is close to what the fused-fold and
stencil work already reaches, this is not worth the churn and the issue closes
with that finding recorded. If it is far above, it becomes a plan.
notes:
CORRECTION from the sized-grid-adr.16 port: the 4.6x recorded above for
offsetCoord is inflated, and the honest figure is 3.25x.

Both sides of that pair consumed the result with isJust, which never demands
the coordinate offsetCoord constructs. On the NP side that did not matter --
the cold branch of unsafeOrdinal's guard sat in the middle of the fold and
nothing could be dropped around it -- but on the Int side GHC deleted the
whole position reconstruction, leaving four in-range tests. The tell is in the
numbers already recorded here: 204 us is exactly what the ported library
measures when the result is discarded, and 369 us when it is demanded.

Re-measured old library against new, identical source on both sides, the
result summed through coordPosition: 1.20 ms -> 369 us, 3.25x.

Everything else in the RESULT table stands, and the port reproduces it:
neighbours 2.6x (16.4 MB -> 2.6 MB, exactly), tabulate 2.25x -> 2.31x
measured, index 1.60x -> 1.64x, imap 1.41x -> 1.40x, ifoldl' 1.53x -> 2.07x,
onBoundary 2.2x -> 2.08x, coordDistance 1.7x -> 1.61x, (.+^) four corner reads
1.33x -> 1.34x, torus walk 2.68 MB -> 20 B against the predicted 17 B.
close_reason: Spike done. Ceiling measured at 1.26x-5.1x over the current representation with nothing slower; findings in the issue notes, harness in spike/adr8-intcoord/, plan filed as sized-grid-adr.16.

title: imapGrid forces every coordinate live at once, which the boxed imap deliberately does not
description:
`imapGrid` materialises every coordinate at once:

    imapGrid f (Grid v) = Grid (VG.imap (\i x -> f (allCoordVector VG.! i) x) v)
      where allCoordVector = V.fromListN (coordSpaceSize @cs) allCoord

The boxed `imap` instance a few lines below deliberately does not do this, and
the note above it says why in so many words: `V.zipWith` fuses with
`V.fromList allCoord` so the coordinates die in the nursery, and using
`fromListN` instead forced 90,000 coordinates live at once, cost 23% more
allocation and ran 59% slower. Measured, and the note ends "Leave it alone."

`imapGrid` is the same function for grids whose element type cannot support
`FunctorWithIndex` -- which is to say, it is the *only* indexed map an unboxed
grid has -- and it does the thing the note warns against, plus a bounds-checked
`VG.!` per cell into the coordinate vector.

Fix: give it the same shape as the instance. `VG.imap` over a fused coordinate
stream, or a `zipWith` against `V.fromList allCoord`, whichever the generic
vector API allows here (the awkward part is that `v` and the coordinate vector
are different vector types, which is presumably why it was written this way).

This is gameOfLife's inner loop -- its whole step is one `imapGrid` -- so the
example programs are the workload to measure, alongside adding an
`imapGrid 300x300 unboxed` case to bench/Main.hs, which does not currently
cover it.

No signature change, no type-safety question.
close_reason: Closed

title: Ix (Coord cs) done lawfully: the survey's proposed instance is NOT lawful
description:
From the sized-grid-90f survey. This entry corrects that survey: it was
filed under "Tier 1: the machinery is already written", and it is not.

== The correction

The survey proposed

  range   = allCoord
  index   = coordPosition
  inRange = const (const True)

That is unlawful. base's Data.Ix documents the laws an implementation may
assume, and the first is

  inRange (l,u) i  ==  elem i (range (l,u))

Ix's methods all take a BOUNDING PAIR (l,u) naming a contiguous sub-box, not
the whole space. The proposal ignores that pair. Concretely, for a
Coord '[Clamped 5, Clamped 5] and bounds (1:|1, 3:|3):

  - inRange returns True for 0:|0, which is not in range (l,u). Law 1 fails.
  - index returns coordPosition 4:|4 == 24, but rangeSize (l,u) is 9, so
    "map (index (l,u)) (range (l,u)) == [0 .. rangeSize (l,u) - 1]" fails.

The consequence is not academic. Data.Array's accessors call unsafeAt with
whatever index returns, so a consumer writing

  listArray (c1, c2) xs

over a sub-box gets out-of-bounds reads with no bounds check to catch them.
That is exactly the class of bug the library's assert-on-unsafeOrdinal policy
(grid-sized.cabal, sized-grid-6os) exists to prevent -- shipping it through a
base class instance would be a bad trade.

== The lawful instance

The same shape base uses for tuples: componentwise on the bounding box.

  range   (l,u) = the cartesian product of the per-axis ranges, first axis
                  most significant (row-major, matching coordPosition)
  index   (l,u) = mixed-radix over the per-axis SUB-BOX sizes
  inRange (l,u) = every axis in its own range

Then index (minBound, maxBound) c == coordPosition c falls out as a theorem
about the full box, which is the survey's original claim recovered as a
special case rather than assumed as the definition.

Two things this needs that the naive version did not:

  - Ix on each axis type (Ordinal, Clamped, Periodic, Reflective,
    Reflect101). All are newtypes over Ordinal; Ix can be derived through
    them once Ordinal has it. Ordinal's is index i = ordinalToInt i -
    ordinalToInt l.
  - Ix's superclass is Ord, so the instance context picks up All Ord cs on
    top of IsCoordList. Ord (Coord cs) exists (Coord.hs:129) and is
    lexicographic first-axis-major, which agrees with row-major
    coordPosition -- so the Ord Ix wants and the order range produces are
    the same order. Worth stating in the Haddock.

Periodic is the interesting axis: is (Periodic 2, Periodic 4) of a Periodic 5
the three-element range [2,3,4], or the wrap-around [2,3,4,0,1]? Ix's laws
force the first (range must agree with rangeSize and with the Ord-contiguous
reading), so Periodic's Ix must NOT wrap even though its Enum and Semigroup
do. Say so in the Haddock; it is the one place a Periodic operation is not
periodic, and the reason is that Ix's contract is about contiguous subranges.

== Payoff

Data.Array and Data.Array.Unboxed keyed by our coordinates, for consumers who
want a boxed array rather than our Grid. array is already in the build plan
(pulled in by lens and containers), so this adds no package.

== Test

quickcheck-classes 0.6.5.0 ships ixLaws (confirmed present); add it via the
existing lawsToTest helper. See sized-grid-5p0.
close_reason: Implemented lawful componentwise Ix for Ordinal, all axis policies, and Coord; added scalar Ix laws plus a multidimensional sub-box regression. Cabal tests pass: 685 tests.

title: Use RequiredTypeArguments to delete Proxy from the public API
description:
GHC 9.10+ has RequiredTypeArguments ('forall n -> ...'), so the Proxy-passing style
throughout this library is now avoidable. Kevin has approved targeting 9.12/9.14
features (2026-08-09).

Current Proxy-taking API:
  - src/SizedGrid/Grid/Grid.hs:190  dropGrid  :: KnownNat n => Proxy n -> Grid '[c m] x -> Grid '[c (m - n)] x
  - src/SizedGrid/Grid/Grid.hs:197  takeGrid  :: KnownNat n => Proxy n -> Grid '[c n] x
  - src/SizedGrid/Coord/Class.hs:37 sCoordSized  :: Proxy (c n) -> Proxy n
  - src/SizedGrid/Coord/Class.hs:41 maxCoordSize :: KnownNat n => Proxy (c n) -> Integer
  - src/SizedGrid/Coord/Class.hs:45 maxCoord     :: KnownNat n => Proxy n -> c n
  - src/SizedGrid/Coord/Class.hs:48 asSizeProxy  :: c n -> (forall m. ... => Proxy m -> x) -> x

After:
    takeGrid :: forall n -> (KnownNat n, n <= m) => Grid '[c m] x -> Grid '[c n] x
    takeGrid 3 g        -- instead of takeGrid (Proxy @3) g

    maxCoordSize :: forall (c :: Nat -> Type) n -> KnownNat n => Integer

Also removes Proxy from test and user code: tests/Main.hs is full of
'Proxy @(Periodic 10)' arguments, and ../aoc passes Proxy around too.

Related modernisation to do in the same pass:
  - default-language: GHC2024 (GHC 9.10+). GHC2024 already implies DataKinds, GADTs,
    LambdaCase, MonoLocalBinds, DerivingStrategies, RoleAnnotations,
    ExplicitNamespaces, DisambiguateRecordFields on top of GHC2021's
    ScopedTypeVariables/TypeApplications/TypeOperators/FlexibleContexts/RankNTypes.
    That deletes most of the 10-20 line LANGUAGE headers on every module.
  - TypeAbstractions ('instance ... where method @a = ...') for the IsCoord instances
    that currently need InstanceSigs + ScopedTypeVariables to bind the type variable.
  - OrPatterns (GHC 9.12) where the coord classes match several constructors alike.
  - DerivingStrategies to make the many 'deriving instance' lines in
    Coord/Periodic.hs:37-42 and Coord/HardWrap.hs:30-36 explicit about newtype vs
    stock vs anyclass.

Sequence after the plugin adoption (sized-grid-h56) so the constraint changes and the
signature changes land together rather than touching every signature twice.
notes:
GHC 9.12.3 spikes done 2026-08-11, before the work was deferred behind sized-grid-5gp. All four forms this issue needs compile:

  1. Visible Nat with constraints after the binder, on a plain function:
       takeIt :: forall m. forall n -> (KnownNat n, n <= m) => [Int] -> [Int]
  2. Passing an in-scope type variable as the required argument: 'takeIt @m k xs'.
  3. Class methods, both 'forall n -> KnownNat n => Integer' and no argument at
     all where the result type already fixes everything.
  4. A rank-2 continuation that itself takes a required type argument,
       withSize :: Int -> (forall m -> (KnownNat m, m + 1 <= 8) => String) -> String
     bound at the call site by an ordinary lambda '\m -> ...'. So asSizeProxy can
     drop its Proxy rather than keeping it in a rank-2 position.
  5. TypeAbstractions in an instance-method equation ('maxC @n = ...') works, which
     is how an instance body names a type variable once the Proxy argument is gone.

Proxy-free Nat reflection: 'fromSNat (natSing @n)' works; 'fromSNat SNat' does not
(ambiguous). Prefer natVal (Proxy @n) where Proxy is already imported for SOP.

Design decisions reached, not yet implemented:
  - maxCoordSize should stop being an IsCoord method and become a standalone
    'maxCoordSize :: forall n -> KnownNat n => Integer'. It cannot depend on c:
    asOrdinal is an Iso' (c n) (Ordinal n), so every lawful instance has exactly n
    inhabitants, and no instance overrides the default. Keeping it a method forces
    either an ambiguous c or 'maxCoordSize (type Periodic) n', because a visible
    type-constructor argument collides with the data constructor of the same name.
  - sCoordSized deletes outright; it is pure Proxy plumbing.
  - maxCoord should lose its argument entirely rather than take 'forall n ->': the
    result type c n already fixes both variables. NOTE: worktree-allcoord has since
    given maxCoord the '1 <= n' constraint this issue would also have added.
  - Rule worth stating in the ChangeLog: visible type arguments only where
    inference cannot determine them.

Blast radius check: ../aoc uses SizedGrid in 8 modules but none of takeGrid,
dropGrid, maxCoordSize, sCoordSized, asSizeProxy or maxCoord, so this break is
contained to this repo plus tests. The per-module LANGUAGE headers are also still
long (14 lines in Coord/Class.hs) despite the cabal file already setting GHC2024 --
almost all of them are now redundant and should go in the same pass.
close_reason: Done on branch worktree-required-type-args (commit d0b07ab). No public function takes a Proxy: takeGrid/dropGrid take a visible Nat, maxCoordSize became a standalone visible-forall function, maxCoord lost its argument entirely, sCoordSized is deleted, asSizeProxy is reifyCoord with a required-type-argument continuation. Minimum GHC raised to 9.10. 64 lines of redundant LANGUAGE headers removed. Clean build, zero library warnings, 129 tests plus README suite pass, no new warnings against master.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
OrPatterns, which this issue also asked for, does NOT apply anywhere here -- recording it so nobody retries.

The one site that looks like a candidate is reifyOrdinal:

    case cmpNat (Proxy @(k + 1)) (Proxy @n) of
        LTI -> func k
        EQI -> func k
        GTI -> invariantViolated ...

Two branches with an identical right-hand side. But LTI and EQI are GADT constructors of OrderingI and each brings different evidence into scope: LTI gives (k + 1) < n, EQI gives (k + 1) ~ n, and 'func k' needs k + 1 <= n derived from whichever one matched. An or-pattern has to type its right-hand side once, with no branch-specific evidence, so it cannot express this. The duplication is load-bearing.

The coord classes have no multi-constructor matches at all any more: Ordinal is a newtype since worktree-ordinal-int, and Coord matches on NP.

title: No benchmarks; performance work is currently unmeasurable
description:
There is no benchmark suite, so every performance claim about this library
(Ordinal representation, allCoord caching, unboxed vectors) is speculation.

Add a criterion (or tasty-bench) suite covering the operations the real workloads hit:

  - index / gridIndex on Grid '[HardWrap 300, HardWrap 300] Int
    (the shape ../aoc/src/2018/11.hs uses)
  - tabulate at the same size
  - imap / ifoldMap' / itraverse -- these rebuild allCoord every call
  - the comonadic step: extend over a FocusedGrid, as in ../aoc/src/2015/18.hs
    and ../aoc/src/2018/18.hs and gameOfLife/
  - coordinate arithmetic in isolation: (.+^), (.-.), toEnum, fromEnum
  - allCoord itself
  - collapseGrid / gridFromList round-trip
  - JSON encode/decode

Record a baseline on GHC 9.12 BEFORE touching the Ordinal representation, so the
refactor can be judged. tasty-bench is the lighter dependency and integrates with the
existing tasty suite.

This gates the Ordinal-newtype issue and the unboxed-Grid issue -- do it first.
close_reason: tasty-bench suite added (bench/Main.hs, 'benchmarks' stanza), covering every operation this issue listed at the consumer's own grid shapes. Baseline recorded at bench/baseline-ghc9.12.3-aarch64-darwin.csv; whole suite runs in 32s. Quantified the two blocked issues: allCoord costs 115x on tabulate-vs-pure and 23x on imap-vs-fmap (uvd), and tabulate allocates 93 MB for a 90,000-cell Int grid whose payload is under 1 MB (upo). Verified on ghc 9.12.3 and 9.14.1.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
DONE. tasty-bench suite added at bench/Main.hs, wired as the 'benchmarks' stanza, and a
baseline recorded at bench/baseline-ghc9.12.3-aarch64-darwin.csv. Whole suite runs in
32 s, so it is cheap enough to re-run on every change. tasty-bench over criterion as
suggested: it shares tasty with the test suite and emits allocation figures, which turn
out to matter more than the times.

Coverage is the list from this issue: index, tabulate, imap/ifoldl'/itraverse, the
comonadic extend, coordinate arithmetic ((.+^), (.-.), toEnum/fromEnum), collapseGrid /
gridFromList round trip, and JSON encode/decode. Shapes are the consumer's, not invented:
300x300 from ../aoc/src/2018/11.hs, 100x100 from ../aoc/src/2015/18.hs and 2018/18.hs.

BASELINE, GHC 9.12.3, aarch64-darwin, -O1:

  coord arithmetic
    (.+^) x10000, Periodic 300x300                 1.57 ms    11 MB     (157 ns/op)
    (.-.) x10000, HardWrap 100x100                  234 us   3.2 MB     (23 ns/op)
    toEnum/fromEnum x300, HardWrap 300             7.16 us    77 KB     (24 ns/op)
  allCoord overhead
    tabulate 300x300   [rebuilds allCoord]         23.6 ms    93 MB
    pure 300x300       [does not]                   206 us   704 KB
    imap 300x300       [rebuilds allCoord]         17.7 ms    80 MB
    fmap 300x300       [does not]                   758 us   4.1 MB
  grid access
    index x90000, 300x300                          13.8 ms    72 MB     (153 ns/index)
  indexed traversals
    ifoldl' 300x300                                19.5 ms   107 MB
    itraverse 100x100                               318 us   3.4 MB
  comonad
    extract 50x50                                   154 ns   808 B
    extend neighbourSum 50x50                      5.42 ms    29 MB     (2.2 us/cell)
  collapse round trip
    collapseGrid 100x100                            163 us   2.7 MB
    gridFromList . collapseGrid 100x100             581 us   4.4 MB
  json
    toJSON 100x100                                  338 us   3.7 MB
    fromJSON . toJSON 100x100                      1.65 ms    10 MB

TWO NUMBERS THE BLOCKED ISSUES WERE WAITING FOR:

  sized-grid-uvd (allCoord rebuilt per call). The pairs are deliberately identical apart
  from whether allCoord is built:
      tabulate vs pure   23.6 ms vs 206 us   = 115x slower, 132x the allocation
      imap     vs fmap   17.7 ms vs 758 us   =  23x slower,  20x the allocation
  So allCoord is not a minor overhead on indexed traversal, it IS the cost.

  sized-grid-upo (Ordinal GADT). tabulate allocates 93 MB to fill a 90,000-cell grid of
  Int -- roughly 1 KB per cell. An Int grid's payload is under 1 MB. That two-orders-of-
  magnitude gap is the someNatVal/KnownNat-dictionary traffic this issue predicts, now
  measured rather than assumed.

METHOD NOTE, worth knowing before anyone adds to this file. There is deliberately no
standalone allCoord benchmark. 'allCoord' takes no value arguments, so at a fixed type
it is a CAF; the obvious benchmark builds the list once and then times a pointer
dereference. It reported 1.96 ns for 90,000 coordinates. Wrapping it in a NOINLINE
function behind a Proxy argument does not help -- full laziness floats the list out past
the Proxy lambda, still 1.72 ns. Only -fno-full-laziness defeats it, and that would make
every other benchmark stop resembling how the library is really compiled. The library
itself never gets that sharing, because its instances take the 'All IsCoordLifted'
dictionary at runtime, so the paired-difference framing above measures the real cost.
Both dead ends are recorded in a comment in bench/Main.hs so they are not retried.

Verified: cabal build all warning-free, cabal check clean, both test suites green.

title: mapLowerDim is already a Traversal: give it the type synonym and the law note
description:
From the sized-grid-31z optics survey. Tier C, and the cheapest finding in
it: this function is ALREADY a Traversal and nobody has said so.

  mapLowerDim :: (VG.Vector v x, VG.Vector v y, AllSizedKnown as, Applicative f)
              => (GridOf v as x -> f (GridOf v bs y))
              -> GridOf v (c ': as) x
              -> f (GridOf v (c ': bs) y)                     Internal/Grid.hs:660

Line that up with van Laarhoven:

  type Traversal s t a b = forall f. Applicative f => (a -> f b) -> s -> f t

It is the same type, with `s = GridOf v (c ': as) x`, `t = GridOf v (c ': bs) y`,
`a = GridOf v as x`, `b = GridOf v bs y`. So:

  lowerDim :: (VG.Vector v x, VG.Vector v y, AllSizedKnown as)
           => Traversal (GridOf v (c ': as) x) (GridOf v (c ': bs) y)
                        (GridOf v as x)        (GridOf v bs y)
  lowerDim = mapLowerDim

Zero implementation. This is a type synonym and a Haddock paragraph.

Lawful: the body is `traverse` over `splitVectorBySize` followed by
`VG.concat` (Internal/Grid.hs:667-670), so identity holds
(`mapLowerDim Identity = Identity`, the split and concat are inverse by the
size invariant) and composition holds because `traverse`'s does. The foci are
the disjoint sub-grids and they exactly partition the vector.

== Why saying so is worth doing

The existing Haddock spends 12 lines (Internal/Grid.hs:646-658) warning that
`f ~ []` gives a cartesian product of `n ^ n` grids and is "almost never what
a caller taking slices means", and points at `zipLowerDim` instead. That
warning is really the observation that `[]`'s Applicative is not the zipping
one -- a fact about Applicative, not about grids, and one every lens user
already knows in the form "don't traverse with []". Naming the thing a
Traversal makes the warning land in a vocabulary the reader has.

It also unlocks the ordinary combinators for free: `toListOf lowerDim`,
`lengthOf`, `over lowerDim`, `lowerDim . lowerDim` for the second axis down,
and composition with `_SplitGrid` (companion issue), which reaches the same
foci from the other side -- cross-check the two agree on ORDER before
shipping either.

`zipLowerDim` (Internal/Grid.hs:696) stays as it is: it is
`getZipList . mapLowerDim (ZipList . f)`, and ZipList is not an Applicative
that makes a lawful Traversal (no `pure` that respects the laws), so it is
correctly a function and not an optic.

Cost: none.
close_reason: Closed

title: Klein bottle grid: single-chart atlas with both edges self-glued
description:
A Klein bottle grid: the same single-chart self-glued construction as
sized-grid-00v (Mobius), but with BOTH axes self-glued instead of one --
crossing either edge lands you back on the same chart, on the far side of
that axis, with the OTHER axis reflected.

    walking off the right edge at row y     -> land on the left edge, row
                                                (h - 1 - y)
    walking off the bottom edge at col x    -> land on the top edge, col
                                                (w - 1 - x)

Deliberately filed as a follow-on to sized-grid-00v rather than built
alongside it: a Klein bottle is exactly "Mobius's single-chart self-seam
machinery, with a second non-identity entry for the other axis" -- there is
no new representation question here once Mobius exists, only a second
seam-table entry and a second belt-closure-style property (crossing either
wrapped edge twice returns to the same coordinate; crossing both once each,
in either order, lands in the same place -- the discrete analogue of a
Klein bottle having no orientation anywhere on it, unlike a Mobius strip
which still has one un-glued pair of edges).

Building this after Mobius rather than instead of it is also what makes the
"is SeamTable worth extracting" question (sized-grid-1av) answerable with a
real second example of a self-seam, not a guess: if Mobius's seam function
generalizes to Klein by adding one table entry, that is good evidence
SeamTable's shape is right; if it doesn't, that is exactly the kind of
correction sized-grid-68j hit (the hand-derived cube seam table had a wrong
sign that only a property test caught), worth having on record.

Not attempting a projective-plane grid here even though sized-grid-o1n's
policy table lists it (`Projective -> (antipode c, negate all axes)`) --
that is a different gluing (opposite corner, not opposite edge) and belongs
in its own issue if wanted, not bundled into this one.
notes:
CORRECTION, agreed with Kevin before building: the table this issue spelled out (both edge-pairs reflected) is the projective plane's identification, not a Klein bottle's. Klein reflects exactly one pair -- square model (x,0)~(x,1) and (0,y)~(1,1-y). Built the Klein one; the both-reversed table is now sized-grid-4nl.

Second correction: the law asked for here -- 'crossing both once each, in either order, lands in the same place' -- is false for a Klein bottle. pi_1 is non-abelian; on the grid it shows as a Rolled step before the twisted crossing not being the one taken after it (y -> h-y vs y -> h-2-y). Tested as kleinTwistDoesNotCommute instead.

Same class of error as sized-grid-68j's hand-derived cube seam sign, but caught by reading rather than by a red test.
close_reason:
Implemented Data.Grid.Atlas.Klein (kleinAtlas/kleinSeam/kleinStep) plus Test.Klein's four laws: seam involution, Twisted lap mirrors and closes after two, Rolled lap closes unmirrored, and kleinTwistDoesNotCommute. All 10 grid-atlas tests pass under -Werror. Committed on master as d191ee0, along with the merge of worktree-sized-grid-00v (Mobius) which this needed and which was closed-but-unmerged.

Answers the sized-grid-1av question the Mobius issue set up: SeamTable took a second self-seam with no change to its shape. crossKleinEdge is four equations, kleinStep drives the whole coordinate remap off the reversed bit rather than special-casing the axis, and the two table entries differ only in that bit. No correction needed of the kind sized-grid-68j hit.

Both gluings the description got wrong are recorded in the notes; the projective-plane table it actually described is sized-grid-4nl.

title: Pointwise Semigroup, Monoid and Num for Grid cs a, with the reading written down
description:
From the sized-grid-90f survey.

Representable hands all three over for free, and pointwise is the only
coherent reading at a fixed shape: there is no concatenation to compete with
it, because two grids of the same type cannot be concatenated into a third
of that type. That argument is the whole point, and it belongs in the
Haddock rather than being left for a consumer to guess -- for lists, Maybe
and Map the same class means three different things.

  instance (IsCoordList cs, Semigroup a) => Semigroup (Grid cs a)
    -- liftA2 (<>), i.e. zipWithGrid (<>)
  instance (AllSizedKnown cs, IsCoordList cs, Monoid a) => Monoid (Grid cs a)
    -- mempty = pure mempty
  instance (AllSizedKnown cs, IsCoordList cs, Num a) => Num (Grid cs a)
    -- all six methods pointwise, fromInteger = pure . fromInteger

Note the constraint asymmetry, and keep it: Semigroup needs only
IsCoordList because zipWith needs no size evidence, while Monoid and Num
need AllSizedKnown because mempty and fromInteger have to conjure a grid out
of nothing (the same reason Applicative carries it, Internal/Grid.hs:203).
Do not level them up to a common context.

== On Num specifically

sized-grid-90f rejected Num (Periodic n) on the grounds that the product of
two POSITIONS is meaningless and that abs and signum have no reading. Neither
objection transfers here. Grid cs a is a container of values, not of
positions; the Hadamard product is what every array library means by (*);
abs and signum are pointwise and total. It is a different question with a
different answer, and the survey's rejection should not be read across.

If Num is dropped anyway, drop it on its own -- Semigroup and Monoid do not
depend on it.

== Test

semigroupLaws, monoidLaws and semigroupMonoidLaws from quickcheck-classes on
Grid cs a at a Monoid element type. See sized-grid-5p0.
close_reason: Added documented pointwise Semigroup, Monoid, and Num instances for Grid and validated them with focused laws and properties.

title: Build atlas-topology: extract SeamTable/HalfEdge per sized-grid-1av's design
description:
Implementation task for the design recorded in sized-grid-1av. Not started -- do not pick this up without explicit go-ahead, since it involves creating a new package boundary (new .cabal, new git-tracked directory).

Scope when ready:
1. New package `atlas-topology`, no dependency on grid-sized or vector -- just base (+ QuickCheck in its test-suite for seamIsInvolution-style properties).
2. Data.Atlas.Topology.Seam (or similar): HalfEdge, SeamTable, seamIsInvolution as specified in sized-grid-1av.
3. Re-point Data.Grid.Atlas.CubeMap's cubeSeam through SeamTable Face (Axis, Extremum); cubeSeamPairsUp becomes/wraps seamIsInvolution. grid-atlas gains a dependency on atlas-topology.
4. cubeStep and the coordinate-arithmetic half stay in grid-atlas untouched -- not in scope, per sized-grid-1av's split.

Trigger to actually start: either a concrete second consumer of SeamTable shows up (a graph/portal-style AoC puzzle, a Mobius/torus topology), or the user explicitly asks to build it regardless.
notes:
Built on branch worktree-sized-grid-b15, commit b51ee00.

New package atlas-topology (base only): Data.Atlas.Topology.Seam exports HalfEdge, SeamTable(..), seamIsInvolution, seamViolations. Two deviations from 1av's sketch, both deliberate:
- seamViolations added alongside seamIsInvolution. It takes the half-edge enumeration as an argument rather than a Bounded/Enum constraint, because a boundary label is typically a product ((Axis, Extremum)) and base gives tuples Bounded but not Enum -- a class-driven version would reject the first real caller. Returning the offenders rather than a Bool is what makes a 24-equation table's failure name the wrong entry.
- Left SeamTable total (a function, not a Maybe/Map). A surface with a real boundary should encode that in its own chart/boundary type instead of making every total table pay for a Maybe.

grid-atlas: cubeSeam :: SeamTable Face (Axis, Extremum); the 24 equations are now the private crossCubeEdge; cubeStep goes through crossSeam. Test.CubeMap's cubeSeamPairsUp is seamViolations over cubeHalfEdges. Verified the check still has teeth by flipping one entry's orientation bit -- it fails and names both ends of the broken seam, which the old assertEqual-per-edge version did not.

atlas-topology's suite: random perfect matchings all pass; negating one half-edge's flip bit is reported as exactly that seam's two half-edges; cylinder/Mobius/badMobius by hand pin down that the two sides of a seam must agree about the twist.

cabal.project gained the package. Not added to flake.nix -- that only builds the root grid-sized package, and grid-atlas is not in it either (pre-existing gap, unchanged).

Follow-up filed: sized-grid-4wn (the coordinate-stepping half 1av left open).
close_reason: atlas-topology built and grid-atlas re-pointed through it; cabal build all and all suites green (commit b51ee00).

title: ChangeLog claims GHC 9.8 support, but base >=4.20 and tested-with both say 9.10
description:
ChangeLog.md (0.3.0.0, near the end) says:

    * Builds with GHC 9.8 through 9.14 via a nix flake

Two things in sized-grid.cabal contradict it:

    line 91  base >=4.20 && <4.23     -- base 4.20 ships with GHC 9.10, not 9.8
    line 29  tested-with: GHC ==9.10.1 || ==9.12.3 || ==9.14.1

GHC 9.8 ships base 4.19, which the bound excludes, so the package cannot build
there at all. Nothing is broken -- the code and the cabal file agree with each
other, and only the prose is wrong.

Noticed while adding coordDistance (sized-grid-lcl): the new code uses foldl'
from Prelude, which is base 4.20+. That is fine under the real bound and would
NOT have been fine under the claimed one, which is what prompted the check.

FIX: either correct the sentence to 9.10, or decide 9.8 is meant to be
supported and lower the base bound plus add it to tested-with. The flake is the
place to confirm which GHCs are actually wired up.
close_reason: Fixed the stale ChangeLog bullet (9.8 through 9.14) to say 9.10 through 9.14, matching base >=4.20 and tested-with in grid-sized.cabal. Chose 'correct the sentence' over lowering the bound since only ghc912/ghc914 are wired up in the flake and nothing targets 9.8.

title: Prefer explicit 'deriving newtype' over unadorned standalone deriving instance
description:
From sized-grid-9e2. The NFData instances added there follow the existing
convention in Clamped/Periodic/Reflective/Reflect101: an unadorned standalone
'deriving instance NFData (Clamped n)' with no explicit strategy keyword,
matching how Show/Random/Enum/Bounded/ToJSON/FromJSON/ToJSONKey/FromJSONKey
are already derived in those same files. GHC infers newtype-via-GND for these
because stock deriving cannot produce them, but the choice is implicit.

DerivingStrategies is already on for every component (implied by GHC2024, per
the comment on the 'lang-base' common stanza in grid-sized.cabal). The
follow-up: convert these standalone deriving declarations -- for NFData and
its existing neighbours -- to state their strategy explicitly, e.g.
'deriving newtype instance NFData (Clamped n)', or fold them into the type's
own header as a second stacked deriving clause,
'newtype Clamped n = ... deriving (Eq, Ord) deriving newtype (...)'.
Explicit strategies stop compiling by coincidence: if a future GHC or
extension change makes some other strategy available first, an unadorned
clause silently picks it up, while an explicit one keeps failing loudly at
exactly the type it was always for.

Scope: at minimum the four axis newtypes (Clamped, Periodic, Reflective,
Reflect101) in src/Data/Grid/Sized/Coord/*.hs. Worth a repo-wide grep for
other unadorned 'deriving instance' declarations while in there.
close_reason: Converted derivable instances to attached explicit strategies; retained explicit strategies for context-sensitive standalone derivations.

title: FocusedGrid fields are lazy; measure strict fields under iterated extend
description:
data FocusedGrid cs a = FocusedGrid
        { focusedGrid         :: Grid cs a
        , focusedGridPosition :: Coord cs
        }

Both fields are lazy. Every other hot path in this library has been measured
and had its allocation driven out; this one has never been looked at.

THE HYPOTHESIS

`duplicate` is `FocusedGrid (tabulate (FocusedGrid g)) p` (Grid/Focused.hs:44)
and `seeks` is `FocusedGrid g (func p)` (Grid/Focused.hs:55). Iterating
`extend` -- which is what every cellular automaton does, hundreds of
generations deep -- builds a chain of these. With lazy fields nothing forces
the grid pointer or the coordinate between steps, so a thunk can accumulate
around either across generations even though `Grid` itself is a strict vector
underneath.

Bang patterns on both fields would force each to WHNF at construction.

WHY IT IS ONLY A HYPOTHESIS

Both fields are newtypes -- `Grid` over `V.Vector` and `Coord` over `NP I cs` --
so WHNF here forces the wrapper and nothing inside it. The vector's elements
and the NP's contents are untouched either way. So the win, if any, is in not
retaining a chain of suspended `FocusedGrid` constructions across generations,
not in element-level strictness. That may be worth a lot or nothing, and this
library's own history says the difference between those two is only ever
settled by measuring: sized-grid-0tj predicted an order of magnitude on the
two-axis benchmark and got 11%.

HOW TO MEASURE

`bench/Main.hs:277` already has `extend neighbourSum 50x50`. That is a single
`extend`, which is the wrong shape for this -- the hypothesis is about
ITERATED extends, so add an n-generation benchmark first
(`iterate (extend rule)` taken to depth ~100, forced) and take a baseline
before touching the datatype.

CAVEAT WORTH CHECKING

`FocusedGrid` derives `Functor`, `Foldable` and `Traversable`. Strict fields
interact with those derivations, and more importantly a strict
`focusedGrid` field makes `fmap` force the grid wrapper where it previously
did not. Nothing in the library appears to rely on a lazily-constructed
`FocusedGrid`, but the comonad law tests (which compare triply-nested
`FocusedGrid`s) are the place a change in forcing behaviour would show up, so
run them.

ACCEPT ONLY WITH NUMBERS. If the iterated benchmark does not move, close this
and record the measurement in the Haddock the way the other performance notes
in this library do -- a documented negative result is worth more than an
undocumented bang pattern.
notes: Added iterate (extend neighbourSum) x100 benchmark (bench/Main.hs) as the shape the hypothesis needed. Baseline (lazy fields): 1,570,443,384 B allocated over 100 generations. With bang patterns on both FocusedGrid fields: 1,570,440,960 B -- noise, and tasty-bench reported wall-clock 'same as baseline' in both directions. Reverted the bang patterns (kept the benchmark) and documented the negative result in the Haddock on FocusedGrid. Full test suite incl. comonadLaws @FocusedGrid still passes (485 tests).
close_reason: Measured: iterated-extend benchmark showed no difference (allocation identical within noise, wall-clock 'same as baseline'). Bang patterns reverted; negative result documented in Haddock per issue's own accept-only-with-numbers instruction.

title: Apply the needle migration to ../aoc when sized-grid-iet reaches master
description:
sized-grid-iet replaced CoordDiff's per-arity tuple family with a coord-shaped
needle: `Diff (Coord cs)` is now `Coord (MapDiff cs)`, so a tuple literal is no
longer a displacement. Five aoc modules use tuple displacements and must be
migrated.

WHY THIS IS A SEPARATE ISSUE, AND WHEN TO DO IT

aoc/cabal.project lists ../sized-grid as a source package, which means aoc
builds against the MAIN sized-grid checkout on master, not against any
.claude/worktrees branch. So aoc keeps working while sized-grid-iet sits on
branch worktree-needle-coorddiff, and breaks the moment that branch merges to
master. Apply this patch WITH the master merge, not before it.

Also: at the time of writing, aoc's working tree had substantial uncommitted
changes (including all eight sized-grid-consuming modules), which is why the
patch was verified out-of-tree rather than applied. Rebase it if those modules
have moved since.

VERIFICATION ALREADY DONE

All eight aoc modules that import sized-grid were type-checked against the
worktree build using the scratch-project workaround in memory
`sized-grid-aoc-cannot-be-cabal-built`:

  - 2016/02.hs, 2017/19.hs, 2018/06.hs,
    2018/11.hs, 2024/04.hs               pass WITH the patch below

LEFT UNCOMMITTED IN ../aoc ON PURPOSE. That repo is the user's own checkout and already carried substantial unrelated uncommitted work across the same five files, so committing would have mixed the migration into it. The changes sit in aoc's working tree; 'git diff' there shows them.
