title: Head and Tail are exported type families with no remaining user
description:
sized-grid-k6n replaced the AllGridSizeKnown type family with a class, and the class matches on 'c n ': as' directly. Head and Tail (src/SizedGrid/Internal/Grid.hs:199-205) existed only to write that family and its four call sites; nothing in the library mentions them now.

They are still exported from SizedGrid.Internal.Grid and re-exported from SizedGrid.Grid.Grid, so they remain public API. ../aoc does not use them (checked: no match for Head or Tail as whole words under aoc/src).

Decide: keep them as generic type-level list utilities, or drop them as surface that exists for no reason. This belongs with the API pass in sized-grid-85n rather than on its own, since removing an exported name is the kind of break that wants to land with the others.
close_reason: Dropped Head/Tail: unused internally and by aoc; smaller public surface

title: _CollapsedGrid: a Prism whose cost is the two RULES pragmas it may stop firing
description:
From the sized-grid-31z optics survey. Tier B: a genuine Prism whose cost is
NOT zero -- read the rewrite-rule note before writing it.

  collapseGrid :: (VG.Vector v a, AllSizedKnown cs)
               => GridOf v cs a -> CollapseGrid cs a          Internal/Grid.hs:380
  gridFromList :: (VG.Vector v a, AllSizedKnown cs)
               => CollapseGrid cs a -> Maybe (GridOf v cs a)  Internal/Grid.hs:406

`CollapseGrid` is the nested-list shape (`CollapseGrid '[] a = a`,
`CollapseGrid (c ': cs) a = [CollapseGrid cs a]`, Internal/Grid.hs:296). A
nested list can be ragged or the wrong length, a grid cannot, so this is a
refinement and a lawful Prism:

  _CollapsedGrid :: (VG.Vector v a, AllSizedKnown cs)
                 => Prism' (CollapseGrid cs a) (GridOf v cs a)
  _CollapsedGrid = prism' collapseGrid gridFromList

== The cost, which is real and is why this is filed separately from the
   other Prisms

Both functions carry phase-controlled INLINABLE pragmas and a RULES pragma
each -- "collapseGrid/boxed" (Internal/Grid.hs:394) and "gridFromList/boxed"
(Internal/Grid.hs:413) -- which bypass a `VG.convert` that is a vector-to-
itself copy when GHC can see `v ~ V.Vector`. The Haddock at
Internal/Grid.hs:387-393 spells out that the phase numbers were chosen so the
rule gets first refusal.

Burying either function behind a `prism'` puts a `Market`/`Choice`
dictionary between the rule's LHS and the call site, and the rules are
written `forall (g :: GridOf V.Vector cs a)` -- i.e. they match on a
concretely-typed argument. Whether they still fire through the optic is an
empirical question, not one to reason about: build with `-ddump-rule-firings`
before and after, on the boxed path, and record the answer in the issue.

If the rules stop firing, the resolution is NOT to drop the pragmas. Export
the Prism and leave both functions as the fast path, with the Haddock saying
which to reach for -- the same split the library already makes between
`indexGrid` and `gridIndex`.

`ugridFromList` (Unboxed.hs:56) is this at `U.Vector`, where the rules do not
apply anyway.

Cost: lens is already a direct dependency; the cost here is optimisation
risk, not a package.

title: Property-test every optic against its laws (the checklist, in one place)
description:
From the sized-grid-31z optics survey. The gate on everything else in it.

Every optic the survey proposes carries a law claim, and the survey found one
shipped optic that violates its laws (`asFocusedGrid`, companion bug issue) by
reading the code -- which is not a repeatable process. The claims should be
properties.

== What to check

Iso (`_CoordTuple`, `_DeltaTuple`, `_CoordCons`, `_DeltaCons`, `_SplitGrid`,
`_SplitHigherDim`, `_Transposed`, `_FocusedGrid`, `translated`):
    view i (review i b) == b
    review i (view i s) == s

Prism (`_Position`, `_GridVector`, `_CollapsedGrid`, `_WeakenedCoord`, and
the already-shipped `_Ordinal`):
    preview p (review p b) == Just b
    preview p s == Just a  ==>  review p a == s
  -- the second needs a generator that produces BOTH matching and
  -- non-matching `s`, or it checks nothing. For `_Position` that means
  -- feeding it negative and oversized Ints, not just valid ones; for
  -- `_GridVector`, vectors of the wrong length.

Lens (`slice`/`prefix`/`suffix`, `focus`, `coordHead`, `coordTail`,
`deltaHead`, `deltaTail`, `gridIndex`, `asGrid`, and whatever
`asFocusedGrid` becomes):
    view l (set l v s) == v            -- put-get, the one asFocusedGrid fails
    set l (view l s) s == s            -- get-put
    set l v' (set l v s) == set l v' s -- put-put

Traversal (`lowerDim`, `tiles`, and `each` from sized-grid-k1t):
    traverseOf t pure == pure
    fmapOf composition -- or, more practically, check that
    toListOf t is the expected partition and that
    over t f . over t g == over t (f . g)
  -- that last one is exactly what would catch someone making `gridWindows`
  -- a Traversal, so include it even though it looks redundant.

== How

`Test.Arbitrary` already exists (tests/Test/Arbitrary.hs) with generators for
the coord and grid types, and `Test.Invariant` is the natural home or model.

sized-grid-90f's verdict already proposes `quickcheck-classes` for the
instance laws it filed; check whether that lands first, since if the
dependency is being added anyway the optic laws can sit beside those tests
rather than in a separate style. quickcheck-classes does not ship optic laws,
so these are hand-written properties either way -- but they are three lines
each.

Marked as related to every optic issue rather than blocking them: writing an
optic and its property in the same commit is better than a separate pass, and
this issue exists so that the checklist is written down in one place rather
than re-derived per optic.
close_reason: Added property-based laws for shipped coordinate, delta, focused-grid, grid-access, slice, prefix, suffix, and ordinal optics; traversal laws were already covered by Test.Tiling.

title: offsetByPosition reads its KnownNat as a run-time Natural on every call
description:
The per-axis step of the checked offset, below the fold sized-grid-135 fixed.

With npOffset in place the axis-list fold unrolls and the remaining cost is all
in the step. From the Core of SizedGrid.Coord.Class at -O1:

    $woffsetByPosition
      = \ @c @n $dIsCoord $dKnownNat c1 ww ->
          case integerToInt# (integerFromNatural ($dKnownNat `cast` ...)) of ds
          { __DEFAULT ->
          case (asOrdinal $dIsCoord $fProfunctorFUN $fFunctorConst ... c1) ...

Two things per call, per axis:
  1. the axis size is recovered from a run-time Natural --- integerFromNatural
     then integerToInt# --- rather than being the literal it is at a concrete
     axis. At the call site the dictionary is 'main81 = NS 300##', so the 300 is
     right there and never folded.
  2. asOrdinal is called through the lens dictionaries ($fProfunctorFUN,
     $fFunctorConst) rather than as the coercion it is.

Compare the (.+^) path on the same shape, which folds the size to a literal:
coordPosition at '[Clamped 300, Clamped 300] is '+# (*# x3 300#) x4'.

EVIDENCE. 'offsetCoord x360000, checked, over Clamped 300x300' in bench/Main.hs
is 199 MB and 57.0 ms after sized-grid-135 (268 MB / 73.0 ms before it), against
66 bytes and 1.92 ms for 'cornerReads', which is the same 360,000 offsets over
the same coords through (.+^). Roughly 550 bytes per checked offset, and the
fold is no longer any of it.

APPROACH, unproven, measure before committing to it. offsetIsCoord's default is
offsetByPosition and the size arrives as KnownNat n on the method rather than
through the instance, so specialisation has no concrete n to fix. Worth trying:
INLINE on the default, or ordinalSize taking the size some way that constant
folds. Note that -fspecialise-aggressively did not rescue the analogous case in
sized-grid-czf, so do not assume a flag will do it.

Affects offsetCoord, offsetCoordUpTo and coordRay, which all bottom out here,
and axisSteps calls offsetIsCoord directly too --- so this is also part of the
neighbourhood cost tracked separately.
close_reason:
Fixed by a one-line INLINE on offsetByPosition (commit e53afc2, branch worktree-bw8-offsetbyposition-knownnat).

offsetCoord x360000, checked, over Clamped 300x300: 56.4 ms / 199 MB -> 6.85 ms / 35 MB. Full suite: 2 improve, 17 unchanged, no regressions. 334 tests, downstream and readme all pass.

THE DIAGNOSIS WAS RIGHT, both halves. Before, the per-axis call was an out-of-line $w$coffsetIsCoord main81 ds3 ww2 -- passing the NS 300## dictionary at run time. After, it is an inline ># x (-# 299# y1) per axis: the size folds to a literal, asOrdinal reduces to coercions instead of applications of $fProfunctorFUN and $fFunctorConst, and the Maybe becomes join points. Zero occurrences of offsetIsCoord remain in the whole benchmark's Core.

WHY INLINE WORKED HERE, given the issue warned it might not. The IsCoordList note establishes that INLINE cannot rescue a fold that is self-recursive and polymorphic in the axis list, and that -fspecialise-aggressively did not either. Neither applies: offsetByPosition is small and not recursive, and sized-grid-135 had already made the axis fold an instance method, so every per-axis call site already held a statically resolved KnownNat. The two results compose rather than conflict -- a class indexed by the axis list fixes the fold, inlining fixes the step the fold then calls directly. Worth remembering as the rule for the rest of this chain.

CHECK THE CORE FROM THE RIGHT ARTIFACT. The issue quoted $woffsetByPosition from the library's own dump, which shows the generic worker that exists for polymorphic callers and is not what a concrete call site runs. The claim only holds up read from the consumer's dump (bench/Main.dump-simpl). A stale library in a shared builddir also produced a misleading dump mid-session; the before/after was settled by building each side into its own builddir.

WHAT IS LEFT of the 35 MB is not the bounds check, which now allocates nothing -- it is the closure the benchmark's own comprehension builds per position.

FOUND ON THE WAY: sized-grid-xv4, the same run-time-Natural read still in axisBoundaryByPosition, the default axisDistanceIsCoord, and Periodic's offsetIsCoord override. Left alone deliberately: no benchmark reaches them, so the change could not be measured.

SIDE EFFECT WORTH RECORDING: extend neighbourSum 50x50 fell 8.88 ms / 28 MB -> 7.01 ms / 25 MB with the neighbourhood fold untouched, because axisSteps calls offsetIsCoord per candidate. sized-grid-5uq's recorded baseline has been updated; it was 9.02 ms / 28 MB and reading against that would now understate the fold.

title: Repo-wide comment trim: strip prose/issue-ID bloat down to code
description: Same treatment as sized-grid-00v's Mobius.hs cleanup, applied across the whole codebase (~50 .hs files, ~3800 comment lines out of ~10000 total). Haddock throughout references bead issue IDs (sized-grid-XXX) and restates design rationale that belongs in commit messages/issue history, not in the source. Strip every module down to: minimal module haddock (1 line, no issue IDs), and per-binding comments only where the WHY is genuinely non-obvious (no restating what the code does, no issue-ID cross-references). Code and behavior must not change; all tests must still pass after.
close_reason: Stripped Haddock prose and bead issue-ID references repo-wide (46 files), keeping only module haddocks and non-obvious WHY comments. 9963 -> 7021 total lines. No code logic changed; full build under -Werror and all test suites (494 tests) verified passing. Pushed on worktree-sized-grid-byi.

title: Constraint hygiene: redundant superclass constraints leak into every user signature
description:
Several instances demand more than they use, and the noise propagates to callers.

  - src/SizedGrid/Grid/Focused.hs:26-32 and :36-42
    Comonad and ComonadStore for FocusedGrid both require 'All Monoid cs, All Semigroup cs'.
    The bodies only use index and tabulate, which need AllSizedKnown + All IsCoordLifted.
    The Monoid/Semigroup constraints appear unnecessary -- verify and drop them.

  - src/SizedGrid/Coord.hs:70
        instance (All Eq cs, All Ord cs) => Ord (Coord cs)
    Eq is a superclass of Ord, but 'All' does not propagate superclasses, so callers
    must write both. Fixable with a Dict-based entailment helper.

  - src/SizedGrid/Grid/Grid.hs:1 sets -Wno-redundant-constraints for the entire module,
    which is why these are not already flagged. Remove the blanket flag; the whole
    point of -Wredundant-constraints (already in ghc-options) is to catch this.

  - AllSizedKnown vs AllGridSizeKnown vs All IsCoordLifted are three overlapping ways
    of saying 'the sizes are known'. ToJSON (Grid) uses AllGridSizeKnown + SListI while
    FromJSON (Grid) uses All IsCoordLifted, for what should be dual operations.
    Consolidate to one constraint synonym.

Measured impact on users: ../aoc/src/2025/04.hs:33 and ../aoc/src/2015/18.hs:31 both
have to carry 'KnownNat (n GHC.* n)' in signatures purely to satisfy AllSizedKnown.
The typelits-plugin issue would remove most of this; this issue covers what remains.
close_reason: Focused.hs Comonad/ComonadStore shed All Monoid/All Semigroup; blanket -Wno-redundant-constraints removed from Grid/Grid.hs with two dead constraints deleted and four soundness constraints kept behind a new 'requiring' helper so the warning stays on. Ord (Coord cs) proved unfixable (GHC cannot induct over AllF for a type variable) and is now documented in place. Constraint consolidation split out as sized-grid-qh9, blocked on h56. Verified on ghc 9.12.3 and 9.14.1.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Worked through all four bullets. Two fixed, one proved impossible, one split out.

BULLET 1 -- Focused.hs Comonad/ComonadStore. FIXED. 'All Monoid cs, All Semigroup cs'
were unnecessary on both instances, exactly as suspected: the bodies only use index and
tabulate, which need nothing beyond Grid's Representable instance. Dropped from both;
library, both test suites and both nix GHCs still build. This was the worst of the four
because Comonad is the only reason to reach for a FocusedGrid at all, so every consumer
was repeating the noise.

BULLET 3 -- the blanket -Wno-redundant-constraints on Grid/Grid.hs:1. FIXED, flag gone.
With it removed GHC reported five constraints, and they split two ways:

  Genuinely dead, removed:
    combineHigherDim  IsCoord c
    splitHigherDim    IsCoord c, KnownNat x
  IsCoord buys nothing here -- a coord's size comes from CoordNat on the IsCoordLifted
  instance, not from IsCoord, so the class could not have justified the n + m or x - y
  in those result types even in principle.

  Load-bearing, KEPT:
    dropGrid/takeGrid  n <= m
    splitHigherDim     y <= x
    gridWindows        Mod (CoordNat big) (CoordNat small) ~ 0
  These are the soundness constraints added in 7bdd829. -Wredundant-constraints only
  looks at whether the BODY uses a constraint, and these are consumed by the caller's
  types, so it flags them wrongly. Drop 'y <= x' from splitHigherDim, for instance, and
  splitting a 5-grid at 9 returns a first component typed 'c 9' holding 5 elements.

  To keep the warning switched on rather than trading one blanket suppression for
  another, those four now name what they are enforcing via a new internal helper,
  SizedGrid.Internal.Type.requiring:

      takeGrid p (Grid v) = requiring @(n <= m) $ Grid $ V.take (natVal p) v

  It is 'id' with a constraint, so it is free at runtime, and it turns an invisible
  contract into a visible one. (Its body has to build a Dict rather than being plain
  'id', or the helper's own constraint gets reported as redundant.) Note it is NOT
  named 'contract' -- Data.Constraint already exports that and Grid.hs imports it.

BULLET 2 -- 'instance (All Eq cs, All Ord cs) => Ord (Coord cs)'. NOT FIXABLE. The
issue proposes a Dict-based entailment helper; that does not work here. Tried it, GHC
9.12.3 says:

    Could not deduce 'AllF Eq cs' arising from a superclass required to satisfy
    'All Eq cs', arising from the superclasses of an instance declaration
    from the context: All Ord cs

'All c cs' expands to the type family 'AllF c cs', and reducing 'AllF Eq cs' from
'AllF Ord cs' needs induction over cs, which the solver will not do for a type variable
-- it works only for concrete lists. Data.SOP.Dict.mapAll can produce the evidence, but
as a VALUE, and superclass evidence for an instance must be discharged at declaration
time where no value is in scope. Both constraints stay; the instance now carries a
comment saying why, so nobody retries this.

BULLET 4 -- consolidating AllSizedKnown / AllGridSizeKnown / All IsCoordLifted. SPLIT
OUT as sized-grid-qh9, blocked on sized-grid-h56.

  First, part of this bullet is stale: ToJSON and FromJSON for Grid are already aligned
  (Grid.hs:135 and :153 both use AllGridSizeKnown + SListI). 7bdd829 fixed that.

  Second, the three constraints are not actually redundant with each other -- they say
  different things, and collapsing them to one synonym would over-constrain APIs like
  'Applicative (Grid cs)' that only need the total size. The real defect is narrower and
  I found the mechanism: AllSizedKnown is a CLASS, so instance resolution discharges it
  from 'KnownNat n' per element and hands back the total size as a value-level Dict,
  whereas AllGridSizeKnown is a TYPE FAMILY that expands into the user's context. That
  single difference is what puts 'KnownNat (n GHC.* n)' in ../aoc/src/2025/04.hs:33 and
  ../aoc/src/2015/18.hs:31 while the FocusedGrid signatures right below them stay clean.
  Details and the two candidate fixes are in sized-grid-qh9.

title: Add a compile-fail test harness for the size invariants
description:
Wave 02 (sized-grid-2h0) tightened takeGrid/dropGrid/splitHigherDim so that misuse is a type error rather than a silently wrong Grid. That is the right outcome, but it means the regression tests for it cannot live in the tasty suite: 'takeGrid (Proxy @9)' of a 3-grid no longer compiles, so it cannot be asserted at runtime.

Right now those cases survive only as comments in tests/Test/Invariant.hs. Nothing would catch a future loosening of the signatures.

Options:
  - 'should-not-typecheck' (uses deferred type errors; brittle)
  - a cabal 'build-type: Custom' / shell script compiling snippets and asserting failure
  - GHC's own '-fdefer-type-errors' plus a runtime catch of TypeError
  - doctest with ':t' expectations

Cases to cover:
  - takeGrid (Proxy @9) :: Grid '[Ordinal 3] -> Grid '[Ordinal 9]   (needs 9 <= 3)
  - dropGrid (Proxy @9) on a 3-grid
  - splitHigherDim remainder annotated as anything other than x - y
  - ShrinkableGrid with a window that does not fit (x + z > y + 1)
close_reason: Added tests/Test/CompileFail.hs: shells out to GHC (-isrc, -fno-code, same extensions/plugins as the library) to compile the 4 snippets under tests/compile-fail/ and assert each is rejected with the expected diagnostic. Verified the harness catches regressions by temporarily loosening takeGrid's n<=m and confirming the test fails, then reverting. -fdefer-type-errors was tried first and rejected: it was observed to swallow the entire enclosing top-level binding rather than scoping the runtime error to the ill-typed subexpression, confirming the brittleness the issue worried about.

title: AffineSpace (Coord cs) folds the axis list with a helper that cannot unroll: 88% of an offset loop
description:
Split out of sized-grid-0tj, which fixed the per-axis half and measured what was left.

360,000 offsets through a two-axis Coord allocate 126 MB after 0tj (was 143 MB). The same
360,000 offsets on a bare Clamped 300 axis allocate 94 KB. So ~88% of the cost is the
Coord layer, not the arithmetic, and 0tj's 11% is all the per-axis fix was ever worth on
this workload.

CAUSE. src/SizedGrid/Coord.hs, the AffineSpace (Coord cs) instance:

    Coord a .+^ Coord b =
        let helper :: All AffineSpace xs => NP I xs -> NP I (MapDiff xs) -> NP I xs
            helper Nil Nil                 = Nil
            helper (I x :* xs) (I y :* ys) = I (x .+^ y) :* helper xs ys
        in Coord $ helper a b

(.-.) has the identical shape. This is the self-recursive polymorphic fold that the
IsCoordList note in src/SizedGrid/Coord/Class.hs documents at length: GHC does not inline
a self-recursive binding, and each call is at a shorter list, so specialising rewrites
only the outermost call and the tail runs through a generic worker that takes the
All AffineSpace dictionary at runtime. Per axis that is dictionary-peeling thunks plus the
NP rebuild. Same defect coordPosition had; moving its fold into IsCoordList as a method
took index x90000 from 27 MB to 38 bytes.

APPROACH, and the decision it needs. The proven fix is a class indexed by the axis list so
the dictionary resolves during instance resolution:

    class All AffineSpace cs => AffineCoordList cs where
        npAdd :: NP I cs -> NP I (MapDiff cs) -> NP I cs
        npSub :: NP I cs -> NP I cs -> NP I (MapDiff cs)

with instances for '[] and (x ': xs). The per-axis step needs AffineSpace x, which
IsCoordLifted does not supply, so this cannot just be another IsCoordList method -- putting
All AffineSpace cs in the *method* signature reintroduces the runtime dictionary peel that
the class was supposed to remove.

The cost is a second breaking change: AffineSpace (Coord cs)'s instance context stops
being All AffineSpace cs. Concrete call sites are unaffected, but polymorphic code that
writes All AffineSpace cs to satisfy the instance must write AffineCoordList cs instead.
In-tree that is gameOfLife/src/Main.hs (3 signatures) and README.md. ../aoc needs checking;
0tj found it builds offsets with coordFromTuple and numeric literals, which would be safe.
Making All AffineSpace cs a superclass keeps every *use* of the instance working -- it is
only the sites that discharge it that move.

VERIFY WITH the two benchmarks 0tj added to bench/Main.hs. 'four corner reads over Clamped
300x300' is the target; 'one Clamped 300 axis (no Coord)' is the control and should not
move. Follow the before/after procedure in that file's header -- do not read against the
recorded CSV.
close_reason:
Fixed by AffineCoordList, a class indexed by the axis list (commit 059f271, branch worktree-czf-affine-coord-list). 360,000 offsets through a two-axis Coord: 28.5 ms / 126 MB -> 2.02 ms / 53 B, with the bare-axis control unmoved at 2.27 -> 2.30 ms / 94 KB. Offsetting a Coord no longer allocates. Full bench suite shows no regression: 3 improve, 15 unchanged.

The predicted breaking change did not materialise in tree, and the reason is worth keeping: All AffineSpace cs is a superclass so every USE still typechecks, and instance resolution succeeds whenever the list SHAPE is known -- including cs ~ '[x, y] with x and y variable, which is how gameOfLife writes drawWorld. Only a fully polymorphic cs that actually uses (.+^) would have to change, and nothing in tree does: the All AffineSpace cs in gameOfLife and README.lhs are redundant constraints GHC already flags (sized-grid-ior). ../aoc never names the constraint.

Split out: sized-grid-135, offsetCoord still has the old shape (extend neighbourSum unmoved at 9.17 ms / 28 MB over 20,000 offsets).
Found on the way: sized-grid-4x1, two aoc call sites do not compile against 0tj's Diff = Int -- 0tj's 'aoc is unaffected' note was reasoned from a grep, not a build.

title: _Transposed and permuted: a bijection on coordinates is a bijection on grids
description:
From the sized-grid-31z optics survey. Tier A: two Isos, one of which
generalises the other.

== transposeGrid is its own inverse

  transposeGrid :: (VG.Vector v a, VG.Vector v Int, IsCoord h, IsCoord w,
                    KnownNat x, KnownNat y, 1 <= y, 1 <= x)
                => GridOf v '[w x, h y] a -> GridOf v '[h y, w x] a    Internal/Grid.hs:515

Transposing twice is the identity, so:

  _Transposed :: (...) => Iso' (GridOf v '[w x, h y] a) (GridOf v '[h y, w x] a)
  _Transposed = iso transposeGrid transposeGrid

The constraint set is symmetric under the swap already (`1 <= x` and `1 <= y`
are both there), so the Iso needs nothing transposeGrid does not.

== The general statement: a bijection on coordinates is a bijection on grids

  permuteGrid :: (VG.Vector v a, VG.Vector v Int, IsCoordList cs)
              => (Coord cs -> Coord ds) -> GridOf v ds a -> GridOf v cs a   Internal/Grid.hs:504

`permuteGrid` takes an arbitrary function and backpermutes. If the function
is a bijection, the result is invertible; today the caller has to supply both
halves separately and nothing checks they agree.

  permuted :: (VG.Vector v a, VG.Vector v Int, IsCoordList cs, IsCoordList ds)
           => Iso' (Coord cs) (Coord ds)
           -> Iso' (GridOf v ds a) (GridOf v cs a)
  permuted i = iso (permuteGrid (view i)) (permuteGrid (review i))

Taking an `Iso'` as the argument is the point: it is the type-level statement
that the permutation is invertible, which is precisely the precondition
`permuteGrid` needs for its result to be a rearrangement rather than a
gather-with-duplicates. `_Transposed` then becomes `permuted _TransposedCoord`.

Note `permuteGrid` builds an index vector of `coordSpaceSize @cs` elements
per call (Internal/Grid.hs:512), so `permuted` costs two of those over a
round trip -- the same as writing it by hand, but easier to do accidentally.
Say so in the Haddock.

Depends on a `tranposeCoord`-shaped Iso existing on the coord side, which is
the companion naming issue (the function is currently misspelled in the
public export list).

Cost: none, lens is already a direct dependency.
close_reason: Closed

title: mapAxis as a Setter now, as a Traversal alongside adr.5
description:
From the sized-grid-31z optics survey. Tier C: free today as a Setter,
better as a Traversal, and the Traversal should wait for adr.5.

  mapAxis :: forall n -> (MapAxis n cs c, VG.Vector v x, VG.Vector v y)
          => (GridOf v '[c] x -> GridOf v '[c] y)
          -> GridOf v cs x -> GridOf v cs y                  Internal/Grid.hs:785

That is `(a -> b) -> s -> t` with `a = GridOf v '[c] x`, `b = GridOf v '[c] y`
-- a Setter's shape exactly:

  axis :: forall n -> (MapAxis n cs c, VG.Vector v x, VG.Vector v y)
       => Setter (GridOf v cs x) (GridOf v cs y) (GridOf v '[c] x) (GridOf v '[c] y)
  axis n = sets (mapAxis n)

Free, and it composes with the other setters, which the bare function does
not.

== Why not a Traversal now

A Traversal would additionally give `toListOf axis` (read the fibres),
`traverseOf` (fallible per-fibre transforms) and everything a Fold gives. It
needs the Applicative version of `mapAxisImpl` (Internal/Grid.hs:726), which
is writable -- the fibres along one axis are disjoint and cover the grid, so
the laws hold -- but the implementation goes through `mapAxisHere`
(Internal/Grid.hs:757), whose body is two `transposeFlat` passes around a
split/concat.

sized-grid-adr.5 is already open against exactly that: "mapAxis/scanAxis
transpose the whole grid twice; scanAxis loses to hand-rolled boxed, wins
unboxed". Generalising the current implementation to Applicative would mean
writing the Applicative version of a body that is about to be replaced.

So: ship the Setter now (one line, no risk), and file the Traversal as part
of adr.5's rewrite rather than ahead of it. Marked as depending on adr.5 for
that reason.

`scanAxis` needs no separate optic: it is already defined as
`scanAxis n f = mapAxis n (scanl1Grid f)` (Internal/Grid.hs:807), so with the
Setter in hand it is exactly `over (axis n) (scanl1Grid f)` and the existing
definition can be left alone or rewritten in those terms, whichever reads
better. That it falls out for free is a small piece of evidence the Setter is
carved at the right joint.

Cost: none, lens is already a direct dependency.
close_reason: Shipped 'axis n = sets (mapAxis n)' as a Setter, exported from Internal.Grid and Data.Grid.Sized, with a setterLaws helper and law tests on axis 0/1 of a 2D grid and the middle axis of a 3D one, plus unit tests that the optic reaches the same fibres mapAxis does and that scanAxis n f == over (axis n) (scanl1Grid f). scanAxis left as it was. Traversal deliberately not written: it needs an Applicative mapAxisImpl and belongs to sized-grid-adr.5's rewrite of mapAxisHere. Commit 1b216cd.

title: Offset should report where it hit the edge, not just Nothing
description:
Inspiration: `Data.Manifold.WithBoundary` in the `manifolds` package.

    (.+^|) :: m -> Needle (Interior m)
          -> Either (Boundary m, Scalar (Needle (Interior m))) (Interior m)

Read it as: either you arrived in the interior, or you hit the boundary --- and here is
WHICH boundary point you hit and HOW FAR along the displacement you got.

sized-grid's `offsetCoord` (src/SizedGrid/Coord.hs:361-382) returns `Maybe (Coord cs)`,
which throws that information away. `Nothing` says an offset left the grid but not where
it left, not on which axis, and not how many steps succeeded first.

WHY THIS MATTERS, from a real call site

../aoc/src/2024/04.hs:64-82 wants "walk three steps in direction d from c, or tell me it
ran off". Because no such operation exists, it embeds the whole coordinate into a grid
one cell larger, offsets three times there, weakens back, and drives the type-level
arithmetic by hand:

    let i, j, k :: Coord '[Periodic (n + 1), Periodic (n + 1)]
        i = strengthenCoord c .+^ d
        j = i .+^ d
        k = j .+^ d
    ... \\ plusNat @n @1 \\ leTrans @1 @n @(n + 1) \\ plusMonotone2 @n @0 @1

Three `Dict` entailments and a `mapMaybe (traverse weakenCoord)` for what is one ray
walk. Every raycasting, beam-tracing or line-of-sight problem has this shape.

PROPOSAL

Add the informative offset alongside the existing one:

    data OffGrid cs = OffGrid
      { lastInside  :: Coord cs   -- final coordinate still on the grid
      , stepsTaken  :: Int        -- how many whole steps succeeded
      }

    offsetCoordUpTo :: ... => Coord cs -> Needle (Coord cs)
                    -> Either (OffGrid cs) (Coord cs)

and derive a ray from it:

    coordRay :: ... => Coord cs -> Needle (Coord cs) -> [Coord cs]
    -- successive offsets until the grid runs out; infinite on an all-Periodic coord,
    -- so document that and let the caller `take`.

`offsetCoord` stays; it is `either (const Nothing) Just . offsetCoordUpTo` and remains the
right answer when the caller genuinely does not care where the edge was.

NOTE ON PERIODIC

A `Periodic` axis never fails, so on an all-`Periodic` coord `offsetCoordUpTo` is always
`Right` and `coordRay` never terminates. Mixed coords are the interesting case: the
bounded axis decides when the walk ends while the torus axis keeps wrapping, which is
already the semantics `offsetCoord` documents at Coord.hs:357-360.

DEPENDS ON the Needle change: this signature should be written against
`Needle (Coord cs)` from the start rather than against `Diff (Coord cs)` and then
migrated. If the Needle issue is rejected, this one is still worth doing against
`Diff (Coord cs)`.
design:
SHIPPED, with one deviation from the sketch above.

WHAT LANDED

    data OffGrid cs = OffGrid { lastInside :: Coord cs, stepsTaken :: Int }

    offsetCoordUpTo :: (All IsCoordLifted cs, AllDiffSame Integer cs)
                    => Int -> Coord cs -> Diff (Coord cs)
                    -> Either (OffGrid cs) (Coord cs)

    coordRay :: (All IsCoordLifted cs, AllDiffSame Integer cs)
             => Coord cs -> Diff (Coord cs) -> [Coord cs]

THE DEVIATION: offsetCoordUpTo carries a step count

The sketch had `offsetCoordUpTo :: Coord cs -> Needle (Coord cs) -> Either ...`. With
a single displacement and no count, the Left of a failed offset can only ever report
the coordinate it started from and zero steps --- it is `Maybe` again with an extra
allocation, and `stepsTaken` has nothing to count. The count is what makes the field
mean what OffGrid documents. Argument order follows `axisSteps`/`stepsWithin`/
`mooreNeighbours`: the radius-like number first.

The alternative considered and rejected: subdivide one displacement into its
primitive lattice steps (divide by the gcd of the components), so `offsetCoordUpTo`
keeps the two-argument shape and reports partial progress along a single `d`. It is
the closer analogue of manifolds' scalar, but it is surprising --- (2,3) would report
no partial progress and (2,4) would, for reasons about lattices rather than about
grids --- and every real call site wants a step budget instead.

Related decision: a step is a whole `d`, not a subdivision. On a lattice there is
nothing between `c` and `c .+^ d` unless `d` is a multiple of something shorter, so a
caller who wants the finer walk passes the finer `d`.

DIRECTION OF DEFINITION

`offsetCoord` stays the primitive; `offsetCoordUpTo` iterates it. The sketch had it
the other way (`offsetCoord = either (const Nothing) Just . offsetCoordUpTo`), but the
axes answer for a single displacement --- `offsetIsCoord` applies a whole `Diff` per
axis --- so the single offset is the honest bottom of the stack and counting steps is
iteration above it. The proposed relation is kept as a law and a property test on a
bounded, a torus and a mixed coord.

RAY SEMANTICS

`coordRay` excludes the start, for the reason the neighbourhoods exclude their centre:
every caller wants what is ahead, and `take k` then means "the first k cells along the
ray", shorter than k exactly when the grid ran out. It is infinite on an all-Periodic
coord and on a zero displacement (standing still never leaves, even on a bounded
coord); documented and tested by taking a prefix rather than guarded against. That
second case is easy to trip over --- an early property test hung on it.

WHERE lastInside IS AN EDGE

With a one-cell step, `lastInside` is on the boundary and `axisBoundaries . lastInside`
names the edge the walk met, which is the "which axis" the issue asked for. With a
wider step the walk can leave from the interior, so the guarantee is only "the last
coordinate that was inside". Both directions are pinned by tests.

ACCEPTANCE

Met, and verified out-of-tree. The aoc rewrite drops strengthenCoord, weakenCoord,
all three Dict entailments and the pad grid, switching the axes to Clamped --- which
is what the pad was simulating. Its documented examples still answer 18 and 9, and old
and new agree on all four answers over 300 random 12x12 grids. 2532/1941 could not be
produced directly: input/2024/04.txt is not in the repo. The patch is recorded in
sized-grid-4yw, to be applied WITH the merge to master (aoc builds against the main
checkout, not against a worktree branch).

NOTE FOR sized-grid-448 (coord + heading)

448 says to revisit "if the boundary-policy work makes 'what happens to a heading at an
edge' a question the library is already answering". It now half-does: a walker that
meets an edge gets back which edge and how far it got, which is the stop half of
stop/reflect/turn. Reflect and turn are still unmodelled, and there are still only two
consumers, so 448 stays parked.
acceptance_criteria: ../aoc/src/2024/04.hs can drop strengthenCoord/weakenCoord and its three Dict entailments (plusNat, leTrans, plusMonotone2) in favour of a single ray walk, and still produce 2532/1941.
close_reason: Shipped: OffGrid, offsetCoordUpTo and coordRay, with offsetCoordUpTo carrying a step count. aoc migration patch recorded in sized-grid-4yw.

title: Enable -Werror in CI to catch warnings on a cold cache
description:
sized-grid-ior found 8 warnings (README.lhs, tests/Main.hs) that a normal
incremental build never showed, because GHC only warns on files it actually
recompiles and the dev's local dist-newstyle was stale. A clean
'cabal build all --enable-tests --ghc-options=-fforce-recomp' rebuild today
(2026-08-18) shows those 8 are already gone -- fixed incidentally by later
refactors (e.g. sized-grid-4xh's AllSizedKnown/AllGridSizeKnown merge) -- but
nothing would have caught them at introduction time, and nothing stops the
next batch from landing silently the same way.

sized-grid-rt9's .github/workflows/ci.yml runs
'cabal build all --enable-tests --enable-benchmarks' but without -Werror, so
CI builds clean even when warnings are present -- it only ever logs them.
Adding -Werror there would have caught the original 8 at PR time regardless
of dist-newstyle caching, because -Werror promotes a warning to a build
failure for any file GHC actually recompiles; it doesn't need a cold cache to
work, it just needs the file to be rebuilt, which CI always does for changed
files.

Blocker: turning on -Werror repo-wide today breaks the build. Confirmed via
'cabal build all --enable-tests --ghc-options="-fforce-recomp -Werror"':
  - sudoko/src/Main.hs:1:1 -Wmissing-export-lists (module Main has no export list)
  - ising-example/src/Main.hs:72:1 -Wunused-top-binds (totalEnergy defined but not used)

grid-sized (lib+tests+readme), grid-atlas, and atlas-topology are all clean
under -Werror right now.

Plan:
  - fix the two example warnings above (or scope -Werror to just the library
    and test-suite components, leaving the gloss example executables out, if
    that's preferred)
  - add -Werror to the 'cabal' matrix job's build step in ci.yml (and/or to
    each package's ghc-options so `nix flake check` inherits it too)
close_reason: Baked -Werror into every package's ghc-options (grid-sized, grid-atlas, atlas-topology, gameOfLife, sudoko, ising-example) rather than as a CI-only flag, so it applies to nix flake check, the CI cabal matrix, and any local build alike -- it fires on any file GHC actually recompiles, cache or no cache. Fixed the two example warnings found while filing this issue (sudoko missing-export-lists, ising-example unused-top-binds totalEnergy) plus 4 more unused-top-binds in sudoko (rowAtPoint/columAtPoint/squareAtPoint/allValues) discovered once -Werror was actually turned on. Per user direction, wired those four into main as a demo rather than deleting the solver scaffolding; filed sized-grid-5is to write the real solver. Also hit and fixed a GHC-9.14-only deprecation (-Wpattern-namespace-specifier on Data.Grid.Sized.Coord's export list) that only nix flake check's ghc914 build surfaced -- silenced via a per-version cabal conditional since the 'data' keyword replacement doesn't parse on 9.10/9.12. Verified clean: nix flake check passes, full cabal test suite (485+4+... tests) passes.

title: ising-example and gameOfLife cannot use UGrid: they are comonadic over sum types
description:
Correction to a premise carried through sized-grid-up6. Its notes repeatedly named
ising-example and gameOfLife as 'the stronger cases' for an unboxed grid -- 'bulk map/zip over
numeric grids end to end'. Read at implementation time, they are neither.

Both are comonadic cellular automata over two-constructor sum types:

  ising-example/src/Main.hs:  data Spin = Up | Down
  gameOfLife/src/Main.hs:     data TileState = Alive | Dead

Two independent blockers, either sufficient:

1. Neither element type has an Unbox instance, and neither example writes one. Data.Vector.Unboxed
   cannot hold them as they stand.

2. More fundamentally, both are written through FocusedGrid and extend:
     totalEnergy po = sum . extend (singleEnergy po) . view asFocusedGrid
     applyRule       = over asFocusedGrid ...
   'duplicate' on FocusedGrid is 'tabulate (FocusedGrid g)' -- a grid OF grids -- and a grid is
   never an unboxed element. The comonadic formulation is structurally boxed. ising also uses
   'sequence $ pure getRandom' (Traversable + Applicative, both unavailable unboxed) and
   'gridIndex c %~ flipSpin', a single-cell update, which up6 measured as gaining nothing.

So the genuine beneficiary of the unboxed representation is the summed-area-table shape --
../aoc/src/2018/11.hs -- and workloads like it, not these two.

Worth doing, if anything: derive Unbox for one of these element types via Word8 and convert the
rule to a non-comonadic bulk formulation, purely to have an in-tree example of the unboxed API on
something other than Int. That is an example-writing task, not a library one, hence low priority.
Do not use these two as justification for further unboxing work without re-reading them.
close_reason: gameOfLife's TileState now derives Unbox via Word8 (DerivingVia/As); applyRule rewritten as a non-comonadic imapGrid+indexGrid bulk pass over UGrid, replacing the extend/FocusedGrid formulation. Full app (tick, mouse edit, render) runs on UGrid. Tests pass (485/485), all packages build. ising-example untouched -- gameOfLife alone satisfies the 'one in-tree unboxed example beyond Int' ask.

title: Missing API: first-class axis selector for mapAxis/scanAxis
description:
Split out of sized-grid-7uj. Sealing the Grid constructor covered every bullet of that issue except the last: 'add the length-preserving combinators people actually want: mapAxis / scanAxis / prefix sums along a dimension'.

What landed instead was 'scanl1Grid', a row-major scan over the whole grid, which composes with the existing 'mapLowerDim' to give per-row scans:

    runIdentity (mapLowerDim (Identity . scanl1Grid (+)) g)

That is enough to retire the reach-through at ../aoc/src/2018/11.hs:31, but only because the summed-area-table build-up transposes between passes:

    transposeGrid . rowPrefix . transposeGrid . rowPrefix

so the 'other' axis is reached by rotating the grid rather than by naming the axis. That works for 2D and gets awkward past it -- there is no transposeGrid for an arbitrary pair of dimensions, only the 2D one.

What is missing is a way to name a dimension and act along it:

    mapAxis  :: <axis selector> -> (Grid '[c n] a -> Grid '[c n] b) -> Grid cs a -> Grid cs b
    scanAxis :: <axis selector> -> (a -> a -> a) -> Grid cs a -> Grid cs a

The design question that stopped this landing with 7uj is the selector itself: a type-level index into cs, with the machinery to prove the resulting slice type. Worth doing only if a second consumer wants it -- one 2D call site does not justify the type-level apparatus.
notes:
Implemented mapAxis/scanAxis in Data.Grid.Sized.Internal.Grid, exported from Data.Grid.Sized. Proceeding without waiting for a second consumer, per explicit direction -- the gate in this issue's own description is deliberately not being honoured here.

Axis selector: a Nat, resolved through a new `MapAxis (n :: Nat) (cs :: [Type]) (c :: Type) | n cs -> c` class (fundep-determined axis type, not an associated type family -- the associated-type version hit "Conflicting family instance declarations" between the n=0 and n>0 OVERLAPPING/OVERLAPPABLE instances, because associated-type equations are checked for confluence independently of instance overlap resolution; plain unification through nested instance resolution has no such check).

Recursion: peels outer axes one at a time via mapLowerDim (n>0 case) until the target axis is outermost, then mapAxisHere transposes it against everything else taken as a single block (transposeFlat, a new raw-index-arithmetic generalisation of what transposeGrid does via coordinates), chunks, applies f, and transposes back. Falls back to applying f directly with no transpose when the target axis is already the sole/innermost axis (MaxCoordSize as == 1) -- without that fast path, scanAxis on the last axis of a 300x300 grid cost 2.2x what mapLowerDim . scanl1Grid does, all in wasted no-op transpose copies.

Verified against the untyped-plugin downstream test suite (tests-downstream/Main.hs) that MapAxis instance resolution needs no ghc-typelits-natnormalise/knownnat -- concrete-literal Nat arithmetic (n - 1) resolves without them.

Benchmarked in bench/Main.hs (satBuildAxis) against the existing transpose-trick satBuild: the inner-axis pass is free (fast path), the outer-axis pass (genuine transpose) measured ~25% slower boxed, unaffected/slightly faster unboxed -- documented honestly in both the bench comment and ChangeLog rather than claimed as free.

Tests added to tests/Test/Invariant.hs: well-sizedness on a 3-axis grid at all three positions, and correctness against hand-computed expected grids for scanAxis 0/1/2 on a 2x3x2 grid plus agreement with mapLowerDim . scanl1Grid on 2D.
close_reason: Implemented mapAxis/scanAxis; see notes for design and perf tradeoffs

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Gate re-checked 2026-08-12 and it is still not met. Swept ../aoc for any axis-wise consumer:

    grep -rnE 'scanl1Grid|mapLowerDim|transposeGrid|scanAxis|mapAxis' --include='*.hs' ../aoc

returns exactly two lines, both in the same function, both the known 2D call site:

    src/2018/11.hs:27  makeSAT = transposeGrid . rowPrefix . transposeGrid . rowPrefix . tabulate . power
    src/2018/11.hs:29    rowPrefix = runIdentity . mapLowerDim (Identity . scanl1Grid (+))

Still one consumer, still 2D, still served by the transpose trick. The issue's own standard -- 'worth doing only if a second consumer wants it; one 2D call site does not justify the type-level apparatus' -- says do not build it yet. Deferring rather than closing: the design question is real and the issue is the right place to hold it. Reopen when a 3D+ or second axis-wise consumer appears.

title: Atlas/mosaic: multi-chart grids glued by typed edge transitions
description:
A grid assumes one coordinate system covering one rectangular space. An atlas
(or mosaic) drops that: space is a collection of charts glued along their edges
by transition rules.

    coordinate  =  (ChartId, Coord cs)
    step        =  stay in chart, OR cross a seam into another chart,
                   arriving at a transformed local coordinate with a
                   transformed frame

This is what the cube map, the hexagonal mesh, the multi-room dungeon and the
hyperbolic tiling all are, and none of them is expressible as a boundary policy
on a single `Coord cs` -- see the separable/non-separable issue for why.

WHAT IT REUSES

Everything. A chart is a `Grid cs a`, indexed exactly as now, with all the
unrolling work intact. The atlas layer sits above `index` and decides WHICH
grid and WHICH coordinate before touching a vector. Nothing in
Internal/Grid.hs needs to change, and the vector invariant is untouched.

`gridTiles` (Internal/Grid.hs:543) already cuts a grid into disjoint tiles. It
is the degenerate atlas: same-shaped charts, glued in a line, identity
transitions. That is a good first target -- an atlas whose transitions are all
identity must be observationally equal to the grid it came from, which is a
free property test.

SHAPE OF THE THING

  * Charts may differ in axis type but probably not in shape, at least at
    first. Heterogeneous chart shapes are a second problem.
  * The transition is the seam rule from the sibling issue: destination chart,
    coordinate map, frame transform.
  * A cube map is 6 charts with a fixed D4 transition table. That is the
    smallest interesting non-trivial atlas and it is the one to build first,
    because the answers are all checkable by hand.

PACKAGING

Strong preference for a separate package (`grid-atlas`) depending on
`grid-sized`, not a module inside it. Reasons:

  * grid-sized has a stated thesis -- the coordinate type is the boundary
    policy -- and the atlas is explicitly the layer for the policies that
    thesis cannot express. Keeping them apart keeps both statements true.
  * It cannot destabilise the measured performance work.
  * If the atlas turns out to be the interesting library, it has a fast tested
    tile layer underneath. If it does not, nothing was lost.

NOT SCHEDULED. This is the endpoint, and the two issues it depends on are the
actual work.
notes:
WHY THIS IS THE QUIVER/fgl CONNECTION (from the decomposition-comonad transcript, 2026-08-16).

Quiver and fgl decompose a graph into a Context -- inbound edges, label, outbound edges -- and the rest of the graph. They STORE the edges, because a graph's topology is arbitrary and there is nothing else to do with it.

A grid never stores its edges. Adjacency is COMPUTED from the coordinate, by the boundary policy: neighbours c is derived, not looked up. That is the whole reason Grid cs a can be a flat vector with no per-cell overhead, and it is what makes this library fast.

An atlas is exactly the point where that stops being true. A transition table -- which chart, which coordinate map, which frame element -- is topology that CANNOT be computed from a coordinate, so it has to be stored. That is the same move fgl makes, and it is the first thing in this design that genuinely resembles a graph library rather than an array library.

So the progression is:

    Grid       adjacency computed from geometry, zero storage
    Atlas      adjacency computed WITHIN a chart, stored BETWEEN charts
    Quiver     adjacency stored everywhere

The atlas is the middle term, and it is interesting precisely because it keeps the fast computed case inside each chart and pays for storage only at the seams. That is a better argument for building it than 'Mobius strips are cool', and it should be the framing in any writeup.
close_reason: Shipped v1: new sibling package grid-atlas (grid-atlas/grid-atlas.cabal, added to cabal.project) with Data.Grid.Atlas, restoring gridTiles's own disjoint list as one addressable (ChartId, Coord cs) structure -- Atlas cs k a (sealed newtype over a Vector of Grid cs a), AtlasCoord cs k = (Ordinal k, Coord cs), atlasFromTiles (smart constructor, k fixed to CoordNat big Div CoordNat small at the type level), atlasIndex (total lookup), atlasOffsetHead (steps the tiled axis, crossing into the neighbouring chart on overflow, Nothing at the atlas's own two ends; always the head axis, matching gridTiles's own restriction). Verified: cabal build all, cabal test grid-atlas (exhaustive equivalence check against index on the untiled grid plus a 100-case QuickCheck property on atlasOffsetHead), cabal test grid-sized (473 tests, unaffected), cabal haddock grid-atlas (100% coverage). Deliberately NOT built: heterogeneous chart shapes, a general seam-transition table, any frame transform, and the cube map itself -- filed as sized-grid-68j (blocked on this issue), which is also where sized-grid-ts4 (is this a grid-independent manifold library) gets its second data point.

title: Path is not Offset: relative movement is order-dependent once a seam transforms the frame
description:
`Diff (Coord cs) = Coord (MapDiff cs)` is a displacement: one signed Int per
axis, added componentwise. That is the right representation for a flat space
and it is what the library has (Coord.hs:328).

It is NOT sufficient once a seam transforms the frame, and that is the
representation question sized-grid-448 has been blocked on.

THE PROBLEM

On a flat grid, `N` then `E` then `E` collapses to the displacement (+2, -1).
The order does not matter and neither does the route.

Cross a Mobius seam and it does. Going east twice and then north is not the
same as north then east twice, because the first east-crossing flipped what
"north" means. A displacement cannot record that; it has already summed.

So there are two distinct notions of relative movement and the library
currently has only one:

  Offset / Needle    Coord (MapDiff cs)      commutative, order-free.
                                             Correct exactly on the separable
                                             policies.

  Path               a sequence of steps      order-dependent. The steps are
                                             elementary moves, and each one is
                                             resolved -- and may transform the
                                             frame -- before the next is taken.

`coordRay` (Coord.hs:581) already walks step-by-step rather than summing, so
the library has a path-shaped operation without a path type. That is the hint
this is real: `coordRay c d` cannot be `c .+^ (n *^ d)` on anything with a
seam, and today it is only accidentally fine because nothing has a seam yet.

WHY THIS BLOCKS EVERYTHING ELSE

sized-grid-448 says a heading is "most naturally `Needle (Coord cs)` restricted
to unit steps". That is right on separable policies and wrong on the rest: on a
seam, a heading is not a needle, it is a needle PLUS the frame it is expressed
in. Which is the pair a path carries implicitly and a displacement discards.

So the order is:
    this issue (what is a relative movement?)
      -> the seam rule (what does an edge do to it?)
        -> sized-grid-448 (a walker that carries one)
          -> atlas (charts glued by seams)

DESIGN CONSTRAINTS

  * Do not throw the type-level dimensional structure away. Whatever a Path is,
    it is indexed by `cs` the way `Coord cs` is. A `[Direction]` over an
    untyped list would lose what the whole library is for.
  * A Path must collapse to an Offset where the space is flat, and that
    collapse should be the definition of "this policy is separable" -- which
    ties this back to the sibling issue and gives the separability claim an
    operational meaning rather than a descriptive one.
  * Watch the cost. The offset path is the measured hot path (see the
    unrolling notes in Coord/Class.hs); a Path representation that allocates
    per step would be a real regression for every existing caller. The likely
    answer is that Path is a separate type used only where a seam exists, and
    `Coord cs` keeps its displacement API untouched.
close_reason: Implemented Path cs (src/Data/Grid/Sized/Coord.hs): an ordered list of Diff (Coord cs) steps, with walkPath resolving them one at a time through offsetCoord and pathOffset giving the collapse to a single displacement. Documented precisely where the collapse holds (no wall interrupts) vs. where it doesn't yet (a seam transforming the frame, sized-grid-o1n, not implemented) vs. a third, orthogonal case that already existed (a wall blocking a route even when it doesn't block the net displacement -- demonstrated in tests/Test/Path.hs). Path carries an identity frame transform today since nothing produces anything else; it exists so o1n has somewhere to attach one. Unblocks o1n, sized-grid-yws (tracePath), sized-grid-448.

title: _WeakenedCoord: strengthen/weaken is a Prism at three levels, with a class-indexing wrinkle
description:
From the sized-grid-31z optics survey. Tier B: a genuine Prism, at three
levels, and a friction point in how the classes are indexed.

The pattern is the same each time: widening is total, narrowing is checked,
and they agree on the overlap.

  Ordinal (Ordinal.hs:200, 202):
    strengthenOrdinal :: (KnownNat m, n <= m) => Ordinal n -> Ordinal m
    weakenOrdinal     :: KnownNat m => Ordinal n -> Maybe (Ordinal m)
      ==> _Strengthened :: (KnownNat n, KnownNat m, n <= m)
                        => Prism' (Ordinal m) (Ordinal n)

  Axis (Coord/Class.hs:88, 91):
    strengthenIsCoord :: (KnownNat m, n <= m) => c n -> c m
    weakenIsCoord     :: KnownNat m => c n -> Maybe (c m)
      ==> Prism' (c m) (c n) given n <= m

  Coord list (Coord.hs:811, 829):
    class WeakenCoord as bs where weakenCoord :: Coord as -> Maybe (Coord bs)
    class StrengthenCoord as bs where strengthenCoord :: Coord as -> Coord bs
      ==> _WeakenedCoord :: (StrengthenCoord as bs, WeakenCoord bs as)
                         => Prism' (Coord bs) (Coord as)

Laws: `weaken (strengthen c) = Just c` because strengthening does not change
the index, only the type's claim about its bound; and `weaken c = Just c'
==> strengthen c' = c` for the same reason. `strengthenOrdinal`'s own
Haddock states the argument: "i < n and n <= m give i < m".

== The friction, which should be recorded whether or not it is fixed here

The two classes are both indexed `as bs` meaning "from as to bs", so the
Prism needs `StrengthenCoord as bs` AND `WeakenCoord bs as` -- the same two
type lists in opposite orders in the two constraints. That reads badly and
will read worse at a call site with a type error in it.

Options, in order of preference:
  1. Leave the classes alone and eat the two-constraint signature. Cheapest,
     and the awkwardness is confined to one type signature in the library.
  2. Add a single `CoordEmbeds small big` class with both methods and a
     default implementation of each in terms of the existing classes. Better
     call sites, one more class in an API that already has a lot of them.
  3. Re-index one of the two classes. Breaking, and the current naming
     ("weaken as into bs") is defensible on its own terms.

Take (1) unless writing it makes a case for (2).

What it buys: `bigCoord ^? _WeakenedCoord` is "is this coordinate of the big
grid also a coordinate of the small one", which is the interesting half of
sub-grid work, and `review` is the embedding. Composes with `_Position`
(companion issue) to go straight from a raw index in one space to a coord in
another.

Cost: none, lens is already a direct dependency.
close_reason: Implemented the requested lawful optics, renamed _WrappedCoord to _CoordAxes, and validated tests.

title: Named type aliases for common separable coord products (Torus, Cylinder, ...)
description: sized-grid-3u1's doc note on IsCoordList calls out that every product of separable axes is free: `'[Periodic 10, Clamped 5]` is a cylinder, `'[Periodic w, Periodic h]` a torus. Consider adding named type aliases in Coord.hs for the common cases (e.g. `type Torus w h = Coord '[Periodic w, Periodic h]`, `type Cylinder w h = Coord '[Periodic w, Clamped h]`) so callers can name the topology instead of spelling out the axis list. Pure sugar -- no new capability -- so scope and naming need a pass before committing to public API surface.
design:
Design discussion (2026-08-18), before implementing:

1. Alias the axis list (`cs :: [Type]`), not `Coord` directly.
   `Grid`, `FocusedGrid`, and `Coord` are all parametric over the same
   `cs :: [Type]` (see `GridOf v (cs :: [Type]) a`, Internal/Grid.hs:162).
   aoc call sites spell out the axis list at `Grid`/`FocusedGrid`/`Coord`
   alike, so `type Torus w h = Coord '[...]` only sugars the minority of
   `Coord`-typed signatures. Prefer:

     type TorusAxes w h    = '[Periodic w, Periodic h]
     type CylinderAxes w h = '[Periodic w, Clamped h]

   so it drops into `Grid (TorusAxes w h) Cell`, `Coord (TorusAxes w h)`,
   `FocusedGrid (TorusAxes w h) Cell` uniformly.

2. Cylinder-style (mixed) names are inherently 2D-only and don't generalize.
   Past two axes, "which axes wrap" has to be stated per-axis anyway, which
   is exactly the axis list the alias was meant to save writing out. Don't
   imply a general pattern -- scope the mixed-product aliases explicitly to
   the 2-axis case in the haddock.

3. Torus *does* generalize to n dimensions (every axis periodic is a
   coherent n-torus, e.g. periodic boundary conditions in a 3D sim). If
   that's wanted, it needs a type family over a `[Nat]` list rather than a
   fixed 2-arg synonym:

     type family MapPeriodic (ns :: [Nat]) :: [Type] where ...
     type TorusAxesN ns = MapPeriodic ns

   This is more machinery than a plain `type` synonym -- treat it as a
   separate decision from the 2D aliases, not a default inclusion.

4. Naming convention still needs pinning down before committing to public
   API surface: for `CylinderAxes w h`, which parameter is the wrapping
   (circumference) axis and which is the clamped one? Document the
   convention explicitly wherever the alias is defined.

Net: scope this issue to the 2D axis-list aliases (TorusAxes/CylinderAxes)
as the concrete deliverable; the n-D torus type family is an optional
follow-on, not bundled in.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
A reason these aliases could carry a property rather than only a name, if
wanted later. Recording it here rather than filing an issue, because it is
speculative and should not be built before a caller wants it.

Only Periodic's (.+^) is a total group action. Clamped/Reflective/Reflect101
are retractions: measured at n=7 over 567 (p,u,v), (p .+^ u) .+^ v ==
p .+^ (u+v) holds 567/567 for Periodic but 487/567, 407/567, 407/567 for the
others -- and 269/269 for all four when restricted to routes no wall
interrupts. See sized-grid-8nz for why this is forced by the Z^n/G structure
(translations descend to the quotient only when G commutes with them) and so
cannot be fixed.

That means TorusAxes is exactly the case where pathOffset fuses
unconditionally and step order does not matter, which is precisely what
tests/Test/Path.hs 'collapseTests' already checks on '[Periodic 5, Periodic 5]
and 'wallTests' shows failing on '[Clamped 5, Clamped 5].

If that distinction is ever wanted in a type rather than in a test, the shape
is an empty marker class, not a newtype and not a type synonym:

    class IsCoord c => Boundaryless c
    instance Boundaryless Periodic

It is the type-level form of Periodic's existing axisBoundaryIsCoord _ =
Nothing, costs nothing at run time, and is open to any future
translation-quotient axis. Then All Boundaryless cs on a fusion-dependent
signature means "summing the path first is safe", and TorusAxes satisfies it
by construction.

Two non-options, for the record:
  - A type synonym CANNOT carry a distinct instance. Verified on GHC 9.12.3:
    'type Torus n = Periodic n' plus separate instances for Torus and Periodic
    is rejected as "Duplicate instance declarations". Synonyms are transparent,
    so TypeSynonymInstances only lets you WRITE a synonym in an instance head;
    it resolves to the same instance and gives no discriminating power. This
    does not affect the aliases proposed in this issue, which are pure naming
    -- it only rules out hanging behaviour off them.
  - A newtype would work, but wraps the type that is already correct and adds
    coercion noise at every call site to express what the empty class
    expresses for free. Newtypes earn their keep when one representation needs
    two behaviours (Sum/Product); Periodic has one behaviour and it is the
    right one.

Not proposed now: ../aoc uses neither pathOffset nor walkPath, so nothing is
currently asking for the guarantee to be type-level.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Correction to the Boundaryless sketch in the comment above, and where it went.

The sketch's `All Boundaryless cs` does not typecheck with the class declared
at the container kind. IsCoord is indexed by Nat -> Type, but cs :: [Type]
holds Periodic 10, not Periodic. GHC 9.12.3:

    Couldn't match kind 'Nat -> *' with '*'
    Expected kind '[*]', but 'cs' has kind '[Nat -> *]'

The class has to sit at kind Type, mirroring the IsCoord / IsCoordLifted
split. A marker class has no methods with n quantified, so one lifted class
suffices -- no container-level twin is needed.

Also, the closing "nothing is currently asking for it" is not by itself a
reason to defer: the library is meant to serve consumers not yet thought of.
The property does earn its keep independent of ../aoc, because it changes a
type rather than only documenting one -- walkPath goes from Maybe (Coord cs)
to Coord cs on a boundaryless axis list.

Split out to sized-grid-2r3 with the corrected shape, its laws, and measured
evidence (3360/3360 fusion agreement at '[Periodic 5, Periodic 7]). This
issue stays scoped to the naming aliases; TorusAxes satisfies All Boundaryless
by construction and CylinderAxes does not, which is the sharpest thing those
aliases could come to mean.
