title: Periodic's Enum wraps modulo n-1, so toEnum 2 :: Periodic 3 is 0
description:
src/SizedGrid/Coord/Periodic.hs:42-44

    toEnum x = Periodic $ fromJust $ numToOrdinal $
        (fromIntegral x) `mod` (maxCoordSize (Proxy @(Periodic n)))

'maxCoordSize' is natVal - 1, not natVal, so the period is one short. Every
other operation in the module uses 'maxCoordSize + 1' correctly, so it is the
only place with the off-by-one.

Consequences: fromEnum . toEnum is not the identity on the type's own range
(toEnum 4 :: Periodic 5 == 0), and toEnum 3,4,5 :: Periodic 3 gives [1,0,1]
rather than [0,1,2]. Not caught before because the coordinate enumeration path
('allCoordLike') goes through Ordinal's Enum, not Periodic's, and HardWrap's is
derived from Ordinal's.

Found while rewriting these lines for sized-grid-upo.
acceptance_criteria: fromEnum . toEnum == id on [0, n); toEnum wraps with period n. Regression test in tests/Test/Ordinal.hs.
close_reason: Fixed in commit 'Make Ordinal a newtype over Int' on branch worktree-ordinal-int; 100 tests pass, zero warnings

title: -O2 on the library silently strips unsafeOrdinal's assert unless -fno-ignore-asserts is restated after it
description:
Measured under sized-grid-adr.6. Adding -O2 to the library re-enables -fignore-asserts, because -O implies it and the last flag on the command line wins. The library's deliberate -fno-ignore-asserts (sized-grid-6os) is written before any optimisation flag cabal appends, so a naive 'ghc-options: -O2' silently defeats it.

Evidence: a downstream consumer calling 'unsafeOrdinal 99 :: Ordinal 5' and forcing it:
  base (-O1, -fno-ignore-asserts)          -> ASSERT FIRED
  -O2 appended after                       -> NO ASSERT: got 99
  -fexpose-all-unfoldings only             -> ASSERT FIRED
  -O2 + unfolding flags appended after     -> NO ASSERT: got 99
  -O2 with -fno-ignore-asserts restated last -> ASSERT FIRED

Fix: whenever an optimisation flag is added to the library stanza, -fno-ignore-asserts must come after it. Anyone adding -O2 later in a cabal.project 'package grid-sized' stanza reintroduces the bug, since project ghc-options are appended after the .cabal's.
close_reason: Closed

title: (BUG) The readme test-suite does not compile: README.md still uses asFocusedGrid
description:
c0bc2df dropped asFocusedGrid from IsGrid (sized-grid-3au) but left README.md:144 using it:

  applyRule rule = over asFocusedGrid $
      extend $ \fg -> rule (extract fg) $ map (\p -> peek p fg) $
          neighbours $ pos fg

README.lhs is a symlink to README.md and is the readme test-suite's main-is,
so this is a build failure, not a stale doc:

  README.lhs:144:23: error: [GHC-88464] Variable not in scope: asFocusedGrid

CI's matrix job runs 'cabal build all --enable-tests --enable-benchmarks'
(.github/workflows/ci.yml:146), so master is red on this today. Found while
working sized-grid-djh; nothing in that change touches it, and the failure
reproduces on c0bc2df alone.

applyRule is polymorphic over 'grid cs' via IsGrid, so the replacement has to
go through asGrid, which survived: focus the grid, extend, take the grid back.
The working tree at the time this was filed had an uncommitted
'focusedAtZero :: IsCoordList cs => Grid cs a -> FocusedGrid cs a' in
Focused.hs, which is what that rewrite wants:

  applyRule rule = over asGrid (focusedGrid . extend step . focusedAtZero)

Whether focusedAtZero ships is the open question -- it is the same 'focus at
the origin because there is nowhere else to start' that asFocusedGrid was
criticised for hiding, but as a named function rather than a lens it is
honest about it.
close_reason: i fixed it

title: Property-test that zeroPosition agrees with mempty/zeroV where both exist
description:
Surfaced while answering a question about whether a standard "zero"
typeclass (Monoid, AdditiveGroup, etc.) could replace IsCoord.zeroPosition.

IsCoord.zeroPosition is the only zero-like operation every axis type
(Clamped, Periodic, Reflective, Reflect101, Ordinal) honestly implements.
Monoid's mempty only exists for Clamped and Periodic; AdditiveGroup's
zeroV only exists for Periodic (deliberately -- Clamped saturates instead
of wrapping, so it has no additive inverse and would be dishonest as a
group, the same reason asFocusedGrid was unlawful, sized-grid-3au).

Coord/Class.hs documents the relationship with a default:

    zeroPosition :: (1 <= n, KnownNat n) => c n
    default zeroPosition :: Monoid (c n) => c n
    zeroPosition = mempty

but nothing checks that an instance which defines zeroPosition
explicitly (or picks up a Monoid default) actually agrees with mempty
and zeroV on the axes where more than one of these is defined:

  - Clamped n: has both zeroPosition and Monoid -- check zeroPosition == mempty
  - Periodic n: has zeroPosition, Monoid, and AdditiveGroup -- check
    zeroPosition == mempty == zeroV

This is a cheap addition to isCoordLaws in Test/Utils.hs (or a sibling
helper it's composed with), gated on the relevant Monoid/AdditiveGroup
constraints so it only runs where applicable.
close_reason: Closed

title: Is the atlas/seam layer a general discrete-manifold library, not a grid-specific one?
description:
sized-grid-fh2 (atlas: charts glued by seam transitions), sized-grid-o1n (seam
rule: boundary resolution returns a coordinate AND a frame transform) and
sized-grid-1bm (space-group framing: grid space = Z^n/G) together describe
something that doesn't actually mention cell contents anywhere load-bearing:

  * ChartId + Coord cs is a coordinate on a discrete space built from charts.
  * A seam is a transition (ChartId, Coord) -> (ChartId, Coord) plus a frame
    transform, i.e. an element of a groupoid of chart-gluings.
  * Z^n/G (sized-grid-1bm) already states the single-chart case as a quotient
    by a group; the multi-chart atlas is the same idea one level up -- a
    manifold built from charts and transition functions, which is exactly the
    textbook definition of a manifold's atlas, just discrete.

None of that needs `Grid cs a` specifically. A chart could be any
Representable/indexed structure, or nothing at all (bare coordinate topology
with no payload, useful for pathfinding/graph problems). grid-atlas v1 is
being built AS a grid-specific instantiation on purpose -- concrete and
checkable beats an abstracted-too-early library -- but the question is real:
once there's a second concrete consumer (the cube map, or something from
../aoc), does the ChartId/Seam/transition-table machinery want to be pulled
out into its own package with no grid-sized dependency, something like a
'manifold' or 'atlas-topology' library that grid-atlas (and potentially
non-grid consumers) depend on?

NOT to be resolved now. Revisit once grid-atlas has at least two concrete
atlases built (the degenerate/tiled one and the cube map) -- that is the
minimum evidence needed to see which parts of the design are actually
grid-independent versus which only look that way with one example.
close_reason: Resolved via decision sized-grid-jtt: evidence bar met (two atlases exist), but no real non-grid consumer exists to drive an extraction, so machinery stays in grid-atlas until one does.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
The second data point this issue asked for now exists: sized-grid-68j (cube map, Data.Grid.Atlas.CubeMap) shipped alongside grid-atlas v1's tiled atlas. Both are grid-specific instantiations, so the extraction question can now actually be compared against two real designs instead of one:

- Tiled atlas (fh2): AtlasCoord = (Ordinal k, Coord cs), transitions are all identity, atlasOffsetHead only ever moves the head axis.
- Cube map (68j): AtlasCoord = (Ordinal 6, Coord cs) with cs fixed to '[Ordinal n, Ordinal n], transitions are a hand-written 24-entry table keyed on Face/Axis/Extremum, cubeStep applies a coordinate remap AND a heading frame transform.

What's grid-independent in the cube map's design, on this evidence: Face/Axis/Extremum/Heading and cubeSeam's shape (source seam -> destination seam + orientation bit) don't mention Grid or cell contents anywhere load-bearing -- a chart could be any Representable, or nothing. What's still grid-specific: cubeAtlas and cubeStep both hard-code cs = '[Ordinal n, Ordinal n] and go through Atlas/AtlasCoord.

Not resolving the extraction question itself here -- that's still a real design decision (new package vs. staying put) worth deciding deliberately rather than as a side effect of closing 68j. Flagging that the evidence bar this issue set is now met.

title: Grid is boxed-vector only; no unboxed/storable representation for numeric grids
description:
src/SizedGrid/Grid/Grid.hs:40 hardcodes Data.Vector (boxed).

For the numeric workloads this library is aimed at, that is the wrong default:
  - ising-example/src/Main.hs is a Monte Carlo spin simulation
  - gameOfLife/src/Main.hs is a cellular automaton
  - ../aoc/src/2018/11.hs builds a 300x300 Int summed-area table
All of these want Data.Vector.Unboxed and get boxed Ints with a pointer chase each.

The complication: Functor/Applicative/Monad/Representable/Traversable all require the
element type to be unconstrained, so Grid cannot simply switch to Unboxed.

Options:
  1. Parameterise over the vector type:
       newtype GridOf v (cs :: [Type]) a = GridOf (v a)
       type Grid = GridOf V.Vector
     Keep the current instances for the boxed version; give the unboxed version the
     instances it can support (Foldable-like ops via a Vector.Generic constraint,
     no Functor). Costs an extra type parameter in every signature.
  2. Leave Grid boxed and add a separate SizedGrid.Grid.Unboxed with a monomorphic
     API (map/zipWith/fold/index taking Unbox constraints). Less elegant, far less
     disruptive, and covers the actual use cases.

Recommend option 2 first -- it is additive and non-breaking. Revisit 1 only if the
duplication becomes painful.

Prerequisite either way: benchmarks, so the win is measured rather than assumed.
close_reason: Closed

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Baseline landed (sized-grid-amf). Relevant figure for the unboxed-Grid case: a 300x300
Grid of Int costs 93 MB of allocation to build via tabulate and 72 MB to read back via
index over allCoord, against a true payload under 1 MB. Most of that is Ordinal and
Coord boxing rather than the vector itself, so sized-grid-upo should land first --
switching the vector to unboxed cannot help while every element access still constructs
a boxed Coord. Benchmarks to watch: 'tabulate 300x300', 'index x90000' and 'fmap
300x300' in bench/Main.hs.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Unblocked in principle by the sized-grid-upo work: Ordinal is now a newtype over
Int, so a Coord's components are machine words rather than GADTs carrying
dictionaries. That was the stated prerequisite for an unboxed or storable Grid.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Measure-first spike (bench-spike/, branch worktree-up6-measure-unboxed, ghc 9.12.3 aarch64-darwin).
Minimal UGrid over Data.Vector.Unboxed vs the real Grid, same shapes, same workloads, both
sides through coordPosition/allCoord so the coord machinery cancels.

  operation (300x300 Int)   boxed              unboxed            delta
  tabulate                  14.2 ms / 20 MB    1.90 ms / 9.6 MB   7.5x faster
  index x90000              765 us  / 26 B     751 us  / 41 B     none
  map then sum              1.52 ms / 4.1 MB   92.5 us / 18 B     16x faster
  foldl'                    312 us             86.8 us            3.6x faster
  row prefix scanl1         1.68 ms / 4.2 MB   845 us  / 5.5 MB   2x faster
  transpose                 14.6 ms / 18 MB    2.24 ms / 9.6 MB   6.5x faster
  SAT build (2018/11)       57.3 ms / 64 MB    13.3 ms / 40 MB    4.3x faster
  SAT solve, 360k reads     35.2 ms / 157 MB   36.4 ms / 157 MB   none

Conclusion: the win is real but it is NOT where up6's description assumed. It is entirely in
BULK operations that touch the vector wholesale (3.6x-16x). Per-coordinate access wins exactly
nothing -- 'index' and the SAT solve are identical to within noise, because their cost is the
Coord arithmetic and not the vector read.

That settles the API shape: an unboxed grid wants map/zipWith/fold/scanl1/tabulate/transpose,
and there is no point optimising an indexed read path.

Caveat on the fmap row: part of that 16x is fusion U.map/U.foldl' get and the derived
Functor/Foldable on Grid do not, so read the SAT build (4.3x on a whole real workload) as the
honest headline. Caveat on index: both benchmarks walk row-major, which is the prefetch-friendly
best case for boxed. The consumer's real access patterns are also near-sequential, so this is
representative rather than flattering.

Separate finding, filed as its own issue: the SAT solve burns 157 MB for 360,000 reads (~436 B
per read) and that is all coordinate arithmetic ((.+^) over allCoord), not the grid.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
From the sized-grid-zzj evaluation (closed): if this lands on vector-sized rather than raw Data.Vector.Unboxed, note that vector-sized 1.6.1 indexes with Data.Finite's Integer-backed alias, not an Int-backed one:

    index (Vector v) (Finite i) = v `VG.unsafeIndex` fromIntegral i
    generate f = Vector (VG.generate i (f . Finite . fromIntegral))

So an Ordinal -> Finite conversion at that boundary allocates an Integer per index, and that cost is inherent to vector-sized rather than to Ordinal -- switching Ordinal's representation would not avoid it. Given the spike above already showed per-coordinate access wins nothing and the whole win is in bulk operations, the cheap route is to keep the bulk API off the index path entirely (map/zipWith/fold/scanl1/tabulate/transpose over the underlying vector) and not route reads through Finite at all. Raw Data.Vector.Unboxed, as the spike used, sidesteps the question.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Ordering: sized-grid-0tj should land first. Decomposing the solve loop showed (.+^) is 93% of
it, with a 14.8x ceiling, against up6's 4.3x on the build. On ../aoc/src/2018/11.hs as a whole
(1 build + 17 solves) up6 alone is 1.04x, 0tj alone is 6.6x, both together 11.6x. up6 is still
worth doing -- it is most of what is left once 0tj lands -- but it is the second half, not the
first. Full numbers and root cause on sized-grid-0tj.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Follow-up: evaluated forking vector-sized. Recommendation is DON'T -- and don't
depend on it either. Use raw Data.Vector.Unboxed, as the spike above did.

Maintenance status (checked 2026-08-13): dormant, not dead.
  - Last commit 2024-02-01 (~2.5 years ago); not archived; 6 open issues, 2 open PRs.
  - Last release 1.6.1 uploaded 2024-02-07 by koz_ross, not the author (expipiplus1).
  - Last FEATURE release was 1.6.0, January 2022 (~4.5 years ago). The two releases
    since were life support -- bounds bumps and foldl' future-proofing contributed by
    Bodigrim, i.e. an ecosystem caretaker keeping it compiling.
  - tested-with maxes at GHC 9.2.1.
  - BUT it builds fine on GHC 9.12.3 -- verified by compiling against it; 1.6.1 is
    already in the nix GHC package set. The presburger lesson recorded in
    sized-grid.cabal is that the risk is a dep that stops BUILDING on a GHC we need,
    not one that stops adding features. vector-sized is not there.

The strong version of the fork idea does work, and deserves credit: fork it and swap
Finite n for our own Ordinal n, and finite-typelits disappears along with the
KnownIntegral/Limited constraint wall documented in sized-grid-zzj. That would give an
Int-backed index under plain KnownNat, the vocabulary the rest of the library speaks.
So the fork genuinely can solve the representation problem.

It fails on three other counts:

1. It duplicates a size proof we already have. Grid is
   'newtype Grid (cs :: [Type]) a = Grid (V.Vector a)' -- a flat vector carrying our
   own type-level size machinery (cs, Coord, Ordinal, AllGridSizeKnown). A type-level
   size tag IS vector-sized's whole value proposition. Adopting it puts a
   Vector (product-of-cs) a inside a Grid cs a: two independent size proofs to keep in
   agreement, plus the product constraint relating them. AllGridSizeKnown already
   carries KnownNat (MaxCoordSize cs) as a superclass, and sized-grid-oxb is open work
   to REMOVE a KnownNat (n * n) from signatures. Same direction as the finite-typelits
   migration, same reason to decline.

2. Cost: 9,521 lines across 12 modules, with deps on adjunctions, comonad,
   distributive, binary and primitive -- owned forever, on our GHC upgrade schedule.
   Ordinal.hs is ~200 lines.

3. It buys nothing the spike above needs. All measured wins (7.5x tabulate, 16x
   map/sum, 4.3x SAT build) are bulk operations over the underlying vector, which never
   touch an index type. The spike also found per-coordinate access wins nothing --
   and the indexed read path is exactly the surface vector-sized would provide.

A fork would be justified if we wanted to EXPOSE a size-tagged vector in the public
API, or if vector-sized broke on a GHC we need and upstream stayed silent. Neither
holds. If the second ever does, the proportionate fix is a bounds-bump PR or a Hackage
revision -- which is precisely what the last two releases were.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Re-priced after sized-grid-czf landed, on the real consumer rather than by projection.

WHOLE PROGRAM, ../aoc/src/2018/11.hs (1 SAT build + 17 solves), same binary shape
both sides, aoc's nix devshell, GHC 9.12.3 aarch64-darwin:

  against master (pre-0tj, pre-czf)   0.72 s   2.91 GB allocated   MUT 0.645 s
  against 0tj + czf                   0.28 s   1.07 GB allocated   MUT 0.207 s

2.6x end to end. That is the coordinate work finished; up6 is what is left.

WHERE THE REMAINING 207 ms GOES. Split by re-benchmarking the two halves of that
program separately (scratch package, code copied unchanged from 11.hs):

  makeSAT 300x300, the build          78.5 ms
  solve 3, one solve of 360k offsets   8.02 ms
  solve 3 with 'corners' hoisted       4.12 ms

1 build + 17 solves = 78.5 + 17x8.02 = 215 ms, against 207 ms measured. The model
is the program.

So the shares are: build 36 percent, solves 64 percent. And of a solve, only
~2.0 ms is the library's offset path (the 'four corner reads' benchmark, now
2.02 ms / 53 B per 360,000 offsets) -- the other ~6 ms is the caller rebuilding
its four-element 'corners' list inside squareSum, once per position, 90,000 times
a solve. Hoisting it halves the solve. Filed separately.

WHAT up6 IS NOW WORTH HERE. The build is bulk operations over the whole grid --
tabulate, scanl1Grid, mapLowerDim, transposeGrid -- which is exactly the shape
the spike above measured at 4.3x for the SAT build and 7.5x for tabulate. At
that ratio the build goes 78.5 -> ~18 ms, i.e. ~28 percent off the program, 1.4x.
It does NOT help the solves: the spike measured per-coordinate index reads as
unchanged (765 us boxed vs 751 us unboxed), and this split confirms the solve
half is caller-side list building rather than element access.

So: still worth doing, and now the largest library-side item left for this
workload, but as a 1.4x on the build half and not a rewrite of the hot loop. The
stronger cases remain ising-example and gameOfLife, which are bulk map/zip over
numeric grids end to end -- 16x on map/sum in the spike -- rather than
offset-and-read like 11.hs.

Recommendation unchanged: option 2, an additive SizedGrid.Grid.Unboxed with a
monomorphic API, non-breaking.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Option 1 re-evaluated and now RECOMMENDED, reversing the earlier call for option 2. Compiled a
crux module (worktree-up6-generic-grid) against the three things that were not obviously possible.
All three work.

  newtype GridOf v (cs :: [Type]) a = GridOf (v a)
  type Grid = GridOf V.Vector          -- zero-arity, so 'Grid cs' stays partially applicable

1. MIXED REPRESENTATION. The objection that killed option 1 on paper was nested grids: a grid is
   never Unbox, so 'splitGrid :: Grid (c ': cs) a -> Grid '[c] (Grid cs a)' cannot be uniform in v.
   It does not have to be -- the outer vector is always boxed, and that is statable:

     splitGrid   :: (VG.Vector v a, AllSizedKnown cs)
                 => GridOf v (c ': cs) a -> GridOf V.Vector '[c] (GridOf v cs a)
     combineGrid :: VG.Vector v a
                 => GridOf V.Vector '[c] (GridOf v cs a) -> GridOf v (c ': cs) a

   Compiles, and combineGrid . splitGrid roundtrips at v ~ U.Vector. mapLowerDim generalises the
   same way -- it already chunks through a LIST of vectors, so only the element constraint changes.

2. THE BOXED INSTANCE SET SURVIVES, as concrete instances at 'GridOf V.Vector cs'. Functor,
   Foldable, Applicative, Distributive and Representable all carry over with bodies unchanged
   ('deriving newtype' for the first two). Only Traversable needs writing out by hand: GND coerces
   under the applicative m, whose role it must assume nominal. One line.

3. THE PROOFS STILL DISCHARGE through the extra parameter. The ShrinkableGrid instance -- windowFits,
   reifyCoord's existential, sliceGrid's 'off + len <= m' -- typechecks unchanged, and natnormalise
   still fires. GHC additionally reports 'VG.Vector v a' as REDUNDANT on the window helper, which is
   the useful surprise: shrinkGrid only ever moves whole sub-grids, so the shape algebra is
   element-agnostic and does not even need the element constraint.

WHY THIS REVERSES THE RECOMMENDATION. Option 2's cost was mis-stated as 'less elegant'. Its real
cost is that the unboxed module needs its own dropGrid/takeGrid/sliceGrid/splitGrid/combineGrid/
splitHigherDim/mapLowerDim/gridTiles/ShrinkableGrid/collapseGrid -- i.e. the whole shape algebra,
including the windowFits proof and the 'off + len <= m' restatement that took all of sized-grid-wrc
to get right. Two copies of this library's hardest and most safety-critical code, guaranteed to
drift. Under option 1 that code exists once and both representations get all of it.

Option 1's cost is one genuinely ambiguous signature -- gridFromList, whose v is determined by
nothing -- fixed by exporting it monomorphised at V.Vector from Data.Grid.Sized. Every other
function takes a grid as an argument, so v is inferred. That is far cheaper than the original
'an extra type parameter in every signature' framing assumed.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
IMPLEMENTED on branch worktree-up6-generic-grid (commit d921a80), as option 1. All 431 tests
pass (16 new), hlint clean, readme and downstream suites green.

SHAPE. 'newtype GridOf v (cs :: [Type]) a = Grid (v a)', with 'type Grid = GridOf V.Vector' and a
new Data.Grid.Sized.Unboxed giving 'type UGrid = GridOf U.Vector'. The synonym takes no parameters
of its own so 'Grid cs' stays partially applicable; no existing signature in the tree changed. The
constructor is still spelled 'Grid' (different namespace from the synonym), so internal pattern
matches and derived Show output are unchanged.

The Unboxed module is ~30 lines and almost all documentation. That is the result: the shape algebra
is not duplicated, it is shared.

WHAT DOES NOT GENERALISE, and all of it is element-polymorphic by nature: Functor/Foldable/
Traversable are given as 'Functor v => Functor (GridOf v cs)' so any boxed-like vector gets them;
Applicative/Monad/Distributive/Representable are given concretely at GridOf V.Vector. Replacements
exported from Data.Grid.Sized and usable at either representation: tabulateGrid, indexGrid, mapGrid,
imapGrid, zipWithGrid, foldlGrid'. FocusedGrid and Comonad stay boxed-only -- duplicate builds a
grid OF grids.

MEASURED (bench group 'boxed vs unboxed', 300x300 Int, ghc 9.12.3 aarch64-darwin):

  operation             boxed      unboxed   speedup
  tabulateGrid          6.36 ms    1.93 ms     3.3x
  mapGrid then sum       318 us    92.1 us     3.5x
  foldlGrid'             312 us    88.7 us     3.5x
  transposeGrid         5.06 ms    2.15 ms     2.4x
  summed-area build     28.1 ms    13.1 ms     2.1x
  indexGrid x90000       751 us     793 us     none

THE SPIKE'S NUMBERS DID NOT REPRODUCE. It reported 7.5x/16x/6.5x/4.3x on those rows. It compared a
hand-written monomorphic unboxed loop against the library's boxed path, so it credited
specialisation to the representation. Both sides here are the same generic code. The honest ratio
is 2-3.5x, and the 'no change on indexed reads' finding stands exactly as the spike had it -- that
one was right and is the load-bearing one for deciding when to reach for UGrid.

PRAGMAS ARE LOAD-BEARING, and this was the surprise. Without INLINE/INLINABLE nothing specialises
through the VG.Vector dictionary: the summed-area build runs 53.6 ms rather than 13.1 ms. They help
the BOXED path at least as much, since it is the same code -- against e7d6340, tabulate is 60%
faster and fmap 78% faster (mapGrid and a following fold now fuse). So the library was leaving that
speedup on the table before it had a vector parameter at all.

TWO REGRESSIONS, both at conversion boundaries. The four operations that recurse down the axis list
-- collapseGrid, gridFromList, toJSON, parseJSON -- cannot specialise through a recursive call at a
changing cs, so their vector primitives stayed behind a dictionary and ran 60-300% slower. Fixed by
making the recursion monomorphic over a boxed vector with a local splitBoxedBySize; the exported
generic splitVectorBySize inside a polymorphically-recursive function never reduces to its O(1)
slice, and that single helper was most of the gap. What remains is one VG.convert per call:
collapseGrid +9%, toJSON +19%, gridFromList and parseJSON level. Two alternative shapes were
measured and cost more (list recursion: collapseGrid +83%, toJSON +68%; passing vector ops as
arguments: fixes the plain functions, but JSON goes to +74%/+56% because an instance method does not
specialise at its call site the way an INLINABLE function does). The module header records all
three.

Every other benchmark is level with baseline.

HOUSEKEEPING. bench-spike/ is deleted -- its own comment said to remove it once this decision was
made, and it had begun breaking 'cabal build all --enable-benchmarks' by depending on the old
upstream sized-grid from Hackage. Its workloads are folded into bench/Main.hs against the real
implementation. Test.Unboxed runs each operation at both representations and compares, so they
cannot drift. Baseline CSV refreshed.

title: Ordinal's GADT representation costs a KnownNat dictionary + someNatVal allocation per arithmetic op
description:
The central performance problem.

src/SizedGrid/Ordinal.hs:31-32

    data Ordinal m where
      Ordinal :: (KnownNat n, KnownNat m, n + 1 <= m) => Proxy n -> Ordinal m

Every Ordinal value carries a type-level Nat and its dictionary. Consequences:

  - ordinalToNum goes Proxy -> natVal -> Integer -> fromIntegral. Integer, not Int.
  - numToOrdinal (src/SizedGrid/Ordinal.hs:50-61) calls someNatVal (allocates a
    SomeNat, builds a KnownNat dictionary via unsafeCoerce) plus cmpNat, on EVERY
    construction.
  - toEnum = fromJust . numToOrdinal, so enumerating an axis allocates one Nat
    dictionary per element.
  - Periodic's (<>), negateV, (.+^), (.-.) and HardWrap's equivalents all round-trip
    through numToOrdinal. A single coordinate addition allocates a type-level natural.

Observed cost in practice: ../aoc/src/2018/11.hs works on Grid '[HardWrap 300, HardWrap 300]
and iterates 'allCoord' (90,000 coords), each one an NP of two GADTs carrying dictionaries.

Proposal: make it a newtype over Int with a smart constructor.

    newtype Ordinal (m :: Nat) = UnsafeOrdinal { ordinalToInt :: Int }

The only thing the GADT buys at runtime is asSizeProxy (src/SizedGrid/Coord/Class.hs:48-53),
which recovers 'Proxy m' with 'm + 1 <= n'. That is used in exactly one place
(shrinkGrid, src/SizedGrid/Grid/Grid.hs:248-254). Reconstruct the evidence there via
someNatVal at that single call site instead of paying for it on every value.

Expected: coordinate arithmetic becomes machine-word Int ops; Ordinal becomes
unboxable, which unblocks the unboxed-Grid work.

Do this behind the existing _Ordinal prism / numToOrdinal / ordinalToNum API so
most call sites are unaffected. Benchmark first (see the criterion issue).
close_reason: Fixed in commit 'Make Ordinal a newtype over Int' on branch worktree-ordinal-int; 100 tests pass, zero warnings

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Dependency on sized-grid-h56 removed. h56 was retested on 2026-08-09 and deferred --
ghc-tcplugins-extra has no GHC 9.14 release on Hackage, so natnormalise and knownnat
cannot be adopted without dropping 9.14 support. Leaving this blocked on it would block
it indefinitely on an upstream event. The manual Nat plumbing in Ordinal.hs:61/68/79
therefore has to be handled by this refactor itself rather than dissolved by a plugin
first. Still blocked on sized-grid-amf, which is the right gate: benchmark before
rewriting the representation.

Also note sized-grid-j23 (fromJust in Ordinal construction) now depends on this issue --
the seven fromJust call sites collapse into one checked constructor once Ordinal is a
newtype over Int, so they should be fixed here rather than patched separately.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Baseline landed (sized-grid-amf), so this is now measurable rather than speculative.

The strongest single number: 'tabulate' on a 300x300 grid of Int allocates 93 MB and
takes 23.6 ms. The payload of that grid is 90,000 boxed Ints, well under 1 MB. Roughly
1 KB of allocation per cell is exactly the someNatVal / KnownNat-dictionary traffic this
issue describes -- every Ordinal construction builds a type-level natural.

Supporting figures, all GHC 9.12.3 aarch64-darwin -O1:
    index x90000, 300x300      13.8 ms,  72 MB   (153 ns and ~800 B per index)
    ifoldl' 300x300            19.5 ms, 107 MB
    extend neighbourSum 50x50  5.42 ms,  29 MB   (2.2 us per cell, 9 peeks each)
    (.+^) Periodic             157 ns/op, 1.1 KB/op
    toEnum/fromEnum HardWrap    24 ns/op

Compare 'fmap 300x300' at 758 us / 4.1 MB, which touches every cell but constructs no
Ordinals. That is the target the newtype-over-Int representation should be aiming at.

Re-run 'cabal run bench:benchmarks' and diff against
bench/baseline-ghc9.12.3-aarch64-darwin.csv to judge the refactor.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Done in commit "Make Ordinal a newtype over Int" (branch worktree-ordinal-int).

Shipped as proposed: newtype over Int with a nominal role, constructor not
exported, numToOrdinal as the checked entry point and unsafeOrdinal as the one
unchecked one (assert-guarded). asSizeProxy's evidence is rebuilt on demand by
reifyOrdinal at the single call site (shrinkGrid) instead of being carried in
every value. Signatures that gained a constraint the GADT used to smuggle in:
asSizeProxy (KnownNat n), ShrinkableGrid (KnownNat x), maxCoord (1 <= n).

Result, A/B measured in one session:

    (.+^) Periodic 300x300      2.07x faster, 49% less allocated
    toEnum/fromEnum HardWrap    2.50x faster, 61% less allocated
    extend neighbourSum         1.12x faster, 11% less allocated
    (.-.) HardWrap              1.22x faster,  5% less allocated
    tabulate/imap/index/ifoldl' unchanged to within 1%

The estimate in this issue's earlier comment -- that tabulate's 93 MB was
someNatVal/KnownNat traffic -- was wrong, and the benchmark says so plainly.
allCoord shares 600 Ordinals across 90,000 coords, so per-value representation
never dominated the grid-wide operations. The remaining cost is NP allocation
plus coordPosition's Integer arithmetic; both belong to sized-grid-uvd, which
now has the numbers on it.

Also note the measurement trap hit on the way: the recorded baseline CSV was
1.9x off because the machine was busier than when it was written, which made a
2x win read as a 2x regression. bench/Main.hs now documents measuring both
sides in one session.

title: allCoord is rebuilt from scratch on every imap/ifoldMap/itraverse/tabulate
description:
src/SizedGrid/Grid/Grid.hs:67-75

    imap func (Grid v)      = Grid $ V.zipWith func (V.fromList allCoord) v
    ifoldMap func (Grid v)  = foldMap id $ V.zipWith func (V.fromList allCoord) v
    itraverse func (Grid v) = Grid <$> sequenceA (V.zipWith func (V.fromList allCoord) v)

and src/SizedGrid/Grid/Grid.hs:64

    tabulate func = Grid $ V.fromList $ map func allCoord

'allCoord' (src/SizedGrid/Coord.hs:206-212) builds the full coordinate list through
the list monad over an NP, then V.fromList copies it into a vector. This happens on
every single indexed traversal, and each element is a heap-allocated NP I cs whose
components each carry a KnownNat dictionary.

For Grid '[HardWrap 300, HardWrap 300] that is 90,000 NP allocations per imap.

Also src/SizedGrid/Coord.hs:220-237: coordPosition recomputes the per-axis size
product ('sizeOfList') on every call, in Integer, and index calls coordPosition for
every access.

Options, roughly in order of payoff:
  1. Cache the coordinate vector per type in a CAF: 'allCoordVector :: V.Vector (Coord cs)'
     bound at top level so GHC shares it across calls. Needs care to actually float.
  2. Precompute the axis strides once (a small [Int]) rather than folding sizes each
     time in coordPosition.
  3. Better: make imap/ifoldMap/itraverse iterate positions as Int and only
     materialise a Coord when the user function demands one. Most callers use
     fromEnum on the result anyway -- see ../aoc/src/2018/11.hs:40
     '(fromEnum -> r) :| (fromEnum -> c) :| _'.

Depends on the Ordinal representation change for the biggest win.
close_reason: Fixed on branch worktree-allcoord. coordPosition is a single Int pass (was Integer with a per-axis re-traversal); tabulate uses V.fromListN coordSpaceSize; ifoldr/ifoldl' given outright. allCoord itself was not the problem - the V.fromList in the traversals fuses. 24-49% less allocation across tabulate/imap/index/ifoldl'/extend, 110 tests pass, zero warnings. Remainder tracked as sized-grid-0vl.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Quantified by sized-grid-amf's baseline (GHC 9.12.3, aarch64-darwin, -O1). The
benchmark pairs each allCoord-using operation with the closest operation that does not
use it, so the difference is attributable:

    tabulate 300x300  23.6 ms,  93 MB   vs   pure 300x300  206 us, 704 KB   -> 115x, 132x alloc
    imap     300x300  17.7 ms,  80 MB   vs   fmap 300x300  758 us, 4.1 MB   ->  23x,  20x alloc

allCoord is not overhead on indexed traversal, it is essentially the entire cost. Re-run
'cabal run bench:benchmarks' after any caching change and compare against
bench/baseline-ghc9.12.3-aarch64-darwin.csv.

Note there is no standalone allCoord benchmark and it is not an oversight: at a fixed
type allCoord is a CAF and the optimiser shares it, so a direct measurement reports ~2 ns
for 90,000 coordinates. Details in the comment in bench/Main.hs.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Measured correction from the sized-grid-upo work (commit "Make Ordinal a newtype
over Int"). The Ordinal representation is NOT what tabulate/imap/index/ifoldl'
are paying for. A/B with both sides measured in one session:

    (.+^) Periodic          2.07x faster, 49% less allocated
    toEnum/fromEnum         2.50x faster, 61% less allocated
    tabulate 300x300        unchanged: 97,580,033 -> 97,421,177 bytes
    imap 300x300            unchanged: 83,502,208 -> 83,502,303 bytes
    index x90000            unchanged: 75,581,477 -> 75,581,480 bytes
    ifoldl' 300x300         unchanged: 112,040,243 -> 111,881,769 bytes

Why: allCoord is a cartesian product over the per-axis lists, so for a 300x300
grid it constructs 600 Ordinals and shares them across all 90,000 NPs. Ordinal
construction was never the per-cell cost. What is left, and what this issue now
owns in full, is:

  1. the 90,000 NP I cs allocations themselves, rebuilt per traversal, and
  2. coordPosition, which is called per cell and does its arithmetic in Integer
     -- ordinalToNum boxes an Integer per axis, and sizeOfList recomputes the
     stride product per call.

(2) is now a clean win to take: ordinalToInt gives the axis value as an Int
directly, so coordPosition can be Int throughout with the strides precomputed
once. That did not exist before the newtype.

Judge any change here by the allocation columns, not the times -- see the note
added to bench/Main.hs about cross-session drift.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Done. The issue's premise was wrong in an instructive way, so the result is recorded here in full.

allCoord is NOT rebuilt in the sense meant. 'V.zipWith func (V.fromList allCoord) v' fuses: the coordinates are produced and consumed one at a time and never all exist at once. Its real cost is about 67 bytes a cell. I confirmed this by breaking it -- building the coordinate vector from a recursive function, and separately by putting the same list under V.fromListN -- and both made imap 23% more allocation and 59% slower, with ifoldl' copying jumping from 48KB to 18MB. The fused form is now commented as such in SizedGrid.Grid.Grid so it does not get "fixed" again.

What the benchmark gap actually measured was coordPosition, which tabulate/imap/ifoldl' are all handed as their per-cell function: ~800 bytes per call. The old version recomputed the axis-size product with a separate traversal per axis, in Integer.

Changes:
  - coordPosition is one Int pass; the stride of an axis is the size of the axes below it, which comes back up the recursion.
  - tabulate uses V.fromListN coordSpaceSize (its result is a vector regardless, so the exact length just avoids growth doubling).
  - ifoldr/ifoldl' given outright rather than derived from ifoldMap through an Endo chain.
  - New API: coordSpaceSize (MaxCoordSize as a value, needing only All IsCoordLifted) and coordFromPosition (checked inverse of coordPosition).
  - 10 new tests pinning the position/coordinate bijection and that imap/ifoldMap/ifoldr/ifoldl' agree with tabulate and with each other. Mutation-checked: a wrong stride fails 6 of them.

Allocated, before -> after (the deterministic column):
  tabulate 300x300    97,421,177 ->  73,740,888   -24%
  imap 300x300        83,502,303 ->  62,641,438   -25%
  index x90000        75,581,480 ->  54,720,335   -28%
  ifoldl' 300x300    111,881,769 ->  57,600,340   -49%
  extend 50x50        27,045,702 ->  21,808,586   -19%
  extract 50x50              808 ->         608   -25%
  itraverse 100x100   unchanged; everything else unchanged

Times, both sides measured in one session:
  tabulate 47.0ms -> 33.4ms, imap 33.9 -> 22.8, index 27.0 -> 15.0,
  ifoldl' 38.0 -> 15.1, extend 9.39ms -> 6.23ms, extract 298ns -> 167ns

Baseline CSV re-recorded. The "allCoord overhead" benchmark group is renamed to "indexed vs unindexed (the gap is coordPosition, not allCoord)" -- its old name and its pairing are what pointed this issue at the wrong thing.

What is left is sized-grid-0vl: coordPosition's remaining ~550 bytes a call is dictionary plumbing (peeling IsCoordLifted out of All, natVal boxing an Integer, the Iso call for asOrdinal), not arithmetic.
