title: Two obstacles to instantiating PseudoAffine: an orphan on Int, and MapDiff idempotence
description:
Both hit while building the sized-grid-8nz proof of concept. Neither is fatal;
both need a decision. Only relevant if 8nz goes ahead.

== 1. manifolds-core has no Semimanifold Int

It derives Semimanifold/PseudoAffine for Double and Rational only (a CPP
'deriveAffine' macro applied twice). Int is not a manifold as far as it is
concerned, which is defensible -- a Needle is meant to be a vector space over
R, and Int is not one.

Every Diff in this library is an Int, so the instances do not typecheck without
supplying it:

    instance Semimanifold Int where
      type Needle Int = Int
      (.+~^) = (+)
    instance PseudoAffine Int where
      a .-~. b = pure (a - b)
      (.-~!) = (-)

That is an orphan instance on a base type. It is the thing that would make a
grid-sized-manifolds *separate package* (option (b) in 8nz) attractive: the
orphan is then confined to a package a consumer opts into, and cannot collide
in the main library's own dependency cone. ../aoc defining the same orphan
would be an overlap error, so check there before choosing.

Worth asking upstream whether Semimanifold Int is wanted in manifolds-core
before committing to carrying an orphan indefinitely.

== 2. MapDiff (MapDiff cs) ~ MapDiff cs

Semimanifold's semimanifoldWitness default needs
Needle (Needle x) ~ Needle x, and PseudoAffine's needs PseudoAffine (Needle x).
At Coord cs with Needle (Coord cs) = Coord (MapDiff cs), that is

    MapDiff (MapDiff cs) ~ MapDiff cs
    AffineCoordList (MapDiff cs)
    All AdditiveGroup (MapDiff (MapDiff cs))

True -- MapDiff sends every coord to Int and Diff Int = Int, so it is
idempotent -- but GHC cannot see it without induction over the axis list. The
proof of concept punted by writing all four as instance constraints, which
compiles but pushes them onto every downstream signature.

The clean fix is an inductive class over cs that discharges them once, the same
shape as AffineCoordList and IsCoordList already have (and the same shape the
existing note about Nat-indexed class recursion warns about: a fundep, not an
associated type family, or GHC rejects overlapping instances as conflicting).

At a concrete axis list -- which is most code, including ../aoc -- MapDiff
reduces and none of this is visible. It is only polymorphic code that pays.
notes:
Obstacle 2 (MapDiff (MapDiff cs) ~ MapDiff cs) is dissolved by sized-grid-adr.16, not by the inductive class this issue proposes.

adr.16 splits the displacement out of Coord: Diff (Coord cs) stops being
Coord (MapDiff cs) and becomes Delta (MapDiff cs), where Delta is a type of
its own. A vector space is its own needle, so Needle (Delta ds) = Delta ds and

    Needle (Needle (Coord cs)) = Needle (Delta (MapDiff cs))
                               = Delta (MapDiff cs)
                               = Needle (Coord cs)

holds definitionally. No induction over the axis list, no inductive class, and
nothing pushed onto downstream signatures. The four constraints the 8nz proof
of concept carried as instance constraints go away with it.

Obstacle 1 (the Semimanifold Int orphan) is untouched by adr.16 and is still
the open question here.

title: windowFits is an asserted axiom; try ghc-typelits-presburger to discharge it
description:
`SizedGrid.Internal.Type.windowFits` is the only `unsafeCoerce` in the library:

    windowFits :: forall n y z. Dict (n <= y, z <= (y - n))
    windowFits = unsafeCoerce (Dict :: Dict (0 <= 0, 0 <= 0))

It supplies the two facts `shrinkGrid` needs to call `dropGrid` then `takeGrid`.
Soundness rests entirely on the `x + z <= y + 1` constraint on the
`ShrinkableGrid` instance, which is checked at every call site -- so the axiom is
believed true, but it is asserted rather than derived, and an `unsafeCoerce`
producing a `Dict` is the single place where a mistake in that reasoning would
be silent.

The module comment already names the candidate fix and nobody has tried it:

> That wanted is a `<=` goal from `<=` givens over a truncating subtraction,
> which needs ghc-typelits-presburger; it stays an asserted axiom.

This is a bounded spike, not a redesign. Add `ghc-typelits-presburger` to the
`common lang` plugin list next to `natnormalise` and `knownnat`, delete
`windowFits`, and see whether the `shrinkGrid` call site still compiles.

Two acceptable outcomes, and both are worth having:

- It works: the library's last asserted axiom goes away, and
  `SizedGrid.Internal.Type` shrinks to just `requiring`.
- It does not: the comment gets upgraded from "needs presburger" (a guess) to a
  record of what was actually tried and how it failed, so the next reader does
  not re-run this spike.

Note the constraint that sank sized-grid-h56 applies here too: `-fplugin` is not
transitive. A plugin enabled for this library says nothing about a downstream
consumer. That is fine for `windowFits` specifically, because the goal is solved
*inside* this library at the `shrinkGrid` definition rather than being re-emitted
into a consumer's context -- but confirm that before concluding, because it is
exactly the assumption that made h56 look like a fix when it was not.
design:
The arithmetic the axiom stands in for, from the module comment:

At the use site the window offset `n` comes from `reifyCoord` on a coord of size
`x`, so `n + 1 <= x`, and the `ShrinkableGrid` instance requires
`x + z <= y + 1`. Together:

    n + 1 + z <= x + z <= y + 1        so   n + z <= y

which gives both `n <= y` (drop stays in range) and `z <= y - n` (the window fits
in what is left).

The first conjunct is ordinary linear arithmetic. The second mentions `y - n`,
GHC's *truncating* subtraction on Nat, over an existential `n` -- that is what
natnormalise will not do. Presburger arithmetic can express truncating
subtraction by case analysis on `n <= y`, and here the `n <= y` case is exactly
what the first conjunct establishes, which is the reason to expect this to work.

Verify rather than assume: check that ghc-typelits-presburger's current release
supports GHC 9.10/9.12/9.14 before adding it, since its GHC support has
historically lagged. If it only covers part of the tested-with range that is a
reason to reject, and should be recorded as such.
acceptance_criteria: Either windowFits is deleted and SizedGrid.Internal.Type exports only 'requiring', with the full test suite green on the tested-with GHCs; or the module comment records the concrete presburger attempt and why it failed, so the spike is not repeated.
close_reason:
Done, but not the way the issue predicted -- no plugin was added.

Presburger was tried first and it DOES discharge the goal: commit ae643ea has the
working change, all suites green on 9.12.3. It was rejected on the criterion this
issue's own design section set out. ghc-typelits-presburger 0.7.4.2 is bounded
'ghc <9.13', as is the ghc-tcplugins-extra 0.5 beneath it, with no 9.14 branch
upstream (last release supports 9.12). With it in build-depends GHC 9.14.1 fails
to resolve outright, [Cabal-7107] -- verified against a real 9.14.1 compiler, and
verified that removing that one dependency is what makes 9.14 resolve again. That
is precisely the trap that left h56 deferred; natnormalise and knownnat escaped it
by moving to ghc-tcplugin-api, and presburger has not moved.

The axiom turned out not to need a solver at all (commit 7bf7531). Probing
natnormalise showed the real limitation is broader than the issue assumed: it is
not just the truncating subtraction, it will not chain two '<=' givens at all and
fails on a bare 'a <= b, b <= c => a <= c'. But it does cancel constants from both
sides. So:

  - 'sliceGrid off len' replaces 'takeGrid len . dropGrid off', stating the bound
    as 'off + len <= m' rather than 'len <= m - off'. The truncating subtraction
    never appears. It is also V.slice's own precondition, so that bounds check
    cannot fire. Same elements: [off, off+len).
  - 'windowFits' keeps its name but is derived, not asserted, from plusMonotone1
    and leTrans in Data.Constraint.Nat. 'constraints' was already a dependency.

Net result: no unsafeCoerce in src/, no new dependency, GHC 9.14 kept.

Honest limit on the claim: plusMonotone1 and leTrans are themselves unsafeCoerce
inside 'constraints'. What changed is that the reasoning is machine-checked --
those are general lemmas about + and <=, where windowFits was a bespoke
three-variable claim about this library's window invariant, asserted whole. GHC
now verifies the composition yields 'n + z <= y' from the givens.

Verified on GHC 9.12.3 with -fforce-recomp: library, three examples and benchmarks
warning-free; 315 tasty tests, readme suite and the plugin-free downstream suite
all pass. The downstream suite passing is what shows the goal is solved at the
definition rather than re-emitted into a consumer's context.

Filed sized-grid-ior: tests/Main.hs and README.lhs have 8 pre-existing warnings
that only show on a cold build (confirmed present at c697f1b, so not from this
work).

'sliceGrid' is exported from SizedGrid.Internal.Grid but NOT added to the public
SizedGrid.Grid.Grid list -- deliberately left out of scope; worth deciding
separately, since dropGrid and takeGrid are both public and this is the more
useful primitive.

title: _CoordCons and _DeltaCons: cons/uncons as an Iso, and why lens's Cons class does not fit
description:
From the sized-grid-31z optics survey. Tier A: a genuine Iso, and a note on
why lens's own class does not fit.

  coordSplit  :: Coord (c ': cs) -> (c, Coord cs)     Coord.hs:182
  appendCoord :: c -> Coord cs -> Coord (c ': cs)     Coord.hs:339
  deltaSplit  :: Delta (d ': ds) -> (d, Delta ds)     Delta.hs:89
  appendDelta :: a -> Delta as -> Delta (a ': as)     Delta.hs:203

  _CoordCons :: (IsCoordLifted c, IsCoordList cs)
             => Iso' (Coord (c ': cs)) (c, Coord cs)
  _CoordCons = iso coordSplit (uncurry appendCoord)

  _DeltaCons :: Iso' (Delta (d ': ds)) (d, Delta ds)

And the two degenerate ends, which complete the family:

  _SingleCoord :: IsCoordLifted c => Iso' (Coord '[c]) c
  _EmptyCoord  :: Iso' (Coord '[]) ()

== Do NOT instantiate lens's `Cons` for these

`Cons s t a b` gives `_Cons :: Prism s t (a, s) (b, t)` -- the tail has the
SAME type as the whole. A `Coord (c ': cs)`'s tail is a `Coord cs`, a
different type, so the class simply does not typecheck here.

That is a feature, not an obstacle. `Cons` is a Prism because a list can be
empty and the match can fail; `Coord (c ': cs)` has a head and a tail by
construction, so the bespoke version is an Iso -- strictly stronger. Same for
`Snoc`, which additionally has no cheap implementation: the last axis is the
least significant digit, so uncons is a `quotRem` by the tail stride
(Coord.hs:184) while unsnoc would be a `quotRem` by the last axis size and a
rebuild of everything above it.

The pattern synonyms `(:|)` and `(:^)` already cover the matching half; this
covers the composing half.

Cost: none, lens is already a direct dependency.

title: CI: tests/Test/Ordinal.hs fails to compile on GHC 9.10.1 -- reifyCoord's result type is untouchable
description:
`cabal build all` fails on GHC 9.10.1 while compiling Test.Ordinal (job runs 372s, so this is a real compile error, not a solver failure). GHC 9.12.3 is green.

Root cause is the single [GHC-83865] at tests/Test/Ordinal.hs:87:29 (and again at 97:19):

    Couldn't match expected type 'a0' with actual type 'Integer'
      'a0' is untouchable
        inside the constraints: (KnownNat m, (m + 1) <= 5)
        bound by a type expected by the context:
          forall (m1 :: Nat) -> (KnownNat m1, (m1 + 1) <= 5) => a0

reifyCoord (Data.Grid.Sized.Coord.Class:58) is

    reifyCoord :: KnownNat n => c n -> (forall m -> (KnownNat m, m + 1 <= n) => x) -> x

so `x` is bound outside an implication that carries givens. On 9.10 OutsideIn treats an unsolved `x` metavariable as untouchable from inside that implication, so `x ~ Integer` (from natVal) cannot be solved there. The three [GHC-39999] ambiguity errors at 84:5, 86:7, 86:8, 92:5 and 94:7 are downstream of that -- the numeric literals have nothing to fix their type to.

Fix: annotate the reifyCoord *application* (`... :: Integer`), which fixes `x` before the continuation is checked. Annotating the continuation body would not work -- that unification still happens inside the implication.

Note the obvious-looking fix of annotating only assertEqual's expected argument ([0 .. 4] :: [Integer]) treats the symptom; the untouchable error is at the reifyCoord call.

Verified: compiles under -Werror and all 49 Ordinal tests pass on 9.12.3.
close_reason: Closed

title: bench gate failed on indexGrid x90000 boxed (41% slower than baseline)
description:
Run 32213722072 (job 95951213763, bench, 2026-08-19T03:53Z) failed the benchmark gate:

    indexGrid x90000           boxed:                      FAIL
      938  us +- 50 us, 280 B allocated, 22 B copied, 79 MB peak memory, 41% more than baseline

--fail-if-slower is 25%, so this tripped it. The unboxed variant of the same benchmark (indexGrid x90000 unboxed) came in "same as baseline" in the same run, which is evidence pointing at shared-runner noise rather than a real regression in indexGrid -- nothing in the boxed-vs-unboxed path was touched recently in a way that would explain a boxed-only slowdown.

ci.yml's own comments (around the bench job) already call out that 25% is a provisional threshold picked before there was real run history on GitHub's shared runners, and say to tighten it "once there is a run history showing what this runner's spread actually is." This failure is a data point for that: worth collecting a few more gate failures/passes before deciding whether to widen the threshold, exclude boxed indexGrid as noisy, or otherwise adjust.

Immediate unblock: rerun the bench job / dispatch with refresh-baseline if this turns out to be a one-off, per the escape hatch documented at the top of ci.yml.

title: The other IsCoord defaults still read their KnownNat as a run-time Natural
description:
sized-grid-bw8 fixed offsetByPosition with a one-line INLINE: the checked offset went from 56.4 ms / 199 MB to 6.85 ms / 35 MB, and in the Core the per-axis call went from $w$coffsetIsCoord main81 ds3 ww2 to an inline ># x (-# 299# y1). The same shape is still in its siblings in src/SizedGrid/Coord/Class.hs.

WHAT IS LEFT. The Core of SizedGrid.Coord.Class still shows integerToInt# (integerFromNatural ($dKnownNat cast ...)) in:
  1. axisBoundaryByPosition, the default for axisBoundaryIsCoord.
  2. the default axisDistanceIsCoord.
Both read ordinalSize @n out of the method's KnownNat dictionary, for the same structural reason bw8 documents: IsCoord is indexed by c alone, so n arrives on the method rather than through the instance.

A third, different in kind: Periodic's own offsetIsCoord override is 'Just (c .+^ d)'. Its body folds, because AffineSpace (Periodic n) takes KnownNat n from its instance context --- but the method is still an out-of-line call taking the dictionary, so a Periodic call site does not get what Clamped now gets.

WHY NOT DONE IN bw8. bw8 was scoped to offsetByPosition, and nothing in bench/Main.hs reaches onBoundary or axisDistance. An INLINE on them could not have been measured, and this codebase does not take unmeasured performance changes --- the whole point of the before/after procedure in that file's header.

APPROACH. Add the benchmarks first: an onBoundary sweep over Clamped 300x300 and an axisDistance one, both shaped like checkedCornerReads so the displacement depends on an argument and cannot be floated into a CAF. Then the same one-line INLINE, verified in the Core rather than assumed.

ORDERING with sized-grid-5uq. axisSteps calls both offsetIsCoord and axisDistanceIsCoord, so part of this may land there instead. bw8 already took 'extend neighbourSum 50x50' from 8.88 ms / 28 MB to 7.01 ms / 25 MB without touching the neighbourhood fold, purely through the offsetIsCoord axisSteps calls.
notes:
APPROACH CHANGED BY sized-grid-knm (commit 66d50ee).

knm expected to fix a quadratic scan and instead found that the caller being out
of line was the whole cost: one INLINE on axisSteps, 6.51 ms / 22 MB -> 2.12 ms /
9.9 MB. So for this issue, check the caller before the class default.

Concretely: this issue's plan is an INLINE on axisBoundaryByPosition and on the
axisDistanceIsCoord default. But onBoundary and axisDistance are themselves free
functions over IsCoordList, and if they are out of line the pragma on the default
buys nothing at a call site -- which is exactly the trap knm's premise fell into.
Dump the Core of the new benchmarks first and see which frame the dictionary is
still being passed at.

The benchmark plan in this issue stands unchanged; nothing in bench/Main.hs
reaches onBoundary or axisDistance, and knm did not add anything that does.

The Periodic offsetIsCoord override noted here is now the more interesting half:
Clamped's path folds completely at a concrete axis after knm, so a Periodic call
site is where the remaining gap is, and it is measurable as soon as a Periodic
neighbourhood benchmark exists.
close_reason: Fixed: axisBoundaries/axisDistances now go through new IsCoordList methods npBoundaries/npDistances (unroll like npOffset) instead of generics-sop's hcmap/hczipWith, plus INLINE on the axis-level defaults. onBoundary x360000 101ms/363MB -> 14.0ms/95MB; coordDistance x360000 67.9ms/359MB -> 15.6ms/106MB. Periodic neighbourSum benchmark added but left unmoved -- Periodic's offsetIsCoord override is a separate remaining gap, now measurable. Commit c30b91b, 485 tests pass.

title: One seam-driven stepper: cubeStep, mobiusStep and kleinStep are the same algorithm
description:
grid-atlas now has three hand-written step functions and they are the same function with different names.

EVIDENCE, not a hunch. Diff Klein.hs against Mobius.hs with the axis
constructors renamed apart and the only surviving differences are the
haddocks, Mobius's extra Maybe, and Mobius hardcoding the crossing branch
that Klein drives off the table. Axis, Heading, sideSign, signSide and the
atlas-builder are byte-identical. cubeStep (CubeMap.hs:196) is the same
skeleton again: same in-range test, same free/fixed split, same 'reflect the
free coordinate iff reversed', same 'newSign = negate (sideSign destSide)'
heading rule. kleinStep's crossing branch IS the general single-chart case;
mobiusStep is it with one axis's half-edges unglued.

SHAPE

    seamStep :: SeamTable chart (Axis, Extremum)
             -> (ChartId k -> chart) -> (chart -> ChartId k)
             -> AtlasCoord cs k -> Heading -> (AtlasCoord cs k, Heading)

with the chart-id mapping being identity-ish for the k = 1 surfaces and
indexFace/faceIndex for the cube. Partial surfaces (Mobius's clamped axis)
are the Maybe-shaped variant, or the SeamTable haddock's own suggestion:
instantiate chart or boundary with a Maybe-ish type so an unglued half-edge
is representable in the table rather than special-cased in the stepper.

TWO REAL DESIGN POINTS, both found while writing kleinStep

  * Square vs rectangular charts. cubeStep has one 'size' because a cube
    face is n-by-n; kleinStep carries wSize and hSize separately. Those are
    not interchangeable -- a seam that maps axis U to axis V needs the two
    charts to agree on the size of the axis it lands on, which a rectangle
    only satisfies when the seam preserves the axis. Klein's seams do (its
    destAxis always equals axis), the cube's do not. So a generic stepper
    either demands square charts or states the size-agreement condition as
    a precondition on the table.

  * Whose size does the reflection use. kleinStep reflects with the
    SIBLING axis's size on the source chart, which is correct only because
    destAxis == axis there. The general rule is the FREE axis's size on the
    DESTINATION chart. Getting this wrong is invisible on the cube (all
    sizes equal) and invisible on Klein (source and dest axis agree), which
    makes it exactly the sort of thing to fix while writing the generic
    version rather than after.

Belongs in grid-atlas, not atlas-topology: the stepper needs Coord and
Ordinal, which is the line b15 drew. What moves is the coordinate
arithmetic the three modules currently repeat, leaving each surface as its
seam table plus its atlas builder.
notes:
Done by sized-grid-4wn (commits c4bf2d0, cba2dd8, d8cf8a2), which landed the same conclusion from the other side: 4wn asked whether cubeStep's chart-boundary detection generalizes, yve asked why three steppers are one function. Same answer.

The shared half is Data.Grid.Atlas.Rect's rectStep, in grid-atlas as yve says. Not the signature yve sketched: it takes raw (Int, Int) positions and a per-axis size function rather than an AtlasCoord and a chart-id mapping, so it needs no chart-id round trip at all -- the caller unwraps its own Ordinal or Clamped, which it was going to do anyway, and CubeMap keeps indexFace/faceIndex to itself.

Both design points yve found are handled:

  * Square vs rectangular is a documented precondition on the table (both boundaries of a seam have the same length), not a squareness demand. That is what lets one function serve an n x n cube face and a w x h strip.
  * The reflection uses the free axis of the DESTINATION, which is the general rule yve identified; d8cf8a2 says so in the haddock, since no test in the repo can distinguish it.

Partiality is the Applicative the gluing answers in: Identity for the cube and the bottle, Maybe for the strip's clamped axis. That avoids the Maybe-shaped variant yve weighed. The other option it weighed -- an unglued half-edge representable in the table -- is still open as sized-grid-1yn.

Per-chart sizes were considered and rejected: Atlas cs k a gives every chart the same shape cs, so uniform sizes are a type-level fact, not an assumption.
close_reason:
Duplicate of sized-grid-4wn, which was closed while this session was working and pushed to origin/master as c4bf2d0 + cba2dd8. Data.Grid.Atlas.Rect's rectStep is exactly the generic stepper proposed here, and Klein now goes through it.

Both design points this issue raised are already handled there, checked rather than assumed:

  * Rectangular charts: rectStep takes sizeOf :: Axis -> Int, so w and h are
    independent.
  * Whose size the reflection uses: it is sizeOf (otherAxis destAxis) --- the
    free axis on the DESTINATION --- which is the correct general rule and
    not the one Klein's hand-written version happened to need.
  * The precondition that falls out of those two (a seam may only swap axes
    between edges of equal length) is written up in Rect.hs's own 'What a
    caller must guarantee' section.

Nothing left to build. All 10 grid-atlas tests, including this session's four
Klein laws, pass against the merged result.

title: translated: the torsor structure of a boundaryless Coord, as an Iso
description:
From the sized-grid-31z optics survey. Tier C: the torsor structure, stated
as an optic. Companion to sized-grid-qfg and sized-grid-4il, which are about
the same fact from the algebraic side.

On an axis whose boundary policy never refuses a step -- `Periodic`, the
`Boundaryless` case -- translating by a fixed displacement is a BIJECTION on
coordinates. Every coordinate has a unique preimage: subtract the
displacement.

  translated :: (IsCoordList cs, AllDiffSame Int cs, All Boundaryless cs)
             => Diff (Coord cs) -> Iso' (Coord cs) (Coord cs)
  translated d = iso (.+^ d) (.+^ negateV d)

Today the only route is `offsetCoord :: Coord cs -> Diff (Coord cs) -> Maybe
(Coord cs)` (Coord.hs:~530), which returns `Maybe` because on a Clamped or
Reflective axis the step really can fail. On a fully boundaryless coord list
that `Maybe` is always `Just` and the caller pays a `fromJust` or a redundant
case for a total function.

The constraint already exists and must be used rather than re-invented:
`All Boundaryless cs`, which is what `walkPathTotal` carries for exactly this
reason (Coord.hs:634, and its Haddock at Coord.hs:629 spells out the
argument -- "a step can never leave the grid, so there is no Maybe").
`Boundaryless` has `Group` as a superclass (Coord/Class.hs:160), so the
inverse displacement is available; `Periodic` is the instance
(Periodic.hs:106).

What has to be settled before writing it:

  1. Whether `(.-^)` is total under that constraint or the inverse is better
     written `(.+^ negateV d)`. Both should work; pick whichever survives the
     `AllDiffSame Int cs` plumbing with fewer constraints.
  2. The interaction with sized-grid-7kh, which is open on what `Periodic`'s
     Needle should be -- shortest signed route or non-negative residue. The
     Iso is correct under either, since both agree on which coordinate you
     land on, but the Haddock must not say anything that presumes an answer.
  3. `walkPathTotal` (Coord.hs:611) is `c .+^ pathOffset p` under the same
     constraint, so a whole Path is also an Iso on boundaryless coords. Add
     it in the same pass if it is free.

What it buys: `over (translated d) f`, `translated d . translated e` folding
to a single translation, and -- the real one -- a compile-time witness that
this particular grid's geometry makes the step total, in the same currency
the rest of the library uses. It is also the natural argument to `permuted`
(companion issue), giving "rotate the whole grid by d" as an Iso on grids.

Marked as depending on nothing, but do it AFTER qfg lands or alongside it, so
the two agree on the constraint's name.

Cost: none, lens is already a direct dependency.
close_reason: Closed

title: Decline ComonadTraced: displacements are AdditiveGroup not Monoid, and the fundep forecloses Path
description:
`FocusedGrid` has `Comonad` and `ComonadStore` (Grid/Focused.hs:42,50). The
obvious third instance is `ComonadTraced`, for relative rather than absolute
addressing: `trace d w` reads the cell a displacement `d` away from the focus.
It is worth writing down why that instance should NOT be added, because the
reasons are precise and they are both checkable.

REASON 1: A DISPLACEMENT IS AN AdditiveGroup, NOT A Monoid

    class (Comonad w, Monoid m) => ComonadTraced m w | w -> m

`Monoid m` is the obligation. The library's displacement type is
`Diff (Coord cs) = Coord (MapDiff cs)` (Coord.hs:328), so `MapDiff cs` is a
list of `Int`, one per axis. And:

    instance All Semigroup cs => Semigroup (Coord cs)     -- Coord.hs:164
    instance (All AdditiveGroup cs) => AdditiveGroup (Coord cs)  -- Coord.hs:171

`Int` has no `Semigroup` instance in base, so `Coord '[Int, Int]` has no
`Semigroup` and no `Monoid`. It DOES have `AdditiveGroup`, which is exactly why
`AffineSpace (Coord cs)` asks for `All AdditiveGroup (MapDiff cs)`
(Coord.hs:326) and not for a monoid.

So the instance does not typecheck as stated. Making it typecheck means either
`Sum`-wrapping every axis of every displacement -- `Coord '[Sum Int, Sum Int]`,
a second displacement type that no existing caller uses -- or an orphan
`Semigroup Int`, which is not on the table. Neither is worth a class instance.

This is not a defect. Addition on displacements is a group, and the library
says so with the strictly stronger class. `ComonadTraced` asks for less
structure in a shape that happens not to fit.

REASON 2: THE FUNDEP FORECLOSES THE THING WE ACTUALLY NEED

    | w -> m

One canonical trace monoid per comonad. So `FocusedGrid cs` may be traced by a
displacement OR by a path, never both.

sized-grid-ghj is the finding that the library needs BOTH: a displacement is
order-free and correct on separable policies, a path is order-dependent and is
what a seam requires. Committing `FocusedGrid` to one of them via a fundep
closes off the other permanently, and it would do so before the representation
question in ghj has been answered.

WHAT TO DO INSTEAD

Plain functions. They give the same fusion when passed to `extend`, cost no
class, and can coexist:

    traceOffset :: Coord (MapDiff cs) -> FocusedGrid cs a -> Maybe a
    tracePath   :: Path cs -> FocusedGrid cs a -> Maybe a

`Maybe`, not `a`: a walk can leave a bounded grid, and this library does not
clamp silently. That is a third reason the class does not fit -- `trace` is
`m -> w a -> a`, total by signature, so a lawful instance on a `Clamped` or
`Ordinal` axis would have to clamp or bottom. The README rule applies: the
operation takes the coordinate type that licenses totality, or it returns
`Maybe`. `ComonadTraced` offers no way to say that.

`peeks` on `ComonadStore` already covers the total case for anyone who wants
it, since a displacement applied to the focus is just a coordinate function.

THE OPERATION THAT IS ACTUALLY WORTH HAVING

    walkEverywhere :: Path cs -> FocusedGrid cs a -> FocusedGrid cs (Maybe a)
    walkEverywhere p = extend (tracePath p)

Where does a walker starting at EVERY cell and following this path end up? One
`tabulate`, one strict vector, the whole grid answered at once. That is a real
AoC-shaped operation (2016/02 and 2017/19 both hand-roll a version of it, see
sized-grid-448) and it needs no class at all.

BLOCKED ON sized-grid-ghj: the signature above names `Path cs`, which does not
exist yet and whose representation is that issue's subject.
close_reason: Declined ComonadTraced; added traceOffset, tracePath, walkEverywhere as plain functions in Data.Grid.Sized.Focused, with tests in tests/Test/Focused.hs

title: Test.CompileFail's four tests fail on master: the harness can't see the new 'groups' dependency
description:
Introduced by 84c4e50 (Boundaryless, sized-grid-2r3), which added 'import Data.Group (Group)' to src/Data/Grid/Sized/Coord/Class.hs and 'groups' to the library's build-depends.

Test.CompileFail shells out to 'ghc -fno-code -isrc <snippet>', compiling the library source directly rather than through cabal, so it uses the ambient package environment and never sees the test component's package db. 'groups' is not exposed there, so every snippet now dies with

    src/Data/Grid/Sized/Coord/Class.hs:25:1: error: [GHC-61948]
        Could not find module 'Data.Group'

before it reaches the error the test is looking for. All four tests under 'Misuse the compiler now rejects' fail:
  takeGrid past the source length
  dropGrid past the source length
  splitHigherDim remainder annotated as anything but x - y
  shrinkGrid with a window that does not fit

They fail for the wrong reason, which is worse than failing: the harness asserts on a substring of the diagnostic, so a snippet that stopped being rejected at all would now look the same as this. The suite is not testing what it claims until this is fixed.

Verified pre-existing and not caused by sized-grid-adr.6: src/ on that branch is byte-identical to origin/master.

Fix is probably to pass the package db / -package-env to the ghc invocation in tests/Test/CompileFail.hs so it resolves the same dependencies cabal gives the library.
close_reason: Fixed: CompileFail.hs now shells out via 'cabal exec ghc --' instead of bare ghc, so it resolves the same package set cabal gives the library (including groups) instead of the ambient PATH environment. All 5 CompileFail tests pass with their real diagnostics; full suite (530 tests) passes.

title: Pin the interior-only action law with a property test, and say (.+^) is a retraction
description:
The one actionable item from the lawfulness question (sized-grid-8nz). Small,
cheap, and independent of whether manifolds-core is ever adopted.

== What is actually true

(.+^) on Clamped, Reflective and Reflect101 is a partial action made total by
a retraction. The partial action is lawful; the totalisation is not, and
cannot be -- see the sized-grid-8nz comment for the group-theoretic reason.
Measured at n=7 over 567 (p,u,v):

    (p .+^ u) .+^ v == p .+^ (u+v)      all        interior-only
      Periodic                          567/567    269/269
      Clamped                           487/567    269/269
      Reflective                        407/567    269/269
      Reflect101                        407/567    269/269

Failures are exactly at walls, never in the interior, for every type.

== Why this is worth a test rather than nothing

tests/Test/Utils.hs 'affineSpaceLaws' omits associativity. The omission is
correct but silent: nothing in the suite records WHY it is absent, or that the
restricted version does hold. A future reader can neither tell that the
omission was deliberate nor that the boundary is where it bites.

Concretely, the live hazard is pathOffset (src/Data/Grid/Sized/Coord.hs:757).
It is public, returns a Diff (Coord cs), and the obvious thing to do with it is
offsetCoord c (pathOffset p). Its Haddock scopes the guarantee correctly --
"on any route no wall interrupts" -- but that condition is invisible in the
type and unenforced. A caller who sums a path and applies it near a wall gets
a silently different answer from walking it with walkPath. Nothing in the
library does this (walkPath, coordRay and offsetCoordUpTo all route through
the checked offsetCoord, never (.+^)), so this is about protecting callers,
including ../aoc.

== Proposed

1. Add to the law bundle an interior-only action property: for p, u, v where
   offsetIsCoord succeeds at each leg and for the fused jump,
   (p .+^ u) .+^ v == p .+^ (u+v). Passes for all four coord types today.
2. Add a comment in the bundle saying the unrestricted associativity law is
   deliberately absent, that Periodic alone satisfies it, and why the other
   three cannot.
3. In each of the three AffineSpace instances, state that (.+^) is a
   retraction rather than an action, and that associativity fails at walls --
   next to the existing notes explaining why clamping lives in (.+^).
4. Optionally tighten pathOffset's Haddock from prose to a cross-reference to
   the new property, so the condition has a name.

== Explicitly NOT proposed

Dropping the AffineSpace instances for Clamped/Reflective/Reflect101. That
would break AffineCoordList's All AffineSpace cs superclass, AffineSpace
(Coord cs), offsetCoord and every ../aoc call site -- a large blast radius to
satisfy a law that vector-space never states.
close_reason: Closed

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Scope correction: the path-level half of this already exists.

tests/Test/Path.hs already encodes the lawful/unlawful split by choice of test
type, and does it well:

  collapseTests -- "walking a path agrees with offsetting by its sum, on a
    torus", on '[Periodic 5, Periodic 5]: holds for ANY sequence of steps,
    unconditionally, plus "reordering the steps changes neither endpoint"
    (commutativity, which only a torus has).

  wallTests -- "a wall blocks a route even when it does not block the
    destination", on '[Clamped 5, Clamped 5]: out-and-back across the low edge
    fails though it sums to zero, while offsetCoord at the summed pathOffset
    succeeds. The disagreement is pinned by a concrete case.

So proposal item 4 (tighten pathOffset's Haddock) is largely already paid for,
and the hazard is better contained than this issue first claimed: the failure
mode has a named test demonstrating it.

What is still missing is the PER-AXIS level. tests/Test/Utils.hs
'affineSpaceLaws' still omits associativity with no record of why, and nothing
tests that (p .+^ u) .+^ v == p .+^ (u+v) holds in the interior for the three
retracting types. That is the remaining work here -- items 1, 2 and 3 -- and it
is genuinely small.

Retitle in that direction when picking this up: this is about the coord-level
law bundle, not about Path, which is already covered.

title: Data.Grid.Sized.Grid still says Grid twice; fold it into the head module
description:
'Data.Grid.Sized.Grid' says Grid twice, at positions 2 and 4. Fixing the
adjacent stutter (Grid.Grid -> Grid) removed the worse half of the problem but
not this.

DIAGNOSIS. Every sibling of that module earns its last component: .Coord,
.Ordinal, .Focused, .Class, .Unsafe all add information. .Grid adds none,
because the namespace already said grid. That is the whole difference between
'Data.Grid.Sized.Coord', which reads fine, and this, which does not.

The package this one is named after does not have the problem: there is no
Data.Vector.Sized.Vector. The type lives in Data.Vector.Sized itself, and the
head module IS the type's module. Ours is a pure re-export shim instead, so the
type was pushed a level down and had to re-say its own name.

THE FIX IS AVAILABLE, and it is structural rather than a rename. The Grid type
is not actually defined in Data.Grid.Sized.Grid -- it is defined in
Data.Grid.Sized.Internal.Grid, and Data.Grid.Sized.Grid only re-exports the
safe half of it. So Data.Grid.Sized can take that job over directly:

  Data.Grid.Sized          re-exports the safe half of Internal.Grid, AND the
                           other public modules, as it already does
  Data.Grid.Sized.Class    was .Grid.Class
  Data.Grid.Sized.Focused  was .Grid.Focused
  Data.Grid.Sized.Unsafe   was .Grid.Unsafe
  Data.Grid.Sized.Coord    unchanged, and now the shapes agree
  Data.Grid.Sized.Ordinal  unchanged

No import cycle: Class and Focused would import Internal.Grid rather than the
umbrella, which is where the type actually lives anyway.

WHY IT WAS NOT DONE WITH THE RENAME. Merging two modules' export lists is a
different risk class from moving files, and -Wmissing-export-lists plus the
sealed Grid constructor both ride on exactly these module boundaries -- see the
header of Internal.Grid. A rename that is mechanically verifiable should not
carry a change that needs judgement.

BLAST RADIUS, measured 2026-08-14: only four sites name Data.Grid.Sized.Grid at
all --

  gameOfLife/src/Main.hs:19
  ising-example/src/Main.hs:18
  src/Data/Grid/Sized/Grid/Class.hs:7
  src/Data/Grid/Sized/Grid/Focused.hs:6

Twelve sites import the umbrella Data.Grid.Sized instead, as does every call
site in ../aoc. So this is nearly invisible to consumers, which is the argument
for doing it calmly rather than urgently -- but also the argument that it is
cheap whenever it is picked up.

Best sequenced BEFORE sized-grid-h3d migrates aoc, so aoc is disturbed once.
close_reason:
Done on zxz-fold-grid-module (624fc13), based on worktree-rename-grid-sized.

Data.Grid.Sized now publishes the safe half of the hidden Internal.Grid directly, and Class/Focused/Unsafe moved up beside it. The Grid layer is gone.

Two things the issue flagged as needing judgement rather than mechanics, both checked rather than argued:
  - Public export set unchanged: the head module's explicit Grid section is the old Data.Grid.Sized.Grid export list verbatim; diffing the sorted lists gives no difference.
  - Constructor still sealed: from a consumer, 'Grid' at the term level is rejected as an illegal term-level use of a type constructor; sliceGrid and unsafeGridFromVector are both out of scope. A 'module X' re-export would have broken both at once, which is why the head module carries an explicit list.

Class and Focused import Internal.Grid through explicit import lists, so the constructor did not become ambient in two more modules on the way.

Blast radius was wider than the four sites measured: those were the import sites, but eight further Haddock cross-references named the old module, four of them carrying the Data.Grid.Sized.Grid.Grid stutter. All updated. Every rewritten link resolves exactly as it did before; the module links now point at modules that exist.

The two examples collapsed to a single 'import Data.Grid.Sized', since the head module subsumes every sibling they named and listing both is redundant under -Wall.

ChangeLog: the rename entry was amended rather than answered with a second entry. 0.1.0.0 is unpublished, so both changes ship together and a reader should see the shape that lands.

Verified: cabal build all clean with no warnings, all three examples link, 334 tests pass, downstream suite passes (compiles against the public API with no plugins), README suite passes, haddock shows no new unresolved link.

Confirms the comment on this issue: aoc names neither Data.Grid.Sized.Grid nor anything in the Grid layer, so sized-grid-h3d is untouched by this.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text: Correction: the description's last line says this is 'best sequenced BEFORE sized-grid-h3d so aoc is disturbed once'. That is wrong. aoc imports only the umbrella Data.Grid.Sized and Data.Grid.Sized.Coord; it never names Data.Grid.Sized.Grid or anything in the Grid.* layer, so this issue cannot disturb aoc at all. The two are independent and can be done in either order.

title: Evaluate finite-typelits' Finite against the hand-rolled Ordinal
description:
`SizedGrid.Ordinal.Ordinal` is a hand-rolled `Fin`:

    newtype Ordinal (m :: Nat) = UnsafeOrdinal { ordinalToInt :: Int }
    type role Ordinal nominal

`finite-typelits` provides the same abstraction as `Data.Finite.Finite`, and the
overlap is not approximate -- it exports `weaken`, `strengthen`, `shift`,
`unshift`, `finites`, `modulo`, `packFinite` and `getFinite`, which line up
almost name-for-name with `weakenOrdinal`, `strengthenOrdinal`, `allOrdinal`,
`numToOrdinal` and `ordinalToInt`.

This is an evaluation, not a planned migration. Decide it once and write the
answer down, because "should this just be `Finite`?" is the sort of question
that resurfaces every time someone new reads `Ordinal.hs`.

The reason it is worth asking now rather than never: sized-grid-up6 wants an
unboxed/storable grid representation, and the obvious way to get one is
`vector-sized`, which is built on `Finite`. If the library is ever going to meet
`Finite` at its boundary, better to know deliberately than to end up converting
at every call.

The strong argument against, which the evaluation has to clear first:
`Data.Finite.Finite` is `Integer`-backed, and this library deliberately uses
`Int` because the sizes index a `Data.Vector.Vector` and have to fit in an `Int`
anyway (see the comment on `ordinalSize`). Swapping a machine int for a heap
`Integer` in the type that every coordinate is built from would fight the
allocation work in sized-grid-92z and the coordposition benchmarks head-on.

One thing to check before concluding, because it may dissolve that objection:
the Hackage docs for current `finite-typelits` present `Finite` as an alias of a
more general underlying type parameterised by its representation, which suggests
an `Int`-backed variant may be available. Settle that first -- the whole decision
turns on it.

Also confirm what `Ordinal`'s `nominal` role costs to reproduce. That role
annotation is load-bearing here (its comment explains that a phantom role makes
`coerce :: Ordinal 9 -> Ordinal 3` typecheck), and the Hackage docs do not state
a role for `Finite`. If `Finite`'s role is phantom or representational, adopting
it would silently give away an invariant this library is careful about, and that
alone settles the question.
design:
DECISION: keep Ordinal. Do not adopt finite-typelits.

Evaluated against finite-typelits 0.2.1.0 (current on Hackage, x-revision 2),
GHC 9.12.3, with both project plugins (Normalise, KnownNat.Solver) active.

== The two pre-registered objections both DISSOLVE ==

1. Representation width: NOT a blocker. Data.Finite.Integral exports the
   general type, `newtype Finite a (n :: Nat) = Finite a`, with a real
   `instance SaneIntegral Int`. `Finite Int n` is a newtype over Int -- byte
   for byte what `Ordinal m` is. `Data.Finite`'s `Finite n` is merely
   `Finite Integer n`. The Integer concern applies only to the alias.

2. Role: NOT a blocker. Data/Finite/Internal/Integral.hs declares
   `type role Finite nominal nominal` -- nominal in BOTH parameters.
   Verified: `coerce :: Finite Int 9 -> Finite Int 3` is rejected
   ("Couldn't match type '9' with '3'"). Finite guards the size index
   exactly as carefully as Ordinal's `type role Ordinal nominal` does.

So the reason recorded here is neither of the two the issue anticipated.
Two facts found while checking settle it the other way.

== The decisive reason: KnownIntegral does not compose with KnownNat ==

Finite's operations are constrained by `KnownIntegral a n`, not `KnownNat n`,
and the two do not connect in either direction:

  - `KnownNat n` does NOT give `KnownIntegral Int n`. Verified; the error is
    "Cannot satisfy: n <= 9223372036854775807". The lone instance is
    `(SaneIntegral a, Limited a n, KnownNat n) => KnownIntegral a n`, and
    `Limited Int n` reduces to `n <= maxBound::Int`. Neither natnormalise nor
    knownnat discharges that for a polymorphic n -- and polymorphic n is the
    entire point of this library. (Concrete literals are fine; that is not
    the case that matters.)

  - `KnownIntegral Int n` does NOT give `KnownNat n` back. It is an instance
    context, not a superclass, so it never propagates backwards. `natVal` is
    unavailable under it -- and `ordinalSize` calls `natVal`.

A ported signature therefore has to carry BOTH constraints (verified: that
version compiles). That is 88 KnownNat occurrences across 6 modules in src/,
and it does not stop at the library boundary -- aoc's call sites inherit it.
It also pushes directly against sized-grid-oxb, which is work to REMOVE a
constraint from signatures.

The escape hatch, `withIntegral`, recovers KnownNat at runtime via
`someNatVal` + `unsafeCoerce Refl`. Commit 99b4332 removed this library's last
unsafeCoerce. Reintroducing one per call site to satisfy a dependency is a
strictly worse trade than the ~200 lines Ordinal.hs costs to own.

== The motivating premise (up6 / vector-sized) is false ==

The stated reason to ask now was that vector-sized is built on Finite, so the
library will meet Finite at its boundary anyway. It will not meet the Int one.
vector-sized 1.6.1 indexes with Data.Finite's Integer-backed alias:

    index (Vector v) (Finite i) = v `VG.unsafeIndex` fromIntegral i
    generate f = Vector (VG.generate i (f . Finite . fromIntegral))

Adopting `Finite Int n` would remove NO conversion at that boundary -- you
would convert `Finite Int n` -> `Finite Integer n` exactly as you would
convert an Ordinal. Adopting the Integer-backed alias to genuinely match is
the allocation regression this issue feared, head-on against sized-grid-92z.
Either way sized-grid-up6 gains nothing here.

== Consequence for up6 ==

If up6 adopts vector-sized, it needs a small ordinalToFinite/finiteToOrdinal
pair at the boundary, and that conversion allocates an Integer per index
regardless of what Ordinal is. That is a cost of vector-sized, not of Ordinal,
and it should be weighed inside up6.

Do not reopen on representation width or role; both were checked and both are
fine. Reopen only if finite-typelits makes KnownIntegral derivable from
KnownNat for polymorphic n (i.e. Limited becomes discharged automatically),
which would remove the entire cost above.
acceptance_criteria: A written decision recorded on this issue: either Ordinal is replaced by Finite with benchmarks showing no allocation regression, or the issue is closed with the specific reason (representation width and/or role) so the question is not reopened.
close_reason: Evaluated and declined: keep Ordinal. Both anticipated objections (Integer representation, role) turned out NOT to apply -- finite-typelits has an Int-backed Finite and declares 'type role Finite nominal nominal'. It fails on constraint composition instead: KnownIntegral Int n is not implied by KnownNat n (needs undischargeable 'n <= maxBound::Int' for polymorphic n) and does not imply it back, so ported signatures need both constraints across 88 KnownNat sites in src/ plus aoc's call sites, or a per-call-site unsafeCoerce via withIntegral. Separately, the motivating premise is false: vector-sized indexes with the Integer-backed alias, so adopting Finite Int removes no conversion at that boundary. Full analysis in the design field.

value: aoc's FocusedGrid call sites: 'experiment f w' centres f on 'pos w', NOT on any Coord you happen to have in scope. The correct idiom when you hold a separate coord is 'experiment neighbours (seek coord g)'; the idiom when the grid is already refocused (inside extend) is 'experiment neighbours fg'. aoc/src/2025/04.hs got this wrong for months -- 'experiment (filter (/= coord) . ...) g' looks like it centres on coord but centres on the constant parse-time focus (0,0). Grep aoc for 'experiment' before trusting any neighbourhood result; 2015/18 and 2018/18 are the correct pattern.

Building ../aoc requires aoc's OWN nix devshell, not sized-grid's. aoc/flake.nix supplies lapack, blas and zlib for hmatrix; sized-grid's shell does not, so running cabal for aoc from a sized-grid shell dies at 'Missing C libraries: blas, lapack' during hmatrix configure -- a failure that looks like a sized-grid problem but is not. Use: direnv exec ~/workspace/aoc cabal build <targets>. Also note cabal's failure is easy to miss when piping to tail, since the pipeline reports tail's exit status, not cabal's; redirect to a file and check $status instead.

CORRECTION to memory ghc-will-not-unroll-a-fold-over-a: the claim that a fold fails to unroll because its step is a FUNCTION ARGUMENT is wrong. An eliminator with a higher-rank step (cpara_SList, or a clone) DOES unroll and constant-folds to a literal. The real variable is INLINE vs INLINABLE on the wrapper: INLINABLE makes GHC specialise, and specialisation lambda-lifts the higher-rank step into a shared worker holding the per-axis dictionary at run time; INLINE makes it inline at the call site and unroll. What remains true: (a) a SELF-RECURSIVE where-helper can never unroll, since GHC does not inline self-recursive bindings, verified with INLINE; (b) eliminator+INLINE only wins if the INLINE chain reaches a site where the type-level list is CONCRETE -- in sized-grid it does not, because coordPosition is called from polymorphic instance methods (index, gridIndex), and cpara_SList+INLINE measured WORSE than doing nothing (584 B/call, 50 MB on index x90000, vs 320 B / 27 MB baseline); (c) a class method is the robust shape because the instance chain resolves whenever the DICTIONARY is known, at specialisation, not only at inlining.

CORRECTION to memory sized-grid-the-missing-dolt-remote-is-a: drop the 'sort -o .beads/issues.jsonl' half of the session-end export recipe. Checked 2026-08-13 across HEAD..HEAD~3: the committed .beads/issues.jsonl has NOT been sorted in any recent commit, and 'bd export -o .beads/issues.jsonl' already emits a stable order, so re-sorting reorders the whole file against history -- 68 lines of spurious churn for a 3-record change, and it hides what actually moved. Two collations were tried (en_US.UTF-8 and LC_ALL=C) and neither reproduces the committed order, so there is no sort to be consistent with. Just 'bd export -o .beads/issues.jsonl'. The rest of that memory stands: the JSONL is the only off-machine copy, so exporting at session end is load-bearing. To check an export lost nothing, sort BOTH sides into $CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp and diff those -- that isolates the real record changes without touching the committed file.

Design decisions in grid-sized must NOT be gated on whether a current consumer asks for them. The goal is a general library for consumers not yet imagined, so 'nothing is currently asking for it' (a phrase that appears in several issue writeups, usually about ../aoc) is not a reason to defer or descope. Judge a feature on whether it is true, whether it earns its API surface, and what it lets an unknown consumer express -- not on present demand. Stated by Kevin 2026-08-18 while reviewing sized-grid-gyn.

Design decisions in this repo are judged on library-design merits, not on downstream blast radius. When weighing an API change, do NOT spend effort surveying consumers (../aoc, the example packages) to estimate breakage, and do not let 'this would break call sites' argue against the better design. Kevin said so directly while deciding sized-grid-up6: 'forget about blast radius, consumers dont effect the decision'. That steer is what flipped up6 from option 2 (a duplicate unboxed module) to option 1 (parameterise Grid over its vector) -- option 1's only real cost was signature churn, and once that stopped counting, not duplicating the shape algebra and its size proofs was decisive. Consumers are still worth reading to check a PREMISE (e.g. discovering ising-example is comonadic over sum types and so cannot use UGrid at all, sized-grid-dy5); they are just not a cost input.

GHC type-checker plugins are NOT transitive: enabling -fplugin=GHC.TypeLits.Normalise / KnownNat.Solver in sized-grid only affects sized-grid's own modules. It cannot remove 'KnownNat (n * n)' from ../aoc signatures -- aoc solves its own constraints and does not enable the plugins (no 'typelits' in aoc.cabal/cabal.project/flake.nix). Any 'the plugin will simplify callers' reasoning about sized-grid's API is wrong; only an API change does that (see sized-grid-k6n: AllGridSizeKnown is a type FAMILY, so it emits KnownNat (MaxCoordSize ...) at the call site, whereas the AllSizedKnown CLASS solves the same obligation inductively with no plugin). Corollary: AllSizedKnown is load-bearing, not plumbing -- replacing it with a bare KnownNat (MaxCoordSize cs) would push a plugin requirement onto downstream users. Also as of 2026-08-12 natnormalise 0.9.6 / knownnat 0.8.4 DROPPED ghc-tcplugins-extra for ghc-tcplugin-api 0.19 and build on GHC 9.14.1, lifting the old 9.14 blocker; nixpkgs still pins the 0.7.x line so flake.nix needs callHackageDirect overrides.

ghc-typelits-natnormalise does NOT chain '<=' givens. Probed directly on GHC 9.12.3 (sized-grid-wrc): it fails on a bare 'a <= b, b <= c => a <= c'. It DOES cancel constants from both sides ('m + 1 + z <= y + 1' gives 'm + z <= y'). So when a Nat goal will not solve, the fix is usually to restate it as linear addition rather than truncating subtraction, and to name the transitivity/monotonicity steps explicitly with plusMonotone1 and leTrans from Data.Constraint.Nat -- 'constraints' is already a dependency. Reach for a solver plugin last: ghc-typelits-presburger would work but is bounded 'ghc <9.13' on ghc-tcplugins-extra 0.5 with no 9.14 branch, so it costs GHC 9.14 support.

GHC will not unroll a fold over a type-level list written as a FUNCTION -- a where-helper closed over the dictionary, or generics-sop's cpara_SList with the step passed as an argument. Both are polymorphically recursive (the function calls itself at a shorter list), so GHC specialises the outermost call, stops, and leaves one shared worker taking the All c dictionary at run time. INLINABLE does not help, and neither does -fpolymorphic-specialisation -fspecialise-aggressively (measured: the worker comes out byte-for-byte identical). Only an INSTANCE METHOD gets the per-axis dictionary resolved at compile time, because then there is one statically-known instance per axis. This is why sized-grid's IsCoordList carries sizeAndPosition as a method rather than coordPosition having a where-helper: 320 B/call -> 0 B, and index over 90,000 coords went 27 MB -> 38 B. Applies to any generics-sop NP fold in this codebase.

grid-sized: ComonadTraced does NOT fit FocusedGrid, and the reason is checkable rather than aesthetic (sized-grid-yws, 2026-08-16). ComonadTraced demands 'Monoid m'. The library's displacement is Diff (Coord cs) = Coord (MapDiff cs), i.e. one Int per axis, and 'instance All Semigroup cs => Semigroup (Coord cs)' (Coord.hs:164) therefore needs 'Semigroup Int', which base does not provide. Displacements ARE an AdditiveGroup (Coord.hs:171), which is why AffineSpace (Coord cs) asks for All AdditiveGroup (MapDiff cs) (Coord.hs:326). So the instance does not typecheck without Sum-wrapping every axis into a second displacement type. SECOND, INDEPENDENT REASON: the class has fundep 'w -> m', one trace monoid per comonad, so choosing displacement permanently forecloses Path -- and sized-grid-ghj is the finding that the library needs both. THIRD: trace :: m -> w a -> a is total by signature, so a lawful instance on a Clamped or Ordinal axis would have to clamp or bottom, against the README rule. Use plain functions (traceOffset, tracePath returning Maybe); they fuse identically under extend and can coexist. Do not revisit unless Path lands and turns out to be the single canonical movement type after all.

grid-sized decision, manifolds dependency (2026-08-16). Kevin DECIDED to take the manifolds dependency despite GPL-3, on the grounds that grid-sized is essentially personal use and downstream licensing does not matter. THE FACTS THAT WERE WEIGHED: manifolds and manifolds-core are both GPL-3 while grid-sized is MIT, so linking relicenses the combined work; manifolds proper was last released to Hackage 2023-07-04 and its staticDimensionalLinmapCategory flag still bounds singletons-base <3.3 (GHC 9.8 and below) against this project's GHC 9.10 floor. WHAT IS ACTUALLY REACHABLE: manifolds-core (0.6.1.1) is the small package holding Math.Manifold.Core.PseudoAffine, and its only deps are base, vector-space, call-stack and equational-reasoning -- vector-space is ALREADY a dependency, so manifolds-core costs two new deps and is plain Haskell2010, unlike manifolds proper. So the practical move is manifolds-core only. WHAT IT BUYS: little on its own. Semimanifold/PseudoAffine is four methods, manifolds-core ships a CPP macro making every AffineSpace instance a Semimanifold with Needle = Diff, and grid-sized already has AffineSpace (Coord cs) with Diff = Coord (MapDiff cs). PseudoAffine's (.-~.) :: x -> x -> Maybe (Needle x) is the same shape grid-sized independently reached with offsetIsCoord. IF IT PAYS OFF it will be through FibreBundle/ParallelTransporting (sized-grid-448) and the seam rule (sized-grid-o1n), not through the base classes. Revisit only if grid-sized is ever meant for public release.

grid-sized dependency-cost check: read dist-newstyle/cache/plan.json before arguing about whether a Haskell dependency is 'new'. deepseq, hashable, semialign, semigroupoids, array and primitive are ALREADY in the build plan as transitive deps of aeson/lens/adjunctions/vector, so naming them in build-depends adds zero packages to the build. universe-base and finitary are the only genuinely new ones among the instance candidates surveyed in sized-grid-90f.

grid-sized design decision, boundary policy placement (recorded 2026-08-13, from reviewing Chris Penner's 'grids'). WE PUT IT IN THE COORDINATE TYPE: Periodic/Clamped/Ordinal are axis types, so a grid's edge behaviour is fixed at construction and every operation on it inherits that meaning. THE ALTERNATIVE, which grids takes, is a value-level argument at the operation: 'autoConvolute clampBounds f g' vs 'autoConvolute wrapBounds f g' over the same grid type, with omitBounds :: f (Coord dims) -> Compose f Maybe (Coord dims) changing the RESULT FUNCTOR to carry the partiality. WHAT EACH BUYS: theirs lets one grid be read under several policies at different call sites, and expresses total-or-Maybe per operation. Ours guarantees a given grid always means the same thing at its edges, so a Periodic grid cannot be accidentally read as clamped three functions deep, and the Maybe appears only where the type could not promise a way back. WHY OURS: the policy is a property of the space, not of the question being asked about it -- a torus does not stop being a torus because this particular fold would rather clamp. The cost is real and should be stated when it bites: reading one grid under two policies requires converting the coordinate type rather than passing a different argument. NOT A REASON TO REVISIT unless that conversion shows up as a genuine ergonomic problem at an aoc call site.

grid-sized perf evidence lives in bench/baseline-ghc9.12.3-aarch64-darwin.csv (mean ps + allocated bytes per case). Read it before proposing any optimisation here: it already rules out the obvious suspects. index/(.+^) are effectively free (tens of bytes total for 360k calls) because IsCoordList's per-axis folds are class methods that unroll and constant-fold; the remaining cost is concentrated in operations that build an intermediate list or Coord per cell (onBoundary 98MB, coordDistance 78MB, tabulate 10MB, extend 15MB). CI builds the benchmarks but never runs them against that baseline.

MaxCoordSize's (c n) type-application match is NOT fragile -- do not 'fix' it to go through CoordNat. Checked 2026-08-12 against GHC 9.12.3 with a standalone reproduction. The worry: 'type family MaxCoordSize ((c n) ': cs) = n * MaxCoordSize cs' (src/SizedGrid/Coord.hs:303) matches a type application, so it looks like it would get stuck when the axis head is a rigid type variable x rather than a concrete 'Clamped 5'. It does not. IsCoordLifted carries 'x ~ CoordContainer x (CoordNat x)' as a superclass (src/SizedGrid/Coord/Class.hs:198), and that given equality refines x into application form, so the clause matches with c := CoordContainer x and n := CoordNat x. Verified: 'App (x ': xs) ~ (CoordNat x * App xs)' is provable from 'IsCoordLifted x' and NOT provable without it (negative control fails with GHC-18872), so the test has power. A CoordNat-based definition compiles equally, so it is a wash -- and the current poly-kinded '(cs :: [k])' signature is strictly more general than a CoordNat version, which would be pinned to '[Type]'. That superclass equality is exactly what IsCoordLifted exists to provide.

Prior art for grid-sized: Chris Penner's 'grids' (Hackage 0.5.0.1, last upload 2019-03-10, BSD-3, dead). Same concept, opposite design axis. WHERE IT PUTS BOUNDARY POLICY: a value-level argument to autoConvolute -- clampBounds, wrapBounds, omitBounds -- not the coordinate type. omitBounds has signature 'f (Coord dims) -> Compose f Maybe (Coord dims)', i.e. the policy changes the RESULT FUNCTOR. That is grid-sized's total-or-Maybe thesis expressed per-operation instead of per-type; it buys one grid type convolvable under several policies at different call sites, and costs the guarantee that a given grid always means the same thing at its edges. WORTH TAKING: (1) the 11-line '?!' operator turning a type-level Bool into a TypeError, filed as its own issue; (2) partitionFocus :: Grid window a -> (a, Grid window (Maybe a)), splitting a window into focus and neighbours-with-a-hole, which is the shape Conway actually wants; (3) the Centered class enforcing odd window extents at compile time. WHAT VALIDATES OUR THESIS: grids' Enum instance has 'fromEnum (Coord [i]) = clamp 0 (highestIndex @n) i' -- it SILENTLY CLAMPS out-of-range indices, the exact failure grid-sized's README thesis is written against; its toEnum calls 'error "Index out of bounds"'; convolute has an 'error' escape hatch called criticalError; and window/ is built on 'coerceCoordDims = unsafeCoerce', reinterpreting a Coord at different dimensions. Its Coord is a newtype over [Int], so arity is checked at runtime by a Maybe-returning smart constructor rather than structurally.

sized-grid-2g0 collapseGrid/gridFromList fixed via RULES at v ~ V.Vector (angle not in original issue): each already carries VG.Vector v a as a real function argument (not hidden behind a class dict), so a RULE "collapseGrid/boxed" [~1] forall (g :: GridOf V.Vector cs a). collapseGrid g = nestByShape @cs (unGrid g) matches the whole call and skips VG.convert entirely -- needs phase control ([~1] on rule, [1] on the functions INLINABLE) or the simplifier inlines the body first and the rule never fires (GHC warns "may never fire"), same idiom as map/build fusion in base. Confirmed VG.convert = unstream . stream and Data.Vectors own fusion rules turn unstream (stream v) into clone v not v, so a plain "rewrite VG.convert at v~w" rule (the issues original angle a) is a dead end -- rewriting the top-level function instead is what works. gridFromList needed v pinned via explicit type application (gridFromList @V.Vector @cs @a cg) since v only appears in the result type and RULES cannot annotate a whole LHS call. Measured with tasty-bench --baseline: collapseGrid 9% less than baseline, exactly cancelling the regression; gridFromList unchanged (was already level). toJSON/parseJSON do NOT get this treatment: they are class methods, so a RULE only sees the single opaque ToJSON/FromJSON dictionary, not the AllSizedKnown cs / ToJSON a pieces nestedToJSON needs, and RULES pragmas do not accept their own class context (parse error on =>). Reaching them needs a real internal v-to-boxed-conversion class whose constraint would leak into the ToJSON/FromJSON instance context -- exactly the leak the issues own angle b/c discussion flagged, confirmed empirically now rather than just by inspection. Net: collapseGrids +9% regression is gone for free, toJSONs +19% and parseJSON remain -- issue left open for that residual.

sized-grid: a Grid traversal restricted to some subset of cells needs no library function. Grid cs is TraversableWithIndex (Coord cs) (src/SizedGrid/Internal/Grid.hs:192), so the index is the coordinate and any Coord predicate filters it: 'itraversed . indices (not . onBoundary)' is the interior as a read-write IndexedTraversal, 'indices isCorner' the corners. Check for this composition before adding a named traversal to the Grid API.

sized-grid indexed traversals: 'V.fromList allCoord' inside V.zipWith FUSES -- the coordinate list is streamed, never materialised, and dies in the nursery. Replacing it with anything the simplifier cannot see through (a vector from a recursive function, or the same list under V.fromListN) forces 90,000 live coordinates: measured +23% allocation and +59% time on imap 300x300, and ifoldl' copying went from 48KB to 18MB. Do not 'fix' allCoord in imap/ifoldMap/itraverse. tabulate is the exception -- its result is a vector regardless, so V.fromListN there is a small win.

sized-grid: 'interior' (not onBoundary) and 'has a full 3^d-1 Moore neighbourhood' are the same set only on bounded (Clamped/Ordinal) axes. On a Periodic axis shorter than the neighbourhood diameter -- e.g. Coord '[Periodic 2, Periodic 2] -- every cell is interior yet has 3 neighbours, not 8, because axisSteps dedups offsets -1 and +1 onto the same cell. Documented on interiorCoords; pinned by a test in tests/Test/Boundary.hs.

sized-grid: IsCoord's 'asOrdinal :: Iso' (c n) (Ordinal n)' carries NO KnownNat n, and that makes two of its four laws unfalsifiable. An instance cannot build an Ordinal n at all -- unsafeOrdinal and numToOrdinal both need the size -- so the only ordinal it can return is the one it was handed. Consequences, established by mutation testing on 2026-08-13 (sized-grid-6p4): 'view asOrdinal . review asOrdinal == id' and 'asOrdinal lands in [0,n)' CANNOT fail for any instance; they are the law written down, not tests. The one direction with teeth is 'review asOrdinal . view asOrdinal == id', which a non-injective instance (an extra field dropped on the way out and invented on the way back) does falsify. 'reifyCoord agrees with asOrdinal' also has teeth, because reifyCoord does have KnownNat n and Ordinal overrides it. Do not add more asOrdinal round-trip properties expecting them to catch anything.

sized-grid displacements: Diff (Coord cs) is Coord (MapDiff cs) -- a coord again, one Diff per axis -- NOT a tuple. Changed 2026-08-12 by sized-grid-iet, which deleted the CoordDiff family and its seven per-arity instances. Consequences: (1) there is no arity ceiling any more; CoordDiff stopped at six axes, so a 7-axis Coord had no Diff, no AffineSpace and no offsetCoord. (2) IsProductType (CoordDiff cs) (MapDiff cs) is gone from every signature that offsets, including offsetCoord's -- that is why generics-sop no longer appears in contexts that have no other reason to mention it. The AffineSpace instance now asks for (All AffineSpace cs, All AdditiveGroup (MapDiff cs)). (3) A tuple literal is NOT a displacement: write ((-1) :| (-1) :| EmptyCoord), or coordFromTuple (-1,-1) / coordToTuple. Those two functions are arity-generic and are the only signatures left carrying IsProductType; keeping the conversion OUT of the class is deliberate, since an implicit coercion is what put the constraint in every consumer's context to begin with. The design follows manifolds' Needle: associated type, products get theirs structurally.

sized-grid neighbourhoods: generate them PER AXIS, not by offsetting whole coordinates. Each axis enumerates the values reachable within r steps and keeps each value once at its true (minimal) step count; the cartesian product of per-axis-distinct sets is automatically distinct, and the centre is the only entry whose summed distance is 0. That buys deduplication with no nubOrd and no Ord (Coord cs), centre-exclusion with no Eq (Coord cs), and the correct WRAPPED distance on a torus. It also drops the constraint list from vonNeumanPoints' EIGHT (Enum/Num/Ord/All Integral (MapDiff cs)/AllDiffSame/All AffineSpace/Ord (CoordDiff cs)/IsProductType) to 'All IsCoordLifted cs' alone, and makes them work on Ordinal axes, which the AffineSpace-based versions never could -- Ordinal has no AffineSpace instance. Do not 'simplify' this back to mapping offsetCoord over a list of deltas: that reintroduces every one of those constraints and the duplicates.

sized-grid perf: before redesigning an algorithm for speed, check whether the function is out of line. axisSteps (sized-grid-knm) was blamed for a quadratic dedup scan and the fix was one INLINE pragma worth 67%, beating the algorithmic change that had been designed for it. Same defect three times now: czf, bw8, knm. The shape to look for is a polymorphic helper over IsCoord/IsCoordLifted with no pragma -- out of line it folds nothing it calls, so offsetIsCoord stays a dictionary call, asOrdinal stays applications of $fProfunctorFUN instead of a coercion, and the size is read from a run-time Natural. Verify in the Core (cabal build --builddir=dist-core --ghc-options='-ddump-simpl -ddump-to-file -dsuppress-all -dsuppress-uniques'), and measure both sides in one session -- the recorded baseline CSV does not transfer.

sized-grid session hygiene: sessions work on a .claude/worktrees branch. Check 'git branch --no-merged master' at session start BEFORE picking up an issue. Merge the SAME session you write the work -- historically nobody did, and four branches once held work whose issues were already CLOSED. As of 2026-08-11 master is at 53b86cd with no unmerged branches.

HOW TO MERGE FROM A WORKTREE SESSION: you cannot do it from inside the worktree. The harness refuses git commands aimed at the shared checkout (including ones the user types with the '!' prefix, which run in the same sandbox), and git will not let a worktree update a branch checked out elsewhere. Call ExitWorktree with action 'keep' first; the session returns to /Users/kevin/workspace/sized-grid and normal git works.

EnterWorktree branches from origin/master (worktree.baseRef defaults to 'fresh'), so if the beads auto-export commits to master DURING your session -- which it does -- your branch is behind and 'git merge --ff-only' fails. Use 'git merge --no-ff'. Do NOT rebase: the branch is already pushed, so rebasing would need a force-push, and rebasing your own merge commit replays it into the same .beads conflict.

DO NOT run 'git pull --rebase' before pushing master, despite CLAUDE.md saying to. It tries to flatten the merge commit and dies on the .beads/issues.jsonl conflict; 'git rebase --abort' recovers. Just check 'git status -sb' says ahead-N and push.

.beads/issues.jsonl CONFLICTS ON EVERY MERGE, because the auto-export hook writes it in the main checkout while you work. Resolve it by regenerating, never by hand: 'bd export -o .beads/issues.jsonl' then 'git add'. Dolt is the source of truth and already holds both sides. Note the export orders memory lines non-deterministically, so a diff that touches only memory lines is noise, not a real change.

Each branch merges cleanly against master individually, so a clean 'git merge-tree' proves nothing; conflicts are between branches and the dangerous ones are semantic (a branch adding an export list while another adds top-level functions to the same file merges clean and leaves them unexported).

sized-grid/generics-sop performance trap: getting 'sList' from an 'All c xs' dictionary is NOT free. SListI is All Top, so sList is computed by cpara_SList -- an allocating fold over the whole type-level list -- on every call. Core confirms it: 'case cpara_SList ($p2All $dAll) Proxy $WSNil sList1 of'. Any per-cell function that dispatches on 'case sList :: SList xs of' pays this per cell. Recursing structurally over an NP value instead (as coordPosition does) has no such cost. Same applies to the 'let irred = $p1All $dAll' thunks GHC emits to peel IsCoordLifted out of All at each level.

sized-grid-up6 option 1 (parameterise Grid over its vector) vs option 2 (a separate hand-written
unboxed module) was RE-EXAMINED EMPIRICALLY after option 1 shipped, because the original argument
for option 1 was partly wrong. Option 2 was built as a working prototype against pre-change master
(e7d6340) and compiled. Findings, so the follow-ups do not have to redo this:

OPTION 2 WORKS. Full port of the shape algebra to Data.Vector.Unboxed: 25 top-level functions,
~246 lines, including a second 'ShrinkableUGrid' class carrying the windowFits application.
Nothing was blocked. The copy-paste is mechanical apart from two things:
  - splitGrid/combineGrid need mixed representation (outer boxed, inner unboxed), because a grid
    is never Unbox. Same insight option 1 needed; under option 2 it is hand-written.
  - shrinkGrid needs 'sliceGrid', which is DELIBERATELY WITHHELD from the public Data.Grid.Sized.
    So an option-2 unboxed module cannot be the standalone additive public module the issue
    described -- it must import from the hidden Data.Grid.Sized.Internal.Grid, or live inside it.

PERFORMANCE IS A WASH (300x300 Int, unboxed, both with pragmas):
  operation      option2 mono   option1 generic
  tabulate         1.84 ms         2.02 ms
  map then sum     92.3 us         91.7 us
  foldl'           86.6 us         86.6 us
  transpose        2.12 ms         2.26 ms
  SAT build        13.9 ms         14.3 ms
  index x90000      786 us          788 us
Option 2 is ~5-9% ahead on tabulate/transpose, otherwise identical.

THREE CLAIMS FROM THE ORIGINAL DECISION THAT WERE WRONG OR OVERSTATED:
1. 'Option 2 duplicates the windowFits proof.' No. windowFits lives in Internal.Type and is shared
   either way; option 2 duplicates its 3-line APPLICATION. And the size bounds are type-checked, so
   a copy-paste that gets 'off + len <= m' wrong fails to COMPILE rather than silently producing a
   wrong grid. The dangerous kind of drift is largely prevented by the types. The realistic drift
   is a FEATURE GAP -- the unboxed module quietly lacking an operation the boxed one gained.
2. 'The INLINABLE work is a benefit of parameterising.' No, it is orthogonal. Option 2 needs the
   identical pragmas, because Unbox a is a dictionary too -- without them the prototype was 6-20x
   slower on some rows (uindex 16.8 ms vs 786 us). The 60%/78% boxed speedup on tabulate/fmap was
   available without touching the representation at all.
3. 'Option 1 costs only signature churn.' It also cost the collapseGrid +9% / toJSON +19%
   regression (sized-grid-2g0), AllowAmbiguousTypes, four recursion helpers, and the gridFromList
   annotation. Option 2 touches no existing code, so it would have had NONE of these.

WHERE THE BALANCE ACTUALLY LIES. Option 1's surviving advantage is narrower than originally
claimed: every future shape operation is written once rather than twice, in a repo that is actively
adding them, and Storable / strict-boxed representations come free. Option 2's advantage is no
regression, simpler code, better inference and better error messages. It is a genuine judgment
call, not the clear win the original decision presented. Note also that the u-prefixed names in the
prototype are NOT forced -- a real option 2 would use identical names for qualified import, the
vector-package convention -- so 'option 1 gives one name per operation' is not a real point against
option 2.

The prototype was throwaway and lived in a job tmp dir that is now gone; that is deliberate, per
the lesson of bench-spike. Rebuilding it is about 20 minutes from this description if ever needed.
